# Venous Thromboembolism (VTE):  Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT) And Pulmonary Embolism (PE)

# Introduction

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) are overlapping parts of the same disease process, venous thromboembolism (VTE).  Approximately 50% of patients with DVT have concurrent PE; similarly, ~50% of patients with PE have a concurrent or residual DVT.  In addition to acute morbidity and mortality (eg, right ventricular failure), DVT/PE can cause a range of chronic problems (eg, postthrombotic syndrome, pulmonary thromboembolic hypertension).

# Pathogenesis and risk factors

## Pathogenesis

The adjective "deep" in "deep venous thrombosis" refers to formation of clots within the internal venous system of the pelvis and legs (eg, iliac, deep femoral, popliteal, soleal, and gastrocnemius veins).  Risk factors for clot formation are described in Virchow triad ((Figure 1)):

-   Venous stasis (eg, immobility, long air travel or car rides, chronic venous insufficiency, heart failure)
-   Endothelial inflammation or damage (eg, surgery, infection, indwelling venous catheters)
-   Hypercoagulability (eg, active malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, estrogen therapy, polycythemia, inherited thrombophilias \[eg, protein S deficiency\])

The clinical risk factors for VTE ((Figure 2)) map onto Virchow triad.  For this reason, lower extremity orthopedic procedures (eg, femoral fracture and fixation) are a setup for DVT due to direct trauma to the venous system, systemic and local inflammation from surgery, and immobilization.  Similarly, any underlying systemic inflammation (eg, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease \[COPD\], inflammatory bowel disease) increases the risk of DVT.

The elements of Virchow triad are interdependent parts of a complex thromboinflammatory web.  For example, venous endothelial damage induces:

-   release of intrinsic (contact-kinin system) procoagulants (eg, tissue factor, von Willebrand factor).
-   reduced production of surface anticoagulants (eg, prostaglandin).
-   imbalance of fibrinolytic-antifibrinolytic system (decreased tPA, increased PAI-1).
-   exposure of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), such as extracellular DNA/histones, that activate platelets and leukocytes.

Most clots start as microthrombi in the muscular calf veins and extend proximally (ie, "clot begets more clot").  Venous clots are made up mostly of fibrin and trapped red blood cells (ie, "red thrombus") as opposed to arterial clots, which have high platelet content (ie, "white thrombus").  This difference in clot composition affects treatment (eg, anticoagulants for DVT, antiplatelet for arterial thrombi).

## Provoked versus unprovoked

Clinically, VTEs are often classified as provoked versus unprovoked.

-   Provoked VTE (~70%) can be attributed to a transient (eg, surgery) or persistent (eg, chronic hemiparesis) risk factor.
-   Unprovoked VTE (~30%) cannot be attributed to any identifying risk factor.

Genetic (inherited) thrombophilias ((Table 1)) play a larger role in unprovoked DVT (eg, factor V Leiden is present in ~25% of cases), especially when recurrent.

# Clinical presentation

## Manifestations

-   **DVT:**  presents with acute onset (ie, over days) of unilateral leg fullness, pain, and tenderness, often with increased warmth and erythema.  Distal DVTs (eg, popliteal vein) cause calf-limited calf swelling and pain, whereas proximal DVTs (eg, iliac vein) can induce symptoms in the thighs and buttocks.
-   **PE:**  presentation may depend on clot burden and location (eg, segmental versus mainstem pulmonary arteries).  Segmental PEs often cause dyspnea and chest pain lateralizing to the affected lobes.  Chest pain has a pleuritic quality (pleural irritation due to underlying pulmonary infarction).  Massive PE (eg, saddle) can present with hypotension, syncope, or cardiac arrest due to obstructive shock.

## Physical examination

-   **DVT:**  Approximately 50% of concurrent DVTs are asymptomatic (ie, low sensitivity).  When present, unilateral calf edema is the most common finding (objective asymmetry >3 cm, measured 10 cm below tibial tuberosity, is more specific) ((Image 1)).  Palpable venous cord or dilated superficial veins are occasionally seen.  Homan sign (calf pain with foot dorsiflexion), traditionally associated with DVT, is inaccurate.
-   **PE:**  Tachypnea is one of the most common signs.  Large PEs can produce signs of right ventricular strain (eg, parasternal heave, loud P2, jugulovenous distension).  Massive PEs can produce hypotension and cyanosis.

# Diagnostic testing

The following **general** studies are common in the initial evaluation of undifferentiated chest pain and dyspnea.

## Chest x-ray

Chest x-ray is primarily used to evaluate for alternative diagnoses (eg, pneumothorax).  It is usually normal with PE.  Pulmonary infarction (wedge-shaped subpleural opacity) or focal decrease in vascular marking (Westermark sign, reflecting diminished blood flow to the affected lobe) is sometimes observed ((Image 2)).

## ECG

Several findings may be seen on ECG ((Figure 3)).  Sinus tachycardia is the most common finding of acute PE.  The acute right ventricle (RV) strain pattern (ie, new ST-T depression-inversion in anterior precordial \[V<sub>1</sub>\-V<sub>4</sub>\] and inferior \[II, III, aVF\] leads) is more specific.  An S<sub>1</sub>Q<sub>3</sub>T<sub>3</sub> pattern is classic but insensitive (ie, seen in only 15% of cases).  Other findings of acute RV strain include new right axis deviation and right bundle branch block.

## Chemistry

Cardiac biomarkers are used for risk stratification.  Larger PEs cause microscopic necrosis of the RV (ie, ischemia due to high afterload), reflected as elevated troponin-I.  RV dilation also releases elevated brain-type natriuretic peptide (BNP).

## Arterial blood gas (ABG)

For segmental PEs, the ABG classically shows hypoxemia and acute respiratory alkalosis (↓PaCO<sub>2</sub>).  Larger PEs may cause hypercapnia (↑PaCO<sub>2</sub>) despite tachypnea and high minute ventilation, due to increased alveolar dead space (ie, wasted ventilation from nonperfused lobes).

The following **specific** studies can serve for **confirmatory** testing of VTE.

## CT angiography (CTA)

With PE, CTA shows filling defects where thrombi occlude the pulmonary arteries.  A saddle embolus spans the trunk bifurcation, extending into the bilateral mainstem pulmonary arteries ((Image 3)).  Signs of RV strain (ie, enlargement, septal flattening or bowing in the left ventricle \[LV\], contrast reflux into liver) can be seen with large PEs.

## Ventilation/perfusion (VQ) scintigraphy

VQ scintigraphy shows segmental mismatched perfusion (Q; low) and ventilation (V; normal) ((Image 4)).

## Compression ultrasound (aka Doppler or duplex ultrasound)

Shows a noncompressible vein segment (assessed with gentle pressure from ultrasound probe) with reduced or absent blood flow (assessed with Doppler mode) ((Image 5)).  Occasionally, a solid lumen-filing thrombus can be directly visualized.

# Diagnostic strategy

Most patients have an acute, well-defined presentation and seek care in the urgent or emergency care setting.  However, diagnosis can often be delayed, especially in patients with impaired dyspnea or pain perception (eg, elderly, opioids) and medical comorbidities (eg, COPD, heart failure, lung cancer) that feature similar fluctuating daily symptoms.  Some patients can have vague symptoms (ie, generalized weakness).

## Modified Wells score

For patients presenting to an urgent or emergency care setting with acute chest pain, the first step is to judge the pretest probability of VTE using a standard tool such as the modified Wells score ((Table 2)).

-   Patients with high pretest probability (ie, score ≥4):  Proceed to confirmatory testing (eg, CTA PE or VQ scanning).
-   Patients with low or intermediate pretest probability (ie, score <4):  Perform additional stratification with D-dimer testing.  D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product, generated anytime there is clot anywhere (ie, very high sensitivity).
    -   Negative (ie, <500 ng/mL) D-dimer:  PE is excluded (alternative diagnosis should be sought).
    -   Positive (ie, ≥500 ng/mL) D-dimer:  PE is possible (confirmatory testing is required).

In practice, two additional pathways often arise:

-   Presumptive PE via venous ultrasound:  When leg symptoms prompt venous ultrasound, a positive study (ie, DVT present) is diagnostically equivalent to PE because management is the same.  However, the converse is NOT true; in patients with suspected but unconfirmed PE, a negative venous ultrasound has no diagnostic value (eg, the DVT may have embolized or may be located in proximal pelvic veins).
-   Presumptive PE via echocardiography:  For hemodynamically unstable patients (ie, systolic blood pressure \[SBP\] <90 mm Hg) ((Figure 4)), the concern is for a massive obstructive PE versus other causes of shock.  Time is of the essence, and confirmatory imaging may not be safe or possible.  In this situation, bedside transthoracic echocardiogram can visualize signs of acute RV dysfunction (eg, dilation, septal flattening, reduced contractility), providing actionable evidence for PE (ie, enough to administer empiric thrombolytics to treat the PE).

## Special considerations:  PE evaluation in pregnancy

-   For assessment of pretest probability of PE, scoring instruments (eg, modified Wells) are generally avoided due to lack of validation and high prevalence of baseline sinus tachycardia.  Instead, clinical acumen is used.
-   D-dimer testing requires caution.  D-dimer levels rise throughout gestation and reach >500 ng/mL (the traditional cutoff) by the third trimester in 95% of individuals.
-   For confirmatory imaging, CTA is preferred over VQ scintigraphy due to practical considerations (ie, quicker, widely available).  The fetal-absorbed radiation dose is equivalent between the 2 modalities, although maternal breast dose is higher for CTA.

## Special considerations:  PE evaluation with comorbid lung disease

VQ scintigraphy is generally avoided in patients with parenchymal lung abnormalities (eg, pneumonia, emphysema) due to the coexisting ventilation defect, because a corresponding perfusion defect is expected due to hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.

# Important VTE variations

## Upper extremity DVT

-   Primary upper extremity DVT (ie, Paget-Schroetter syndrome) is very rare.  It involves compression of the axillary or subclavian vein at the thoracic outlet and almost exclusively affects muscular young athletes who use their arms extensively (eg, baseball pitchers, swimmers).
-   Secondary upper extremity DVT (ie, provoked) is more common than primary.  It is usually associated with trauma or venous catheters.
-   Upper extremity DVTs are considered equivalent to lower extremity DVT and therefore require therapeutic anticoagulation ((Table 3)).

## Nonthrombotic pulmonary embolism

-   Rarely, pulmonary emboli can be due nonthrombus material, including septic emboli, tumor cells (eg, dislodged atrial myxoma), foreign material (eg, cosmetic silicone injection), venous air (eg, iatrogenic), fat (eg, long bone fracture), and amniotic fluid.
-   Septic embolism most closely resembles traditional thrombotic PE.  The emboli can originate from right-sided infective endocarditis, injection drug use, or septic jugular thrombophlebitis (ie, Lemierre syndrome).  Chest imaging shows multiple pulmonary lesions with potential cavitation, especially when caused by oral anaerobes (eg, *Fusobacterium necrophorum*).

# Differential diagnosis

## Unilateral leg swelling and pain

Several other conditions are on the differential:

-   **Superficial venous thrombosis or thrombophlebitis:**  Clots form within the superficial (eg, saphenous, varicose) veins, causing erythema and induration.  However, in contrast to DVT, calf asymmetry is absent and the inflamed subcutaneous vein typically appears distinct and traceable (ie, tracking).  Superficial thrombophlebitis is treated with supportive measures such as limb elevation, hot compresses, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
-   **Cellulitis (and other skin and soft tissue infections):** Skin infections are associated with leg asymmetry, erythema, and tenderness.  However, the skin is usually exquisitely tender to light touch, additional signs of bacterial infection (ie, suppurative pustules) may be present, and the systemic inflammatory response is more pronounced (eg, leukocytosis with left shift, higher fever \[versus lower-grade temperature elevations seen with VTE\]).
-   **Arterial ischemia:**  Acute limb ischemia is usually due to atherothrombosis (eg, PAD) or cardioembolism (eg, atrial fibrillation).  The unilateral leg pain is sudden, severe, and associated with the 6Ps ((Table 4)).
-   **Others:**
    -   **Ruptured Baker (popliteal) cyst** ((Table 5)):  begins as an asymptomatic bulge in the popliteal fossa.  Acute rupture can closely mimic DVT; however, sudden-onset and calf ecchymosis are relatively specific features.
    -   **Lymphedema (exacerbation):**  is usually bilateral but can be unilateral (eg, prior radiation, surgery, or recurrent cellulitis).  Compared to DVT, swelling is more profound and disfiguring (elephant-like) and involves the entire foot.  Skin changes (eg, lichenification, hyperpigmentation) are expected.  Pain is less intense (often described as "heaviness").
    -   **Venous stasis dermatitis (exacerbation):**  Lipodermatosclerosis refers to acute inflammation superimposed on chronic venous stasis.  It is usually bilateral but can be asymmetric.  Lower extremities demonstrate atrophic scarring, hyperpigmentation, and a tapered, "inverted champagne bottle" appearance due to constrictive fibrosis (from repeated episodes of subcutaneous inflammation) ((Image 6))
    -   **Calf strain:**  A gastrocnemius tear causes severe pain that begins immediately after a recollectable traumatic episode (eg, explosive movement).  The muscle belly is in spasm (eg, firm to palpation).  Ecchymosis and edema are common, but erythema and warmth are not.

## Acute right ventricular dilation and failure

PE is the most common cause of acute RV dysfunction.  However, 2 other conditions are on the differential:

-   **Pulmonary hypertension (PH)** (acutely decompensated):  In the setting of chronic PH, the RV adaptively hypertrophies so it can tolerate the increased afterload.  Exacerbations of PH (eg, due to medication nonadherence or excess sodium and fluid intake) causes worsening RV pressure and volume overload, resembling acute PE with reduced RV systolic function and dilation.  However, evidence of adaptive RV hypertrophy (eg, RV wall thickening, prominent moderator band) are seen with chronic PH, but not with PE.
-   **RV myocardial infarction:**  Can produce a similar picture to massive PE (sudden chest pain, hypotension, jugulovenous distension, clear lungs).  However, pulmonary artery pressure is low (rather than elevated), and ECG shows an inferior STEMI pattern, which can be confirmed by right-sided precordial leads (V1-4<sub>R</sub>).

# Management:  Guiding principles for anticoagulation

Guidelines for anticoagulation are complex.  A set of principles is presented below.

## Necessity of anticoagulation

There are 2 exceptions to anticoagulation:

-   Distal (ie, below the knee) DVT:  Minimally symptomatic calf-limited DVTs (confirmed by ultrasound) can be treated with NSAIDs and close observations (~25% grow into proximal veins)
-   Incidental subsegmental PE:  Subsegmental PEs are detected on ~10% of chest CT obtained for unrelated purposes; they typically require no specific action.

## Duration of anticoagulation

-   First and subsequent provoked VTE with transient risk factor (eg, surgery):  3 months each time
-   First provoked VTE with persistent risk factor (eg, malignancy):  ≥3 months (duration of risk factor)
-   Recurrent provoked VTE with persist risk factor:  indefinite
-   First unprovoked VTE:  3 months
-   Recurrent VTE with ≥1 unprovoked:  indefinite

## Choice of anticoagulation

-   General:  Direct oral anticoagulants \[DOACs\] (eg, rivaroxaban, apixaban) are most popular due to easy pharmacokinetics
-   Cancer:  Lower molecular weight heparin (LMWH) or DOACs are preferred over warfarin, with stronger evidence for LMWH
-   Pregnancy:  LMWH is the only safe option, as warfarin and DOACs cross the placenta

## Contraindications

-   Absolute contraindication to anticoagulation are active major bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, high risk of rebleeding, and inability to obtain hemostasis (eg, small bowel arteriovenous malformations)
-   In these scenarios, IVC filters are used ((Figure 5)).  They double the risk of DVT (approximately) but halve the risk of PE.  The IVC courses through the abdomen and inferior thorax in a location anterior to the right half of the vertebral bodies.  The renal veins join the IVC at the level of L1/L2, and the common iliac veins merge to become the IVC at the level of L5.

# Risk stratification of PE and management implications

PE suddenly increases the RV afterload.  Because it is a thin-walled ventricle adapted to a low resistance system, the RV does not tolerate rapid change.  Depending on the clot burden, various degrees of acute RV dysfunction can result, allowing stratification into 3 groups ((Table 6)).

## Low risk PE

-   The clot burden is light, usually affecting subsegmental pulmonary arteries.
-   The patient is normotensive (ie, SBP ≥90 mm Hg).
-   RV strain is absent (ie, normal size and contractility).
-   First-line treatment is anticoagulation (eg, heparin bridging to warfarin, DOAC) ((Table 7)).  Patients can be safely discharged home once therapeutic anticoagulation is achieved.

## Submassive PE

-   The clot burden is heavier, usually affecting several segmental pulmonary arteries.
-   The patient is normotensive.
-   RV strain is present on echocardiogram, signified by acute dilation (ie, RV > LV diameter), reduced systolic motion, septal flattening (ie, "D-shaped" RV), and tricuspid regurgitation.  Cardiac biomarkers (ie, troponin-I, BNP) may be elevated due to myocyte necrosis from high wall stress and relative ischemia.
-   Treatment is individualized.  Anticoagulation is generally sufficient.  Local (eg, catheter-directed) thrombolysis, where a fractional dose of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) is infused into target pulmonary arteries, is considered for higher risk patients (eg, intermittent hypotension, elevated troponin-I).  Close monitoring in the hospital is needed to detect progression to massive PE (ie, hypotension, worsening RV function), especially in patients with significant residual DVT.

## Massive PE

-   The clot burden is obstructive, usually affecting mainstem pulmonary arteries.
-   The patient is hypotensive (ie, SBP <90 mm Hg for >15 min, or requiring vasopressors).
-   RV strain is present and often severely dilated (ie, "blown RV").  Cardiac biomarkers are elevated.  Without treatment, a vicious death spiral ensues in which acute RV dilation compromises LV filling, leading to worsening hypotension and decreased right coronary artery perfusion, inducing RV ischemia and further dilation ((Figure 6)).
-   First line treatment is systemic thrombolysis with full-dose tPA, as long as there are no absolute contraindications ((Table 8)).  Some patients may require mechanical clot removal (eg, pulmonary embolectomy).  Obstructive shock is supported with major circulatory assistance (eg, vasopressors, inotropes, or cardiopulmonary bypass in extreme cases).

The impact of clot burden depends on baseline RV function.  Patients with chronic RV failure (eg, pulmonary hypertension due to severe underlying COPD) can quickly decompensate, even with relatively small clots.

# Complications of PE

## Acute complication:  Lung infarction and hemoptysis

Despite having a collateral blood supply (from bronchial arteries), PE can cause lung infarction in roughly one-third of patients.  When present, infarcts appear as a peripheral (subpleural) wedge-shaped opacity (ie, Hampton hump) on chest x-ray ((Image 7)).  The infarcted lung tissue is prone to bleeding.  Minor hemoptysis (ie, <100 mL/day) is common, especially after initiating therapeutic anticoagulation.  Due to the high risk of recurrent VTE in the first 2 weeks, anticoagulation should not be interrupted for non-life-threatening hemoptysis.

## Chronic complication:  Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH)

Recurrent PEs (or incomplete anticoagulation) can result in unresolved thrombi that cause vessel scarring.  On imaging, acute clots (ie, fresh fibrin) are typically smooth and lumen-filling, whereas chronic clots (ie, recanalized fibrin with endothelial hyperplasia) are typically eccentric and plastered into the vessel wall.  Patients present with chronic right heart failure several years after initial VTE.  CTEPH is important to identify because it is often surgically curable (eg, pulmonary thromboendarterectomy).

# Complications of DVT

## Acute complication:  Venous compartment syndrome

Phlegmasia cerulea dolens ("inflammatory blue pain") is a dangerous variant of DVT involving complete obstruction of a proximal (eg, iliofemoral) vein.  Total lack of venous outflow causes severe congestion and inflammation, elevating tissue compartment over arterial perfusion pressure.  The limb can become gangrenous due to ischemia.  Management involves emergent thrombolysis (usually with catheter-directed tPA) and limb decompression (eg, fasciotomy) if necessary.

## Chronic complication:  Postthrombotic syndrome

Chronic venous insufficiency can develop up to 2 years after initial DVT and lead to postthrombotic (aka postphlebitic) syndrome.  Venous valve damage from the release of inflammatory mediators and venous lumen stenosis from wall damage can cause venous hypertension distal to the site of previous thrombus.  Increased venous pressure typically causes progressive lower extremity pain, fatigue, edema, superficial venous dilation, and trophic skin changes (eg, thinning, dryness, discoloration, hair loss).  Management is focused on mobilizing venous flow through exercise (eg, calf pumping exercise, daily walking) and graduated compression stockings. ((Table 9)).  Doppler ultrasonography is sometimes obtained to rule out acute DVT because the symptoms can overlap.

# Primary VTE prevention

Thromboprophylaxis refers to primary prevention of VTE and applies mainly to hospitalized patients who have reduced mobility.  Pharmacological prophylaxis (typically with low-dose low-molecular-weight heparin \[LMWH\] or unfractionated heparin) is used in most patients.  Pneumatic compression devices are used for patients with contraindications to heparin (eg, thrombocytopenia) ((Figure 7)).  The rate of breakthrough VTE in these patietns is 10%-15% despite prophylaxis, and critically ill patients (eg, most inflammation) are at highest risk.

# Summary

Venous thromboembolism (VTE) encompasses deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE).  The pathogenesis involves a triad of venous stasis, endothelial dysfunction, and hypercoagulability, which map onto clinical risk factors such as immobility, surgery or trauma, and systemic inflammation.

Venous duplex compression ultrasound confirms the presence of DVT.  When PE is on the differential (eg, acute chest pain presenting to the emergency department), D-dimer testing is highly sensitive (rules out) and can prevent unnecessary imaging with CT angiography or VQ scan.

Management of VTE almost always involves anticoagulation (eg, direct oral anticoagulants), with very few exceptions (eg, distal calf DVT).  Duration of anticoagulation is based on whether VTE is provoked or unprovoked, among other factors.  Recurrent VTE with persistent risk factors usually require indefinite anticoagulation.  Thrombolytic therapy (eg, tPA) is administered for massive PEs (ie, hypotension, acute RV dysfunction).

articles.title: Vasopressors And Inotropes
articles.markdown:
# Vasopressors And Inotropes # Introduction Blood pressure and organ perfusion are primarily determined by mean arterial pressure (MAP), which is the product of cardiac output (CO) and systemic vascular resistance (SVR).  Vasopressors and inotropes are critical care medications that target these 2 variables to support failing circulation (eg, hypotension, organ hypoperfusion) in shock states.  Vasopressors primarily increase SVR to counteract distributive shock, whereas inotropes primarily enhance CO to support cardiogenic shock. # Relevant physiology ## Adrenergic and nonadrenergic pathways Vasoactive agents include catecholamines, sympathomimetic drugs, and other compounds that act through adrenergic or nonadrenergic pathways: - **Adrenergic** receptors mediate the effects of catecholamines and sympathomimetics.  They include α1 (general vasoconstriction), β1 (positive inotropy and chronotropy), and β2 (skeletal muscle vasodilation, bronchodilation). - **Nonadrenergic** pathways operate through other vasoactive receptors or intracellular pathways.  They include vasopressin, angiotensin II, and phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition. Both adrenergic and nonadrenergic agents can influence SVR and CO. ## Systemic vascular resistance SVR is mostly determined by **arteriolar** diameter, with arteriolar vasoconstriction mainly mediated by the following receptors: - **Adrenergic**:  **α1** receptor, which can respond to a wide range of **catecholamines** including phenylephrine, epinephrine (adrenaline), norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and dopamine (at high doses). - **Nonadrenergic**:  Vasopressin (V1) receptor and angiotensin II receptor. ## Cardiac output CO is the product of stroke volume (SV) and heart rate (HR) (CO = SV × HR).  Both SV and HR are stimulated by the **β1** adrenergic receptor ((Figure 1)). - In the ventricular myocardium, β1 activation increases **contractility** and therefore SV (ie, positive **inotropy**). - In the nodal tissue, β1 activation increases pacemaker automaticity and therefore HR (ie, positive chronotropy). The β1 adrenergic receptor can respond to many agonists, including dobutamine, epinephrine (at moderate to high doses), norepinephrine, and dopamine. Other **nonadrenergic** mechanisms that enhance inotropy include phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition (increases intracellular cAMP), Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase inhibition (indirectly raises intracellular calcium), and calcium sensitization (improves contractility without altering calcium flux). # Therapeutic classification Based on their predominant hemodynamic effect, vasoactive agents are classified into 2 therapeutic groups: vasopressors and inotropes. - **Vasopressors** primarily **increase SVR** (and most also increase CO). - **Inotropes** primarily **increase CO** (and most also decrease SVR). ## Vasopressors (↑ SVR) Vasopressors are defined by their powerful vasoconstrictor effect (↑ SVR).  Therefore, they are used in **distributive (eg, septic) shock**, characterized by **low SVR** and usually normal or high CO.  Vasopressors include: - Adrenergic vasopressors (in order of **α1** specificity): - Phenylephrine (pure α1). - Norepinephrine (α1 > β1 >> β2). - Epinephrine (α1 ≈ β1 ≈ β2). - Dopamine (α1 only at high doses). - Nonadrenergic vasopressors: - Vasopressin. - Angiotensin II. Vasopressors increase SVR and have a slightly positive inotropic effect on CO (eg, norepinephrine and epinephrine have some β1 activity).  Because SVR increases and CO increases to a lesser extent, MAP (= SVR × CO) also increases, improving perfusion pressure to end organs. ## Inotropes (↑ CO) Inotropes are defined by their contractility enhancing effect.  They are used to support patients with **cardiogenic shock** (eg, severe heart failure \[HF\], postischemic stunned myocardium), characterized by **low CO** and usually normal or high SVR.  Inotropes include: - Adrenergic inotropes (in order of **β1** specificity): - Dobutamine (β1 >> β2). - Isoproteronol (β1 ≈ β2). - Epinephrine (β1 ≈ β2 ≈ α1). - Nonadrenergic inotropes: - Milrinone (phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor). - Digoxin (Na+/K+ ATPase inhibitor). - Levosimendan (myofibril calcium sensitizer). (Note that although dopamine and norepinephrine have β1 activity, they are typically classified as vasopressors because their α1 effects are more prominent.) Inotropes increase CO by enhancing myocardial contractility (↑ SV).  Many also have peripheral vasodilatory effects (ie, β2 activity), which can lower SVR.  However, because the increase in contractility (SV) exceeds the drop in SVR, MAP improves overall.  The inotropes dobutamine and milrinone are classified as **inodilators** because they provide both inotropy (which boosts forward flow) and vasodilation (which reduces afterload).  This is helpful in low CO states with high SVR:  The high SVR increases the workload on the already failing heart; lowering afterload decreases this workload, thereby improving tissue perfusion without a major increase in oxygen demand. The following section discusses specific vasopressors and inotropes in more detail. # Vasopressors ## Adrenergic Norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine are catecholamines that share a common biosynthetic pathway ((Figure 2)).  The first, and rate-limiting, step in the synthesis of catecholamines is the conversion of tyrosine to dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA) by tyrosine hydroxylase.  DOPA is converted to dopamine by dopa decarboxylase, which is then converted to norepinephrine by dopamine beta-hydroxylase.  In the adrenal medulla, norepinephrine is rapidly converted to epinephrine by phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase (PNMT), which is upregulated by cortisol.  Phenylephrine, a sympathomimetic drug (ie, not a natural catecholamine), is often included in the same group as catecholamines.  - **Norepinephrine** is a potent α1 agonist (↑↑ SVR) with moderate β1 activity (↑ CO).  It is the **first-line** vasopressor for most patients with distributive (eg, **septic**) shock. - **Epinephrine** has potent α1 (↑↑ SVR), β1 (↑↑ CO), and β2 (bronchodilation, ↓ SVR).  At physiologic levels, its β2 effects dominate, producing net vasodilation in the skeletal muscle; however, at therapeutic doses, its α1 effects dominate, producing net vasoconstriction.  Epinephrine is the preferred agent for **anaphylactic shock**, which features vasodilation, myocardial depression, and bronchospasm.  It is also used as a last-line vasopressor in patients with refractory shock from any cause. - **Dopamine** has dose-dependent receptor activity.  It is a splanchnic vasodilator at low doses (D1 activity), a positive inotrope at moderate doses (β1 activity), and a peripheral vasopressor at high doses (α1 activity).  Dopamine has largely fallen out of favor due to its arrhythmogenic risk at the high doses required for vasopressor effect. - **Phenylephrine** is a pure α1 agonist (↑↑ SVR) with virtually no β1 activity.  Therefore, it is advantageous for patients with shock who have tachyarrhythmias (eg, atrial fibrillation) because other vasopressors with β1 activity may exacerbate the tachycardia. ## Nonadrenergic Noncatecholamine pathways (vasopressin and angiotensin II) can mediate up to 50% of peripheral vasoconstriction.  Vasopressors in this category include vasopressin, terlipressin, and (only available in some facilities) angiotensin II. - **Vasopressin** is agonist at V1 (↑↑ SVR) and V2 (renal water reabsorption) receptors.  It is the **second-line** vasopressor for septic shock for patients who remain hypotensive despite norepinephrine infusion (sepsis may be associated with a relative vasopressin deficiency due to depletion of pituitary stores). - **Terlipressin** is a synthetic analog of vasopression and a selective agonist at splanchnic V1 receptors.  Therefore, it is useful for management of esophageal variceal bleeding and hepatorenal syndrome in patients with cirrhosis. ## Toxicity profiles The major side effects of vasopressors are accidental tissue ischemia (eg, excessive α1 stimulation) and tachyarrhythmias (eg, excessive β1 stimulation). - **Ischemia**:  Vasopressin and epinephrine are the most potent vasoconstrictors and have the highest ischemia risk.  These drugs additionally cause endothelial dysfunction and stimulate intravascular platelet aggregation, which can induce intravascular thrombosis. - **Tachyarrhythmia**:  Dopamine and epinephrine are the strongest β1 agonists and carry the highest tachyarrhythmia risk (eg, atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, ventricular ectopy).  Dopamine has an unacceptably high rate of ventricular arrhythmias, but it is readily available as a premixed infusion on most code carts and can be administered through a peripheral intravenous access (unlike many other vasoactive agents). # Inotropes ## Adrenergic Several adrenergic agents exert positive inotropic (and chronotropic) effects by stimulating cardiac β1 receptors.  They include dobutamine (a sympathomimetic), isoproterenol (a sympathomimetic), and epinephrine (a natural catecholamine). - **Dobutamine** is the most selective β1 agonist (↑↑ CO) but has moderate β2 activity as well (↓SVR).  This combination classifies dobutamine as an inodilator.  It is used for severely decompensated HF or cardiogenic shock.  It is also used as a short-term inotrope during cardiac pharmacologic stress testing. - **Isoproterenol** is a nonselective, balanced β1 (↑↑ CO) and β2 agonist (↓↓ SVR).  Modern use of isoproterenol leverages its positive chronotropic effect.  Isoproterenol accelerates the heart rate in patients with QTc prolongation who are at risk for **torsades de pointes**.  It is also used to support patients with refractory bradycardia while awaiting definitive electrical pacing. - Epinephrine, as discussed above, exerts β1 (↑↑ CO) and α1 activity (↑ SVR) at high doses.  Its use as an inotrope is limited because increased CO comes at the expense of increased SVR (ie, afterload), which is detrimental to left ventricular function.  However, its dual inotrope-vasopressor action is useful for patients with complete circulatory collapse (eg, post-cardiac arrest). ## Nonadrenergic - **Milrinone** is a phosphodiesterase-3 (PDE3) inhibitor, which raises intracellular levels of cAMP and PKA.  This results in dual effects on the heart and peripheral circulation ((Figure 3)).  In the heart, milrinone increases myocardial contractility (ie, ↑ CO).  In the vessels, milrinone induces arterial smooth muscle relaxation (ie, ↓↓ SVR).  This combination of positive inotropy and vasodilation classifies milrinone as an inodilator, making it especially useful for HF, where afterload reduction is beneficial.  Milrinone is renally excreted, so it is typically avoided in patients with diminished GFR. - **Digoxin** is a cardiac glycoside that inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase and promotes intracellular accumulation calcium, which enhances contractility ((Figure 4)).  Separately, digoxin inhibits AV nodal conduction through a central increase in vagal tone.  As a result, it is a useful adjunct for severe HF associated with tachyarrhythmias (eg, atrial fibrillation) that could be exacerbated by other inotropic agents.  Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic window due to its tissue accumulation (eg, lipophilicity), renal excretion, and multiple drug interactions.  Toxicity can take many forms, reflecting its wide tissue penetration ((Table 1)). - **Levosimendan** is a calcium sensitizer.  It binds to troponin C to strengthen interactions between myosin-acting binding, improving contractility without increasing intracellular calcium or myocardial oxygen demand.  This property is theoretically advantageous for patients with underlying ischemic heart disease.  Separately, it binds to potassium channels on vascular smooth muscle, producing a degree of vasodilation.  Levosimendan is used as an inodilator for acutely decompensated HF in Europe, Asia, and Latin America (it is not FDA-approved in the United States due to lack of Phase 3 efficacy data). ## Toxicity profiles The major adverse effects of inotropes are tachyarrhythmias (eg, excessive β1), myocardial ischemia (excessive β1 relative to β2), and systemic vasodilation and hypotension (eg, excessive β2). - **Tachyarrhythmias**:  Isoproterenol, dobutamine, and epinephrine have the highest arrhythmic potential.  This problem is often dose-limiting in heart failure patients, who are already prone to arrhythmias due to their structural remodeling. - **Myocardial ischemia**:  Cardiac workload is increased by β1 stimulation (↑ CO) but decreased by β2 stimulation (↓ SVR).  Dobutamine's β1 effect outweighs its β2 effect, so it raises cardiac workload overall.  Conversely, milrinone has less impact on oxygen demand because it provides greater peripheral vasodilation than dobutamine. - **Hypotension**:  Milrinone induces significant arterial vasodilation, especially when drug clearance is reduced by renal insufficiency (common in heart failure).  Conversely, dobutamine causes less peripheral vasodilation. In clinical practice, the choice is typically between dobutamine and milrinone.  Dobutamine is avoided in patients with major tachyarrhythmias or active myocardial ischemia.  Milrinone is avoided in those with renal impairment or severe hypotension. # Principles of treatment Vasopressors and inotropes are used for hemodynamic support in patients with various forms of shock (ie, hypotension with end-organ dysfunction). ## Distributive shock In distributive shock (eg, **septic shock**), the primary issue is low systemic vascular resistance (SVR) due to widespread vasodilation.  Therefore, **vasopressors** are the first line of therapy.  A general treatment framework is as follows: - Initial volume resuscitation (eg, 30 mg/kg of IV crystalloid solution) is attempted. - If the patient remains hypotensive despite fluids (ie, MAP <65 mm Hg), **norepinephrine** is added as a first-line pressor. - If the patient remains hypotensive despite norepinephrine, **vasopressin** is added as a second-line pressor. - For concurrent cardiac dysfunction (eg, septic cardiomyopathy), an inotrope may be required. ## Cardiogenic shock In cardiogenic shock, the primary issue is low CO, typically accompanied by high SVR.  Therefore, **inotropes** are the first line of therapy.  A general treatment framework is as follows: - Initial trial of aggressive diuresis is attempted, which is sometimes successful in patients with adequate renal perfusion. - If the patient is still oliguric and hypoperfused ("cold and wet"), an inotrope is added.  Either **dobutamine** or **milrinone** are selected depending on individual factors (eg, milrinone avoided with impaired renal function, dobutamine avoided with major tachyarrhythmias). - For patients with tachyarrhythmias (particularly atrial fibrillation) that worsen with inotropic therapy, **digoxin** loading can help to achieve rate control.  Another option is ivabradine, a selective sodium channel inhibitor that exhibits negative chronotropy without negative inotropy. Vasopressors are generally avoided in cardiogenic shock because SVR is already high; further vasoconstriction increases afterload, reducing left ventricular performance. ## Undifferentiated shock When the etiology of shock is unclear, the best empiric vasopressor is **norepinephrine**.  It offers relatively balanced α1 (vasopressor) and β1 (inotropic) effects.  This also makes norepinephrine an attractive agent for **mixed shock** (eg, heart failure with concurrent sepsis). ## Vasopressor-resistant shock Some patients remain hypotensive despite multiple vasopressors and/or inotropes.  This situation indicates decoupling between the drug and the heart or vasculature.  A helpful mnemonic is **OP DEATH**: - **O**bstructive shock. - **pH** low (acidosis, especially with pH <7.15). - **D**rug overdose (especially **beta blockers** or **calcium channel blockers**). - **E**lectrolyte derangements, particularly **hypocalcemia** (eg, ionized Ca2+ <1 mmol/L) and **hyperkalemia** (eg, K+ >6.5 mEq/L). - **A**drenal insufficiency (common in critical illness). - **T**hiamine deficiency (eg, malnutrition, alcohol use disorder). - **H**ypothermia (especially with core body temperature <35°C). Not surprisingly, many of these etiologies overlap with the reversible causes of electromechanical dissociation, which can lead to pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest ((Table 2)). # Complications ## Extravasation injury All vasopressors (except for dopamine) need to be delivered via a central venous catheter because they can cause necrosis from intense local vasoconstriction if accidentally infiltrated from a peripheral IV into surrounding tissues ((Image 1)).  Early signs include pallor, blanching, and pain at the infusion site.  The infusion should be immediately stopped and residual drug aspirated from the catheter.  Subsequent management depends on whether an adrenergic or nonadrenergic extravasation occurred: - **Adrenergic extravasation** (eg, norepinephrine, epinephrine) is managed with **phentolamine**, an α1 antagonist that prevents further vasoconstriction.  The phentolamine can be administered through the original IV or given through multiple subcutaneous injections at the leakage site. - **Nonadrenergic extravasation** (eg, vasopressin) does not respond to phentolamine; instead, it is managed with topical **nitroglycerin** to encourage local vasodilation and with intradermal hyaluronidase to help dissipate the drug into the connective tissue. Surgical grafting may be necessary for full-thickness soft tissue necrosis, which often takes days to become fully apparent. ## Systemic hypoperfusion Any vasopressor has the potential to cause systemic tissue hypoperfusion, including skin mottling, digital gangrene, acute tubular necrosis, and mesenteric ischemia.  Risk factors include: - Prolonged high doses of multiple vasopressors. - Atherosclerotic stenosis (eg, peripheral artery disease). - Disseminated intravascular coagulation. - Use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (eg, selegiline), which inhibit catecholamine clearance. Prevention involves minimizing hypovolemia (to avoid constricting empty vessels) and early detection (eg, lactate monitoring). # Summary Vasopressors and inotropes ((Table 3)) are critical agents used to manage various shock states.  Most of these drugs are administered as continuously titratable infusions in the intensive care setting. - Vasopressors include adrenergic agents (eg, norepinephrine, epinephrine, phenylephrine) and nonadrenergic agents (vasopressin).  They support systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and are indicated for distributive shock (eg, sepsis). - Inotropes also include adrenergic agents (eg, dobutamine, isoproterenol) and nonadrenergic agents (eg, milrinone).  They enhance myocardial contractility and support cardiac output (CO) and are indicated for cardiogenic shock. Many agents have overlapping receptor activities, and their classification depends on the dominant hemodynamic effect. ​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​

Clinical manifestations of digoxin toxicity

Cardiac

  • Life-threatening arrhythmias

Gastrointestinal

  • Anorexia
  • Nausea & vomiting
  • Abdominal pain

Neurologic

  • Fatigue
  • Confusion
  • Weakness
  • Color vision alterations

Reversible causes of asystole/pulseless electrical activity

5 Hs

5 Ts

Hypovolemia

Tension pneumothorax

Hypoxia

Tamponade, cardiac

Hydrogen ions (acidosis)

Toxins (narcotics, benzodiazepines)

Hypokalemia or hyperkalemia

Thrombosis (pulmonary or coronary)

Hypothermia

Trauma

Receptor

Hemodynamics

Indications

Vasopressors

Norepinephrine

  • α1 +++
  • β1 ++
  • SVR: ↑↑
  • CO: ↑

  • α1 +++

articles.title: Upper Airway Cough Syndrome
articles.markdown:
# Upper Airway Cough Syndrome

# Introduction

Upper airway cough syndrome (UACS), previously known as postnasal drip, describes chronic cough that occurs due to nasal and sinus conditions and is one of the most common causes of chronic cough.

# Pathogenesis and clinical presentation

UACS usually results from nasal and sinus conditions, including allergic rhinitis, nonallergic rhinitis, sinusitis, and environmental irritants.  Patients typically have:

-   **Chronic cough** (>8 weeks)
-   **Nasal congestion** and/or **rhinorrhea**
-   Temporary improvement of the cough with nose-blowing or sneezing
-   Worsening of the cough with exacerbation of the underlying condition (eg, periods of high pollen count in patients with allergic rhinitis)

The cough of UACS was previously thought to be due to the production of excessive mucus that accumulates in the throat and triggers a cough to clear these secretions.  As a result, symptoms thought to reflect UACS have included frequent throat clearing, persistent nasal discharge, and a liquid sensation flowing into the back of the throat.  However, it is likely that the underlying rhinologic condition that induces UACS triggers cough hypersensitivity (a neurogenic component) in which mechanical stimulation to the afferent limb of the cough reflex leads to excessive coughing.  This results in coughing out of proportion to secretion production.  For this reason, patients may have a predominantly dry (nonproductive) cough and may not present with excessive mucus.  Cobblestoning, a physical examination finding classically associated with UACS, is not sensitive.

# Differential diagnosis

UACS should be considered in any patient with chronic cough.  In patients who do not smoke, are not on an ACE inhibitor, and have a normal chest x-ray, UACS is one of the 3 most common causes of chronic cough.  In fact, >90% of chronic cough can be attributed to UACS, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), or asthma.  Asthma and GERD can often be distinguished from UACS via history.

-   **Asthma** (especially cough variant asthma):  History often reveals shortness of breath and wheezing in addition to cough.  Cough triggers often include exertion, cold air, and/or respiratory infections.
-   **GERD**:  Heartburn and regurgitation are hallmark symptoms, but GERD can present with isolated throat symptoms including cough, hoarseness, and a sour taste in the mouth.  Throat symptoms due to GERD are often most pronounced in the morning.

There are no specific criteria for a UACS diagnosis.  For patients in whom UACS is strongly suspected, improvement in cough with empiric treatment for the suspected underlying etiology of UACS (as described below) confirms the diagnosis.

In patients unresponsive to empiric treatment of either UACS, GERD, or asthma, further evaluation should be performed, including a chest x-ray (if not previously obtained).  Other possible etiologies of chronic cough may include the following:

-   **Postinfectious cough**:  a very common cause of subacute (2-8 weeks) cough, usually with an antecedent illness; certain viruses (eg, COVID-19) may cause this to be prolonged.
-   **Other pulmonary conditions**:  chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pertussis, *Mycobacterium avium* complex infection.
-   **Neurogenic cough**:  vagal nerve-mediated chronic cough characterized by daytime predominance of hypertussivity (long fits of coughing difficult to stop) and allotussivity (eg, triggered by talking, laughing, nonallergic/nonirritant smells, contact with the external auditory canal).

# Management

Management should be targeted to the most likely underlying rhinologic diagnosis and may include:

-   Allergic rhinitis:  allergen avoidance, intranasal glucocorticoids, intranasal antihistamines, oral antihistamines, and/or allergy immunotherapy.
-   Nonallergic rhinitis:  intranasal glucocorticoids, intranasal ipratropium bromide, irritant avoidance.
-   Chronic sinusitis:  nasal saline irrigation, intranasal glucocorticoids, antibiotics, sinus CT scan; sinus surgery should be considered.

# Complications

Coughing is a violent airway protective reflex.  Chronic cough can lead to significant morbidity, including:

-   Syncope, posttussive emesis after long, uncontrolled fits of coughing
-   Urinary incontinence (stress incontinence)
-   Fatigue, inability to exercise, muscle pain (chest, shoulders, neck), rib fractures
-   Social isolation/ostracization from decrease in social obligations (eg, attendance at religious services, hobby groups, family gatherings) or adverse social interactions (may be especially pronounced since the COVID-19 pandemic)

# Prognosis

With appropriate treatment, the prognosis for UACS is excellent.  Most patients experience significant improvement in symptoms with resolution of the cough.  However, if underlying conditions are not adequately managed, symptoms may persist or recur.

# Summary

Upper airway cough syndrome describes chronic cough that occurs due to an underlying rhinologic diagnosis.  An accurate diagnosis of the underlying condition is the most important step.  Management is targeted to the underlying cause.

# Tuberculosis

# Introduction

Tuberculosis (TB) is a highly prevalent disease, affecting one-quarter of the world population.  TB incidence is falling very gradually, and it remains the leading infectious cause of death across the globe.  This article discusses latent TB infection and active TB disease, encompassing primary, reactivation, and disseminated TB.

# Microbiology

*Mycobacterium tuberculosis* is a gram-positive bacillus with a unique waxy cell wall rich in mycolic acids and lipids that makes it resistant to innate host defenses and many conventional disinfectants.  TB bacilli are transmitted through airborne droplets, leading to initial infection and intracellular replication within alveolar macrophages ((Figure 1)).  *M tuberculosis* has several virulence factors that aid its survival (eg, cord factor inhibits phagolysosomal fusion).  After a few weeks, infected macrophages in the draining lymphatic system display mycobacterial antigens on major histocompatibility complex class II molecules, leading to the stimulation of CD4 T lymphocytes.  Stimulated CD4 cells release interferon-γ (IFN-γ) that activates macrophages, greatly increasing their ability to kill phagocytized organisms.

Specifically, infected macrophages produce IL-12, which stimulates T cells and natural killer cells to produce IFN-γ.  Binding of IFN-γ to its receptor on a macrophage causes transcription of IFN-γ-regulated genes through activation of the JAK-STAT signaling pathway.  The result is upregulation of IL-12 production, enhanced mycobacterial intracellular killing in phagolysosomes, and production of tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α),

TNF-α promotes formation of granulomas, which serve as a barrier to contain the infection but also provide shelter for *M tuberculosis* to persist.  These granulomas consist of large epithelioid macrophages (multinucleated Langhans giant cells) with pale pink granular cytoplasm; the acidic and hypoxic center of the granulomas cause them to appear acellular and cheese-like ("caseating").  The CD14 cell surface marker, which is most specific to the monocyte-macrophage cell lineage, may contribute to pulmonary inflammation.  
Several outcomes are possible, ranging from latency to reactivation to dissemination ((Figure 2)).

# Risk factors

Risk factors for acquisition of new TB are distinct from those of reactivation (or dissemination) of latent TB.

-   Acquisition of new TB:  Mainly determined by contact with an infectious case (eg, prolonged proximity) or risk of constant exposure (eg, some health care workers, incarcerated population)
-   Reactivation (or dissemination) of latent TB:  Mainly determined by immunocompromised status, particularly HIV, medical comorbidities, or iatrogenic immunosuppression (especially tumor necrosis factor-ɑ inhibitors)

# Definitions

Clinically, TB can be discussed from different perspectives:

-   Contagiousness:  active (contagious) or latent infection (not contagious)
-   Disease phase:  primary, secondary (reactivation), or disseminated (eg, miliary)
-   Site of infection:  pulmonary or extrapulmonary
-   Drug responsiveness:  drug-sensitive or drug-resistant

These terms are often combined to provide a higher level of clinical context (eg, latent extrapulmonary TB).  Of note, the terminology is shifting to a simpler system:  "**active TB**" (encompassing primary, reactivation, and disseminated TB) is being replaced by "TB disease"; and "**latent TB infection**" is being replaced by "TB infection" (to denote the need for treatment).

# Clinical pathogenesis and management

## Early (asymptomatic) clearance

In most (>90%) of cases, accidental TB exposure does not lead to TB infection because the bacilli are cleared by alveolar macrophages.  However, a heavy TB inoculum (eg, exposure to an endobronchial TB patient) or prolonged contact (eg, cohabitation with a patient with active TB) can lead to primary TB.

## Primary TB

Primary TB is a local pulmonary infection that occurs when inhaled tuberculous bacilli are not immediately cleared.  The bacilli replicate within macrophages, triggering a **necrotizing (caseating) granulomatous** response.  Usually, patients are asymptomatic or display mild symptoms (eg, low grade fever, malaise, cough) resembling a nonspecific viral respiratory illness.  This infection appears as a rounded opacity or consolidation with a predilection for lower or middle lung zones (due to the settling of airborne droplets), often accompanied by ipsilateral hilar adenopathy (ie, **Ghon complex**).  Cavitation is rare in primary TB because it requires chronic (months to years) tissue destruction and fibrosis.

Due to their relatively mild symptoms, most patients with primary TB are not diagnosed and remain untreated.  Tests for TB infection (eg, interferon-gamma release assay, tuberculin skin test), described in the next section, are negative at this stage because a chronic T-cell immune response has not yet developed.  In rare cases with more severe symptoms (eg, hospitalization for acute TB pneumonia), diagnosis is sometimes possible based on direct detection of TB bacilli (eg, acid-fast bacilli \[AFB\] culture or nucleic acid amplification test \[NAAT\]).

Rarely, primary TB will spontaneously clear, leaving behind a residual scar.  More commonly, the granulomatous response walls off the bacilli but does not fully eradicate them, leading to latent TB infection.

## Latent TB infection

Latent TB infection (LTBI) represents **asymptomatic persistence** of tuberculous bacilli in host tissues (mainly lung granulomas and mediastinal lymph nodes).  Other latent reservoirs include the kidneys, liver, and spleen, which become infected through silent bacteremia.  The bacilli lay dormant (ie, not replicating) and are shielded from destruction by the granuloma.  Although LTBI is asymptomatic, patients can have evidence of prior active TB (eg, stable calcified pulmonary nodules or scarring).

Detection of LTBI is accomplished through **screening**, offered to 2 groups: patients at increased risk of acquiring TB (eg, close contact) and patients at increased risk of TB reactivation (eg, HIV or other immunosuppression).  Screening assays include interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) and tuberculin skin testing (TST):

-   **IGRA** (eg, QuantiFERON) involves incubating peripheral blood with *M tuberculosis* antigens, which stimulates cytokine (mainly interferon-gamma \[IFN-γ\]) release from previously sensitized (eg, memory) T cells.  The test is interpreted as positive, negative, or indeterminate (ie, no response to positive control, possibly due to technical error or anergy/immunosuppression).  IGRAs are the test of choice in most situations because they have higher specificity (eg, it avoids false positives in those with previous bacillus Calmette-Guerin vaccination or nontuberculous mycobacterial infection) and do not require a second visit for skin reading.
-   **TST** (eg, purified protein derivative \[PPD\]) involves injecting *M tuberculosis* proteins intradermally, which provokes a local type IV hypersensitivity response ((Figure 3)) in those with previously sensitized T cells.  This response manifests as an induration, representing dermal granuloma formation, over the following 1-3 days ((Image 1)).  The definition of a positive TST is guided by patient risk factors (ie, smaller induration qualifies as positive in higher-risk patients) ((Table 1)).  For example, ≥5 mm is considered positive for HIV and organ transplant recipients, ≥10 mm is considered positive for health care workers and recent immigrants from endemic countries, and ≥15 is always considered positive.  TST may be preferred over IGRA in resource-limited settings.

All patients with LTBI should be treated with antituberculous drug therapy, which reduces the risk of reactivation by >90% over a lifetime.  The most common LTBI regimens are rifamycin-based (eg, daily rifampin for 4 months) (preferred) or isoniazid-based (eg, isoniazid for 6-9 months) ((Table 2)).  Treatment does not reverse the IGRA or TST result (ie, it eliminates the dormant bacilli but not the immunologic memory).

## Secondary (reactivation) TB

Reactivation TB represents new replication of *M tuberculosis* from previously dormant microscopic granulomas in the lungs.  The risk of reactivation from LTBI ranges from 10% in a lifetime (eg, in immunocompetent patients) to 10% *per year* (eg, in patients with HIV).

**Reactivation** (known historically as "consumption") is the most common and recognizable form of TB, presenting with prominent constitutional symptoms (eg, fever, night sweats, weight loss) and cough.  Chest imaging characteristically reveals upper lobe cavitary lesions ((Image 2)) and coalescent nodules.  Cavitary lesions can erode into bronchial arteries, causing hemoptysis.  The high bacillary load often causes endobronchial spread, contaminating additional lobes.  With longstanding disease, extensive tissue destruction can occur, causing large regions of scarring and retraction, resulting in ipsilateral mediastinal deviation and hemidiaphragm elevation ((Image 3)).  Other thoracic manifestations include pneumothorax, TB empyema, and pericarditis.

In patients with suspected active TB, the first step is to establish **airborne precautions** (eg, N95 mask, negative pressure room) ((Table 3)).  Diagnosis is established by sending sputum (or other infectious fluid) for NAAT as well as AFB smear and culture.

-   **NAAT** (eg, Xpert MTB) is the primary method for detecting TB due to its rapid turnaround and high specificity and sensitivity.
-   **AFB smear and culture** is less sensitive (requires >10<sup>4</sup> CFU/mL to detect) but may be the initial signal in patients with heavy bacillary load (eg, patients with aggressive cavitary disease).  However, NAAT is still needed for confirmation (eg, to differentiate from nontuberculous mycobacteria).

Treatment involves RIPE, a 4-drug regimen that includes the following ((Table 4)):

-   **R**ifampin:  RNA polymerase inhibitor
-   **I**soniazid:  cell wall (mycolic acid) inhibitor
-   **P**yrazinamide:  cell wall (fatty acid) inhibitor
-   **E**thambutol:  cell wall (arabinose) inhibitor

Typically, all 4 drugs are given for 2 months, followed by continuation of rifampin and isoniazid for several more months.  Common adverse effects include hepatotoxicity (all drugs), altered drug metabolism (rifampin is a powerful cytochrome P450 inducer), peripheral neuropathy (an adverse effect of isoniazid prevented with pyridoxine \[vitamin B6\] supplementation), and retinopathy (ethambutol).  Surgery (eg, pneumonectomy) is sometimes needed to remove extensively damaged lung tissue.

## Extrapulmonary TB

*M tuberculosis* can reach extrapulmonary sites, typically via hematogenous spread in the setting of significant immunosuppression (eg, HIV, chronic alcohol use disorder).  Extrapulmonary seeding typically occurs during the reactivation phase of TB, during which there are transient episodes of bacteremia.  Virtually any organ system can be affected.

-   **CNS**:  TB meningitis presents with subacute headache (eg, several weeks) and frequent cranial nerve palsies (eg, ophthalmoplegia) due to basal meningeal inflammation (eg, nuchal rigidity, vomiting) with a thick, gelatinous exudate and vasculitis.  Cerebrospinal fluid outflow and obstruction (with hydrocephalus) may result from tubercular proteins.  Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows elevated protein (100-500 mg/dL), low glucose, lymphocytic pleocytosis, and elevated adenosine deaminase ((Table 5)).  In addition, tuberculomas (TB abscesses) can form in the brain or spinal cord and present with focal neurological symptoms.  Imaging shows ring-enhancing mass lesions, often with central necrosis, typically surrounded by extensive local edema ((Image 4)). 
-   **Abdominal**:  Infiltration of the peritoneal lining can cause TB ascites, characterized by a low serum- ascites albumin gradient (<1.1 g/dL), reflecting the exudative nature of the fluid.  Liver involvement causes granulomatous hepatitis (eg, hepatomegaly, mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic pattern).  Intestinal TB is rare but can present with bowel ulceration and strictures.
-   Reticuloendothelial:  TB can cause splenomegaly, bulky lymphadenopathy, and potential pancytopenia due to bone marrow infiltration.  Cervical TB lymphadenitis (scrofula) involves chronic, large, painless, anterolateral neck nodes that can ulcerate and drain.
-   **Bone and soft tissue**:  The most serious form of skeletal TB is spinal osteomyelitis (ie, Pott disease).  Imaging shows vertebral body collapse, disc edema or herniation, and paravertebral soft tissue masses (inflammatory phlegmon).  Due to its highly destructive course, there is a high risk of progression to permanent deformity (kyphosis) or spinal cord compression and paraplegia.
-   **Other**:  TB can involve the eyes (eg, granulomatous uveitis), skin (eg, verrucous lesions), pericardium (eg, constrictive pericarditis), endocrine glands (TB is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency worldwide), kidneys and urinary tract (eg, renal scarring, ureteral strictures with hydronephrosis), and reproductive organs (eg, chronic prostatitis, epididymoorchitis, salpingitis).

Diagnosis involves invasive sampling (eg, lymph node biopsy) for NAAT and AFB studies.  Despite the hematogenous nature of spread, blood AFB cultures are typically negative.  Treatment is generally similar to that of reactivation TB (ie, RIPE).  CNS disease (eg, TB meningitis) is typically treated with 6-8 weeks of concurrent glucocorticoids (eg, dexamethasone, prednisone) because antituberculous treatment can transiently increase neural inflammation as the bacilli are killed.

## Disseminated (miliary) TB

Miliary TB refers to extensive hematogenous dissemination to multiple organs with innumerable, **small, white nodules resembling millet** seeds.  The tiny nodules can be appreciated on chest imaging ((Image 5)) but are widely present in other locations (especially the liver, retina, brain, adrenals, and bone).  Risk factors include **compromised cellular immunity**, malnutrition, and extremes of age.  Most patients' presentation is subacute with constitutional symptoms (eg, fever, marked weight loss, drenching night sweats, malaise).  In some cases, miliary TB has a fulminant presentation of sepsis and acute multiorgan dysfunction (including acute respiratory distress syndrome).

Despite being widespread, diagnosis of miliary TB is usually more challenging than that of other forms of TB.  Many patients do not produce sputum (eg, small nodules instead of suppurative lung lesions).  Therefore, samples from multiple sites (eg, bronchoscopy, liver biopsy, mycobacterial blood cultures) may be needed to confirm *M tuberculosis* infection.  Treatment is similar to that of other forms of active TB disease (ie, RIPE).

# Special populations

## HIV

TB is highly prevalent in people living with HIV.  Diagnosis can be challenging, because bacillary load tends to be lower (eg, fewer macrophages to carry infection) and patients can have attenuated symptoms (eg, less pulmonary cavitation or lymphadenopathy due to blunted inflammatory response).  Therefore, sensitivity of AFB and NAAT are reduced.  Urinary antigen testing for lipoarabinomannan is emerging as a preferred strategy for detecting TB in those with HIV.

Antituberculous treatment (eg, RIPE) is always initiated upon diagnosis of TB.  However, the timing of antiretroviral treatment (ART) must be carefully considered.  Initiation of ART promotes immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), an intense inflammatory response that occurs as CD4<sup>+</sup> cell count begins to rebound.  TB-associated IRIS is most likely in those with a lower baseline CD4<sup>+</sup> cell count.  In general, ART is delayed for 2 weeks after initiation of RIPE, and prophylactic systemic corticosteroids may be given (eg, when CD4<sup>+</sup> cell count <100/mm<sup>3</sup>) to blunt the IRIS response.  In patients with intracranial TB, ART is delayed for 8 weeks after starting RIPE (to prevent cerebral edema and herniation).

## Multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant TB

Drug-resistant TB is increasing in prevalence globally.

-   Multidrug-resistant (MDR) TB refers to TB infections that are resistant to both isoniazid and rifamycins, the 2 most effective drugs.  Isoniazid resistance is conferred by mutations of *katG* (catalase; isoniazid is only active once it is processed by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase, so mycobacteria can limit its effect by reducing intracellular levels of catalase-peroxidase) or *inhA* (mycolic acid synthase); rifamycin resistance is conferred by mutations in *rpoB* (RNA polymerase).  MDR TB typically emerges from mismanagement (eg, low adherence) of drug-sensitive TB.  A typical treatment regimen usually involves bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid.
-   Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB refers to MDR TB that is additionally resistant to fluoroquinolones and either bedaquiline or linezolid.  Fluoroquinolone resistance is conferred by mutations in *gyrA* (topoisomerase).  XDR TB emerges from mismanagement of MDR TB.  Treatment is complex and usually involves 4 or 5 oral drugs (eg, bedaquiline, delamanid, clofazimine, ethionamide) under scrutiny (eg, directly observed therapy).  In some cases, intravenous aminoglycoside therapy (eg, amikacin) is needed.

To complete coverage of resistance mechanisms:  Ethambutol resistance develops when the mycobacteria increase production of arabinosyl transferase (an enzyme in the pathway to arabinogalactan, a key constituent of the mycobacterial cell wall).  Because pyrazinamide must be converted to an active form by the mycobacterial enzyme pyrazinamidase, drug resistance can occur when pyrazinamidase is altered or eliminated.  Streptomycin, one of the older drugs in the aminoglycoside family, works by interfering with the 16s rRNA of the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, thereby preventing bacterial protein synthesis.  Mutations of the genes that encode ribosomal proteins are responsible for aminoglycoside resistance because they lead to modifications in the ribosomal binding sites for these drugs.  Although sometimes used for tuberculosis, plague, or tularemia, widespread resistance limit its use.

## Pregnancy

Pregnancy has minimal impact on TB progression.  Treatment for LTBI is typically deferred until after delivery.  Treatment of active TB during pregnancy is similar to that of TB in the general population, but pyrazinamide is individualized due to its potential risk of fetal harm (Category C) ((Table 6)).  Mothers can safely breastfeed their infants during treatment.

# Differential diagnosis

## Infectious granulomatous lung diseases

Several pathogens can resemble pulmonary TB, causing prominent constitutional symptoms, caseating granulomas, nodular cavitary lung disease, and hilar lymphadenopathy.  These include nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) and fungi.

-   Common NTM (*Mycobacterium avium* complex \[MAI\]):  Pulmonary NTM infection causes nodules, bronchiectasis, and occasional cavitation.  Incidence is high in thin elderly women (eg, Lady Windermere syndrome).  Compared to TB, MAI infection is usually more symmetric (eg, bilateral middle lobes).
-   Uncommon NTM (*Mycobacterium abscessus, fortuitum,* and *kansasii*):  Like TB, these rarer NTM cause nonresolving pneumonia and pulmonary cavities and tend to disseminate to bone and soft tissue.
-   Fungi:  Systemic mycoses (ie, histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis) can produce chronic upper lobe fibrocavitary lesions.  They can also disseminate to extrapulmonary sites like the reticuloendothelial system, bone, and meninges.

NTMs are AFB that produce positive TST (but a negative IGRA) and are definitively identified by NAAT.  Fungal mycoses are diagnosed by antigen testing or serology.

## Noninfectious granulomatous lung diseases

Several noninfectious conditions can resemble TB, causing pulmonary granulomas, nodules and/or cavitation, and hilar adenopathy.

-   Sarcoidosis:  Pulmonary manifestations can range from diffuse reticulonodular infiltrates and hilar adenopathy (resembling miliary TB) to upper lobe fibrosis and cavitation (resembling reactivation TB).  However, sarcoidosis is usually symmetric, whereas TB lung destruction tends to be unilateral (unless miliary).
-   Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) (bird fancier's lung):  Acute HP typically involves diffuse symmetric upper lobe ground-glass opacities (an uncommon pattern with TB).  Similarly, chronic HP involves symmetric upper lobe fibrosis (unlike TB); the disease is "burned out" at this stage, so constitutional/inflammatory symptoms are uncommon.  Extrapulmonary involvement is not seen.
-   Silicosis:  Chronic silicosis causes upper lobe fibrotic changes and prominent hilar lymphadenopathy.  However, unlike TB, the fibrosis is confluent and symmetric, and lymphadenopathy tends to have dense peripheral (eggshell) calcification.  Extrapulmonary disease is not seen.

The key features of these conditions are symmetric (biapical) lung involvement and the presence of noncaseating (noninfectious) granulomas.

# Summary

Tuberculosis is a global pandemic affecting 25% of the world population.  Pathogenesis involves airborne droplet transmission and replication within alveolar macrophages, resulting in caseating granulomas that allow bacilli to persist for decades.  Diagnosis of latent tuberculosis infection involves tuberculin skin testing or interferon-gamma release assay, and treatment is almost always recommended.  Reactivation tuberculosis mainly occurs in immunocompromised individuals and is marked by significant constitutional symptoms and upper lobe cavitary lesions.  Disseminated (eg, miliary) tuberculosis results from hematogenous spread, particularly to reticuloendothelial organs, bone, and the CNS.  Diagnosis of active tuberculosis is usually accomplished through acid amplification testing of sputum, and treatment typically consists of a 4-drug regimen with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (RIPE).  Differential diagnoses include other infectious and noninfectious granulomatous diseases, such as sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which require distinct diagnostic and management approaches.​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​
