articles.title: Trauma: Penetrating Trauma To The Neck
articles.markdown:
# Trauma: Penetrating Trauma To The Neck # Introduction Penetrating trauma to the neck is a high-risk injury due to the concentration of critical structures, including the carotid arteries, jugular veins, trachea, esophagus, and spinal cord.  Managing these injuries requires careful evaluation because damage to any of these structures can result in life-threatening complications (eg, massive hemorrhage, airway compromise, neurologic  injury).  Physical examination findings (eg, hard or soft signs) and advanced imaging determine the appropriate diagnostic and surgical management.  The presence of "hard signs" (eg, active bleeding, airway obstruction, expanding hematomas) often necessitates immediate surgical intervention.  In contrast, "soft signs" (eg, hoarseness, subcutaneous emphysema) may allow for more conservative management with imaging to assess deeper injury. # Anatomy of the neck The neck is divided into 3 anatomical zones ((Figure 1)), with structures of the upper gastrointestinal and airway systems traversing multiple zones.  Injuries in these zones can impact multiple systems simultaneously: ## Zone I From the clavicles to the cricoid cartilage.  Major structures include the subclavian vessels, carotid arteries, trachea, esophagus, and thoracic duct.  Injuries to Zone I are less common than Zone II but carry high morbidity due to proximity to major vessels and the lungs. ## Zone II From the cricoid cartilage to the angle of the mandible.  This zone contains the carotid arteries, jugular veins, esophagus, trachea, and larynx.  This is the most common zone for penetrating injuries due to its relative exposure (~60%-75% of cases). ## Zone III From the angle of the mandible to the skull base.  Structures include the distal carotid and vertebral arteries, cranial nerves, and the pharynx.  Injuries here are high risk due to potential damage to cranial nerves and major blood vessels. The esophagus runs posterior to the trachea ((Figure 2)) in the cervical region and continues into the thorax.  The trachea is located anteriorly and bifurcates into the bronchi at the level of the sternal angle.  Given this arrangement, injuries to one structure may affect adjacent systems, complicating the clinical presentation and management. # Initial evaluation As with all major trauma, evaluation of a patient with penetrating trauma to the neck should begin with the primary survey (described in detail in another article) that evaluates the patient with a systematic approach (the ABCDE approach). ## Airway Assess if immediate airway protection (eg, endotracheal intubation) is necessary.  Signs indicating urgent airway intervention is needed include: - Significant bleeding or neck hematoma - Hemoptysis - Subcutaneous neck emphysema - Bruit or thrill - Distorted neck anatomy - Stridor or abnormal voice - Difficulty swallowing secretions If a secure airway is urgently required, the most commonly used method is rapid sequence intubation (RSI) (with cervical stabilization when indicated).  This method is appropriate for patients whose airway anatomy is preserved.  If intubation fails, invasive techniques like cricothyroidotomy ((Figure 3)) or tracheostomy are used, especially in cases of distorted anatomy. ## Breathing Assess breathing (eg, stridor, absent breath sounds), listen for any voice changes (eg, hoarseness), palpate for crepitus.  Address any urgent findings (eg, tension pneumothorax) if identified.  Injuries to the lower neck can easily involve the pleura or lung apices because they are positioned high in the thoracic cavity, extending above the level of the clavicles into the base of the neck.  Therefore, neck trauma can result in pneumothorax, tension pneumothorax, or hemothorax. ## Circulation Hemorrhage should be immediately controlled when possible (eg, direct compression).  Consider tension pneumothorax as an alternate cause  of hypotension.  Perform an Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma (E-FAST) examination to evaluate for possible pneumothorax or hemothorax. ## Disability Evaluate the patient's neurologic status because a cervical spinal cord injury can occur with penetrating neck trauma.  In general, routine cervical spine immobilization for penetrating neck trauma is not required but should be applied when there is a neurologic deficit present or when a deficit cannot be ruled out on physical examination (eg, patient is not conscious). ## Exposure Make sure the patient is undressed and other areas of the body are searched for possible injury. Objects impaled in the neck or any other location should never be removed until the patient is in a location with adequate resources and trained personnel equipped to handle rapid hemorrhage (eg, operating room). # Clinical presentation Patients with penetrating neck trauma can have a varied presentation depending on the structure(s) that are injured. ## Vascular injuries - Expanding hematoma, active bleeding, or signs of shock - Pulsatile bleeding or presence of a bruit/thrill - Neurologic deficits such as stroke symptoms, particularly if the carotid or vertebral arteries are involved ## Esophageal injuries - Dysphagia and odynophagia, often associated with subcutaneous emphysema or crepitus in the neck - Hamman sign (a crunching sound heard in the precordium with each heartbeat that occurs due to air in the mediastinum being compressed) - Hematemesis - Fever and signs of mediastinitis in delayed presentations - Features of esophageal perforation are presented in the accompanying table ((Table 1)). ## Cervical spine injuries - Neurologic deficits (eg, numbness, weakness, paralysis) - Vertebral fractures or dislocation on imaging, with potential instability - Airway compromise/difficulty breathing if the injury involves the upper cervical spine ## Laryngotracheal injuries - Dyspnea, stridor, subcutaneous emphysema, and hoarseness - Hemoptysis and coughing - Visible wounds with air bubbling # Diagnosis In addition to a physical examination, diagnosing penetrating trauma to the neck and upper gastrointestinal tract/airways often requires imaging and/or direct visualization. - **Chest x-ray** (usually obtained during the primary survey of all trauma patients):  identifies pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum ((Image 1)), and subcutaneous emphysema ((Image 2)), which can occur with esophageal and tracheobronchial injuries.  Pleural effusions (due to leakage of gastrointestinal fluids, typically a delayed finding) and widened mediastinum may be evident in patients with esophageal injuries.  Foreign bodies may also be visible. - **CT angiography**:  first-line modality for evaluation of penetrating neck trauma.  High sensitivity and specificity in diagnosing vascular injury.  Can also identify esophageal and tracheal injuries better than x-ray but cannot completely rule them out (particularly esophageal perforation). - **Flexible laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy**:  essential in evaluating the aerodigestive tract for penetrating injuries to the esophagus, trachea, or bronchus.  This allows direct visualization of the injury site and helps guide surgical repair. - **Esophagoscopy**:  used to evaluate the esophagus in patients suspected of esophageal injury. - **Esophagogram**:  water-soluble contrast study to evaluate esophageal perforations ((Image 3)). Small, life-threatening injuries can be easily missed; therefore, imaging is essential in the evaluation and management of penetrating neck trauma.  The specific modality and evaluation sequence depends on the clinical presentation. # Management Historically, management of penetrating trauma to the neck was guided by the zone of injury. - **Zone I injuries:**  often explored surgically after confirming vascular involvement via imaging due to the complexity of the anatomy and risk of major vessel injury. - **Zone II injuries:**  typically managed operatively without preoperative imaging, especially if vascular or airway compromise is evident. - **Zone III injuries:**  Surgical exploration may be complicated, and imaging with CT angiography is often required before any intervention. However, this approach is now less favored.  Although the injury zone plays a role in management, physical examination (eg, presence of hard and soft signs) and advanced imaging (eg, CT angiography) have largely replaced the zone-based approach (although the terminology is still used). After securing the airway and managing immediate threats identified in the primary survey, the patient should be examined for "hard signs": ## Hard signs of vascular injury - Severe/uncontrolled hemorrhage - Expanding or pulsatile hematoma - Thrills or bruits - Shock - Abnormal radial pulse - Neurologic deficit ## Hard signs of injury to trachea or esophagus - Air bubbling from wound - Large volume hemoptysis or hematemesis - Respiratory distress If hard signs of injury are present, the patient should be transported immediately to the operating room. ## Soft signs If no hard signs are present, the patient should then be evaluated for the presence of soft signs, which include the following: - Proximity wounds (injury within 1-2 cm of a major vessel) - Minor hematoma/hemorrhage - Minor hemoptysis or hematemesis - Subcutaneous air/mediastinal air - Small, nonpulsatile, nonexpanding hematoma - Dysphonia - Dysphagia Stable patients with soft signs should undergo further testing with CT angiography, evaluation of the esophagus (eg, esophagogram, esophagoscopy), and laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy.  Injuries noted on these examinations (eg, esophageal perforation, tracheal injury) will often require surgical intervention. - **Vascular repair:**  Hemorrhage from neck vessels requires rapid vascular control, typically with ligation or repair depending on the size of the injured vessel. - **Esophageal injuries:**  Most traumatic esophageal perforations ((Figure 4)) necessitate prompt surgical repair.  Depending on the size and location of the injury, primary closure or more complex repairs, such as using muscle flaps, may be indicated to prevent postoperative fistula formation or mediastinitis. - **Laryngeal injuries:**  Laryngeal injuries often require emergency airway management due to risk of obstruction.  Definitive repair is then typically performed to prevent complications such as chronic pain, stenosis, or voice change. - **Tracheal injuries:**  Tracheal lacerations may be closed if small, whereas larger defects or complete disruptions require tracheoplasty. In the absence of any of these injuries, the patient may be observed or discharged depending on the specific mechanism (eg, gunshot, stabbing) of trauma and overall condition of the patient ((Figure 5)). # Complications Complications from penetrating trauma to the neck and upper gastrointestinal tract/airways can be immediate or delayed, significantly affecting morbidity and mortality. ## Immediate - **Airway obstruction:**  common with laryngotracheal injuries.  Can also occur secondarily due to expanding hematomas, nerve injury, or significant edema. - **Hemorrhagic shock:**  Vascular injuries may result in life-threatening hemorrhage, especially from carotid or subclavian artery lacerations. - **Neurologic deficits:**  Cranial nerve or spinal cord injuries can result in permanent neurologic impairment, especially in Zone III injuries.  Vascular injuries to carotid or vertebral arteries can cause strokes and permanent neurologic impairments. ## Delayed - **Mediastinitis:**  Esophageal perforation, if undiagnosed, can lead to mediastinitis, a life-threatening infection with high mortality. - **Sepsis:**  Delayed or missed diagnoses, particularly of esophageal injuries, can lead to sepsis and multiorgan failure. - **Fistula formation:**  Tracheoesophageal fistulas can develop if simultaneous injuries to the trachea and esophagus occur. # Prognosis The prognosis for penetrating trauma to the neck and upper gastrointestinal tract/airways depends on the structures involved and the timeliness of treatment: - **Vascular injuries:**  Rapid surgical intervention for arterial injuries, particularly in Zone I and Zone III, can significantly reduce mortality, though delayed recognition increases the risk of exsanguination. - **Esophageal injuries:**  Early diagnosis and surgical repair are critical to avoid complications like mediastinitis and sepsis.  Delayed treatment carries a high risk of mortality. - **Laryngotracheal injuries:**  Prognosis is generally favorable with early airway management and surgical repair.  Delays can lead to chronic voice changes, respiratory dysfunction, or infection. - **Neurologic injuries:**  Damage to cranial nerves or the spinal cord carries a poorer long-term prognosis. # Summary Penetrating trauma to the neck presents a complex challenge due to the density of vital structures in a small area.  A thorough assessment, including physical examination and advanced imaging, is essential to identify potentially life-threatening injuries.  The management of these injuries has evolved, with less emphasis on the anatomical zone of injury and greater reliance on clinical signs and imaging to guide intervention.  Timely diagnosis and appropriate surgical repair of vascular, esophageal, and airway injuries are important to reduce complications and improve patient outcomes.  Delays in treatment increase the risk of severe complications, including airway compromise, infection, and neurologic deficits. ​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌

Esophageal perforation

Etiology

  • Instrumentation (eg, endoscopy), trauma
  • Effort rupture (Boerhaave syndrome)
  • Esophagitis (infectious/drug-induced/caustic)

Clinical presentation

  • Chest/back &/or epigastric pain, systemic signs (eg, fever)
  • Crepitus, Hamman sign (crunching sound on auscultation)
  • Pleural effusion with atypical (eg, green) fluid

Diagnosis

  • X-ray or CT scan of chest: widened mediastinum, pneumomediastinum, pneumothorax, pleural effusion
  • CT scan: esophageal wall thickening, mediastinal fluid collection
  • Esophagography with water-soluble contrast: leak from perforation

Management

  • NPO, IV antibiotics & proton pump inhibitors
  • Emergency surgical consultation
IV = intravenous.

articles.markdown:
# Trauma: Penetrating Thoracic Trauma # Introduction Penetrating trauma to the chest is a critical emergency that arises from various mechanisms, such as stab wounds, gunshot injuries, or other forms of violence.  This type of trauma can result in a range of life-threatening injuries, including pneumothorax, hemothorax, cardiac tamponade, lung lacerations, and great vessel injuries.  The management of penetrating chest trauma often requires a rapid assessment and intervention, which may include surgical procedures to control bleeding, repair injuries, or decompress the pleural space.  In contrast to blunt trauma, which may lead to injuries such as rib fractures and pulmonary contusions that are often managed nonoperatively, penetrating trauma frequently necessitates immediate surgical intervention due to the direct and often catastrophic nature of the injuries involved.  Early recognition and prompt management are crucial in mitigating complications and improving patient outcomes in cases of penetrating chest trauma. # Anatomy The thoracic cavity ((Figure 1)) is bordered by the clavicles superiorly, the diaphragm inferiorly, the rib cages laterally, the sternum and ribs anteriorly, and the ribs and vertebrae posteriorly. - Central penetrating wounds inside "the box"—delineated superiorly by the clavicles, inferiorly by the costal margins, and laterally by the nipples—are particularly dangerous because of the underlying heart and mediastinal structures.  The right ventricle composes the majority of the anterior surface of the heart and is at risk of injury with penetrating trauma at the mid- and lower-left sternal border.  The left ventricle forms the apex of the heart and can reach as far as the fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line.  All other chambers of the heart lie medial to the left midclavicular line.  The lungs overlap much of the anterior surface of the heart. - Injuries occurring below the scapula (seventh intercostal space) posteriorly or nipple line (fourth intercostal space) anteriorly can potentially penetrate the diaphragm, causing thoracoabdominal injuries. Although the majority of penetrating injuries to the thoracic cavity are limited to structures in the thorax, some (up to 20%) may also include abdominal injuries. # Initial evaluation ## Primary survey The assessment of penetrating trauma begins with the primary survey (ABCDE approach) of trauma management made widely known in advanced trauma life support (ATLS).  The goal of the primary survey is to address injuries that are the most immediately life-threatening.  The primary survey in penetrating trauma is similar to blunt trauma. - **Airway:**  Address any critical airway compromise (eg, occlusion).  The neck should be carefully examined because this is a common area where obstruction can occur (eg, from hematoma). - **Breathing:**  Assess for signs of pneumothorax, hemothorax, or tension pneumothorax,  which are common in penetrating chest trauma.  Signs of respiratory distress, asymmetric breath sounds, and jugular venous distention may indicate these conditions.  If one of these conditions is identified, it should be addressed before moving on in the survey. - **Circulation:**  Hypotension in penetrating trauma often results from hemorrhage.  Hemorrhage should be immediately controlled when possible (eg, direct compression).  Pericardial tamponade and tension pneumothorax should be considered as other causes of hypotension. - **Disability:**  A rapid neurologic assessment with Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) should be performed. - **Exposure:**  Patients should be completely undressed, and the entire body should be searched for occult injuries.  Areas that are often missed include the scalp, axillary folds, perineum, and, in obese patients, abdominal folds. A more detailed description of the primary survey is described in another article. ## Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (E-FAST) The E-FAST is an important sonographic tool in the initial assessment of patients with penetrating chest injuries because it evaluates for the presence of free fluid or air in specific areas of the body following trauma as well as for pneumothorax and hemothorax (E-FAST includes all 4 standard FAST views ((Figure 2)) plus bilateral anterior lung views).  A positive E-FAST is highly specific in penetrating trauma, but a negative E-FAST does not rule out intraabdominal injuries (eg, damage to the diaphragm or hollow organs), and further evaluation through repeated abdominal exams, diagnostic peritoneal lavage, CT scans, or exploratory surgery may be necessary. # Diagnostic work-up In addition to E-FAST, most patients with penetrating trauma will require laboratory evaluation and imaging. ## Laboratory evaluation Although laboratory results are not diagnostic and often lag behind the patient's clinical presentation, they are still important for assessing the extent of injury, guiding treatment decisions, and monitoring for complications.  Tests that may be indicated in patients with penetrating trauma include:  complete blood count, blood type and crossmatch, basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, coagulation panel, arterial blood gas, lactate level, urinalysis, and pregnancy tests. ## Imaging Patients with penetrating trauma to the chest typically have a chest x-ray (CXR).  Further imaging (eg, CT, esophagogram, bronchoscopy) may be indicated depending on location of injury. - **Plain radiographs:**  A supine anteroposterior CXR is obtained, with an upright CXR preferred if the patient is not severely injured.  Important injuries detected on CXR include pneumothorax, hemothorax, rib fractures, and retained ballistic fragments.  Esophageal injuries, hemopericardium, and diaphragm injuries cannot be directly seen on CXR, but associated signs (eg, pneumomediastinum, organ herniation into thoracic cavity) may be evident. - **CT scan of the chest:**  Appropriate for hemodynamically stable patients with penetrating thoracic trauma and typically performed with intravenous contrast.  Indications include: - The trajectory of the object crosses the mediastinum or center of the chest. - Signs or symptoms suggesting injury to the esophagus, tracheobronchial tree, or major blood vessels (eg, pneumomediastinum, widened mediastinum on x-ray). - Signs or symptoms (eg, hypotension, chest pain, shortness of breath) that cannot be fully explained by a CXR. Advantages of CT over CXR include CTs superior sensitivity and specificity in detecting pneumothorax, hemothorax, and injuries to internal thoracic structures. Penetrating thoracic injury near mediastinal structures (eg, within "the box") requires evaluation to rule out damage to the heart, tracheobronchial tree, or esophagus.  This typically involves echocardiography, along with bronchoscopy and esophagoscopy or a contrast esophagogram. Penetrating injuries below the nipple line anteriorly and below the tip of the scapula posteriorly (suspicious for thoracoabdominal injuries) are difficult to evaluate because diaphragm movement can obscure the wound path.  Imaging of the abdomen is often indicated to assess for injuries to abdominal organs (eg, liver, spleen) and major blood vessels (eg, aorta). # Clinical presentation and management Penetrating chest trauma can cause a variety of injuries that necessitate different management. ## Pneumothorax - **Clinical presentation:**  may be asymptomatic or can have dyspnea, tachypnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia, unilateral diminished or absent breath sounds, or unilateral hyperresonance to percussion ((Figure 3)). - **Imaging:**  On CXR, a pneumothorax appears as a visible pleural line with absent lung markings beyond it, and the deep sulcus sign may be seen in supine patients ((Image 1)).  On CT, pneumothorax shows air in the pleural space with a clear collapsed lung edge and no lung markings in the affected area ((Image 2)). - **Management:**  In the majority of cases, tube thoracostomy is indicated.  Occasionally, a small asymptomatic pneumothorax (eg, visible on CT but not CXR) can be observed and serial CXRs obtained to follow any expansion. ## Tension pneumothorax (TP) - **Clinical presentation:**  may be characterized by acute severe dyspnea, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and neck vein distension (due to superior vena cava compression).  TP develops when accumulated air (due to injured lung tissue) causes high intrathoracic pressure that compresses the vena cava and impedes cardiac venous return, resulting in decreased cardiac output and hypotension.  This occurs when a one-way valve has formed, allowing air to flow into the pleural space during inspiration but trapping it during expiration ((Figure 4)). - **Imaging:**  On CXR, mediastinal shift ((Image 3)) away from the affected side, flattening or depression of the diaphragm, and widening of the intercostal spaces is often seen.  There is also an absence of lung markings beyond the visible pleural line. - **Management:**  When TP is suspected, needle decompression (or, if available, emergency tube thoracostomy) should be initiated immediately, followed by placement of a tube thoracostomy ((Table 1)).  Needle thoracostomy can be performed quickly and should precede intubation.  It is typically done in the second intercostal space at the midclavicular line or the fifth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line.  A long, large bore catheter should be used (eg, 14 gauge). ## Hemothorax - **Clinical presentation:**  Diminished breath sounds and dullness to percussion are findings consistent with hemothorax, which may result from injuries to larger intrathoracic structures (eg, aorta, hilar vessels) and/or smaller structures (eg, lung parenchyma, intercostal blood vessels).  Each hemithorax can hold up to 40% of the circulating blood volume, and massive hemothorax (>1,500 mL) can present with signs of hemorrhagic shock and tracheal deviation from mass effect. - **Imaging:**  may appear as a homogeneous opacity in the pleural space ((Image 4)), typically with blunting of the costophrenic angle.  In larger hemothoraces, there may be a fluid level with a meniscus sign, where the fluid line curves upward along the chest wall. - **Management:**  Tube thoracostomy is typically sufficient to manage hemothorax.  Some patients (up to 15%) require emergency thoracotomy for extreme bleeding, including patients with initial bloody output >1,500 mL, persistent hemorrhage (eg, >200 mL/hr for >2 hours) or continuous need for blood transfusion to maintain hemodynamic stability. ## Cardiac tamponade - **Clinical presentation:**  occurs due to rapid fluid accumulation in the pericardial space.  Patients may have hypotension with elevated jugular venous pressure (obstructive shock due to the pericardial fluid preventing adequate cardiac contraction) as well as muffled heart sounds (Beck triad ((Table 2)), only seen in a minority of patients). - **Imaging:**  The condition is best identified on FAST, where blood will be evident in the pericardial space with evidence of right ventricular dysfunction (eg, right ventricular diastolic collapse).  A CXR may not show cardiomegaly because the stiff pericardium does not have time to adapt when fluid accumulates rapidly as occurs in trauma. - **Management:**  Immediate pericardiocentesis or thoracotomy is indicated to prevent decompensation. ## Diaphragmatic injury - **Clinical presentation:**  Common symptoms of a diaphragm injury include abdominal pain (often felt in the upper abdomen), referred shoulder pain, difficulty breathing, vomiting, difficulty swallowing, or shock.  However, some patients may not exhibit any symptoms, and a physical examination alone is not sufficient to exclude a diaphragmatic injury. - **Imaging:**  CXR ((Image 5)) may show abdominal organs within the chest (with or without mediastinal deviation) but is typically nondiagnostic (elevation of the hemidiaphragm may be the only abnormal finding).  CT scans of the chest and abdomen may show direct signs (eg, discontinuity of the diaphragm) or indirect signs (eg, diaphragm thickening, organ herniation) of injury.  Ultrasonography and MRI can also be used to diagnose the condition, but even with imaging, small tears can be difficult to recognize, and diagnosis may be delayed. - **Management:**  Surgical repair is indicated in all left-sided injuries and many right-sided injuries.  Sometimes, small right-sided injuries can be managed nonoperatively (the liver blocks or "tamponades" the injury). Other structures can also be injured in penetrating trauma to the chest.  These include the esophagus, major vessels (eg, aorta, subclavian), and tracheobronchial tree.  Injuries to these structures are discussed in a different article. # Emergency Department Thoracotomy (EDT) Emergency department thoracotomy (EDT) is a critical procedure for resuscitating trauma patients in cardiac arrest or peri-arrest, particularly in cases of penetrating thoracic injuries.  It involves opening the chest (eg, incision and rib spreading) to relieve cardiac tamponade (eg, pericardiotomy), control hemorrhage (eg, aortic cross-clamping), or provide direct cardiac massage to restore circulation.  EDT should be performed only in institutions with appropriate resources (eg, trauma/cardiothoracic surgery).  Overall survival rates are poor; they are slightly more favorable for patients with isolated stab wounds and signs of life upon hospital arrival. # Complications The complications associated with penetrating chest trauma are closely linked to the organs and structures involved.  Common complications include: - **Hemorrhagic shock:**  Rapid blood loss from major vessels in the chest can result in hemorrhagic shock.  This is more common in penetrating trauma due to direct vessel disruption compared to blunt trauma, where bleeding is more likely to be contained. - **Pulmonary complications:**  Persistent pneumothorax, hemothorax, or empyema can occur leading to prolonged respiratory compromise and its associated complications.  Widespread inflammation and lung damage from trauma can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome, which can be life-threatening and require intensive care management. - **Infection and sepsis:**  Penetrating trauma introduces external pathogens into sterile body cavities, increasing the risk of infection and abscess formation, especially in the setting of hollow viscus (eg, bowel) perforation. - **Fistula formation:**  Abnormal connections can develop between organs (eg, esophagus and aorta) due to trauma, leading to complications such as massive hematemesis. # Summary The management of penetrating trauma to the chest requires immediate intervention when life-threatening conditions are present.  Rapid assessment, followed by targeted imaging, can help identify injuries that require surgical management.  Compared to blunt trauma, penetrating injuries more frequently necessitate operative intervention due to the direct damage to organs and vasculature.  The conceptual algorithms for management differ slightly, with penetrating injuries often requiring more aggressive surgical intervention, whereas blunt trauma is more often managed conservatively in stable patients. ​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌

# Trauma: Penetrating Abdominal Trauma # Introduction Penetrating trauma to the abdomen results from an object piercing the body and violating the pleural, peritoneal, or other body cavities.  The nature of these injuries is highly dependent on the velocity, size, and angle of the object.  Common mechanisms include gunshot wounds (GSWs), stab wounds, and shrapnel from explosions.  High-velocity injuries (eg, GSWs) often result in more extensive internal damage compared to low-velocity injuries like stabbings due to the larger cavitation and shockwave effects. The main concern is direct injury to vital structures.  In the abdomen, the liver, kidney, spleen, intestines, and major blood vessels (eg, the aorta) are at risk.  Injury to these structures can cause hemorrhage, peritonitis, and sepsis. In contrast to blunt trauma, which usually results in diffuse injury through the transfer of kinetic energy, penetrating trauma typically causes focal damage along the path of penetration.  Thus, whereas blunt trauma may lead to widespread tissue damage (eg, organ contusions), penetrating trauma involves more precise injuries, often requiring surgical intervention for hemorrhage control or repair of damaged structures. # Initial evaluation ## Primary survey The assessment of penetrating trauma begins with the primary survey (ABCDE approach) of trauma management made widely known in advanced trauma life support (ATLS).  The goal of the primary survey is to address injuries that are the most immediately life-threatening.  The primary survey in penetrating trauma is similar to blunt trauma. - **Airway:**  Address any critical airway compromise (eg, occlusion).  Maintain cervical stabilization if indicated.  The neck should be carefully examined as this is a common area where obstruction can occur (eg, from hematoma). - **Breathing:**  Assess for signs of pneumothorax or tension pneumothorax, which are common in penetrating trauma.  Signs of respiratory distress, asymmetric breath sounds, and jugular venous distention are indicative of these conditions.  If identified, a tension pneumothorax should be addressed (with decompression or chest tube placement) before moving on in the survey. - **Circulation:**  Assess pulses in all extremities, obtain blood pressure, and in unstable patients perform a Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) examination. - **Disability:**  Perform a rapid neurologic assessment with Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). - **Exposure:**  Undress the patient completely, and search the entire body for occult injuries.  Small penetrating injuries (eg, stab wounds, GSWs) can easily be missed. A more detailed description of the general approach to adult trauma is described in a different article. ## Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) The FAST examination is an important sonographic tool used in the initial assessment of patients with penetrating injuries.  FAST ((Image 1)) evaluates for the presence of free fluid or air in specific areas of the body following trauma. - Pericardial effusion/tamponade - Intraperitoneal fluid - Hemothorax In unstable patients, the FAST exam is often performed simultaneously with the primary survey, though it should not delay critical interventions (eg, thoracostomy, thoracotomy, transfer to the operating room).  A positive FAST exam in cases of penetrating abdominal trauma is strongly indicative of injury and is highly specific.  However, its sensitivity in detecting penetrating injuries that require surgery is notably lower compared to its use in blunt trauma cases.  Certain injuries not typically diagnosed by FAST include diaphragm tears, pancreatic lesions, bowel perforations, mesenteric trauma, and abdominal injuries that do not produce free fluid in amounts detectable by ultrasonography (>200 mL).  In many cases of penetrating trauma, further evaluation through repeated abdominal exams, diagnostic peritoneal lavage, CT scans, or exploratory surgery may be necessary. # Diagnostic work-up ## Laboratory evaluation Laboratory testing is often indicated but should be tailored to the specific patient based on clinical suspicion and severity of injury.  Tests that may be indicated include:  complete blood count, blood type and crossmatch, basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, coagulation panel, arterial blood gas, lactate level, urinalysis, and pregnancy tests.  Normal laboratory values do not rule out severe injury and laboratory values may not immediately reflect the clinical condition (eg, hemoglobin drop is often delayed in acute hemorrhage). ## Imaging Most patients with penetrating trauma to the abdomen will require imaging in addition to the FAST exam. - **Plain abdominal radiographs:**  Not typically useful in the management of penetrating abdominal trauma with the exception of GSWs.  In patients with GSWs, plain radiographs are used to determine the path and/or location of projectiles (eg, bullets). - **CT:**  Rapid, sensitive and specific way to identify both visceral and vascular injuries.  The preferred modality to evaluate most traumatic injuries to the abdomen. ## Additional methods of evaluation - **Serial physical examinations (SPE):**  These are primarily used for patients with abdominal stab wounds, although they can also be applied in cases of GSWs when no obvious internal injury is detected on initial evaluation (eg, imaging and physical examination).  SPEs provide a safe and reliable method for monitoring the patient over time to detect signs of intraabdominal injury.  They are typically performed every 6 hours, ideally by the same examiner to ensure consistency.  The patient must be awake, alert, and without any mental status changes to accurately participate in the assessment. - **Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL):**  A bedside procedure used to assess peritoneal penetration and injury to organs in the abdomen, excluding the retroperitoneum.  It is performed by aspirating blood or fluid from the peritoneal cavity and, if necessary, infusing fluid for lavage.  Although once a common procedure, it has largely been replaced by CT.  In stable patients without immediate need for surgery, SPEs or imaging (eg, ultrasonography, CT) are generally preferred. - **Local wound exploration (LWE):**  In asymptomatic patients with abdominal stab wounds, LWE is used to determine if the peritoneum has been violated.  LWE is performed at the bedside with sterile technique, using both sharp and blunt dissection to fully visualize the wound's depth.  If the anterior rectus fascia is intact, the patient can be discharged after wound care, provided there are no other injuries.  However, if the fascia cannot be clearly visualized, further evaluation (eg, SPEs) is necessary.  LWE is rarely used for GSWs due to the difficulty in visualizing the missile tract, though it may be helpful for assessing superficial tangential wounds. - **Diagnostic laparoscopy (DL):**  Diagnostic laparoscopy is a minimally invasive surgical procedure used to visually inspect the abdominal cavity and diaphragm to assess for injuries and determine the need for further intervention, but it may miss some hollow organ injuries and cannot easily evaluate the retroperitoneum.  The role of DL in managing abdominal GSWs is evolving because it helps detect peritoneal violation and inspect the diaphragm.  However, it has limitations in visualizing the posterior diaphragm and detecting subtle hollow viscus or retroperitoneal injuries and may require conversion to open surgery for repair. # Clinical presentation and management For patients with penetrating abdominal trauma, any of the following are indications for immediate exploratory laparotomy ((Figure 1)): - Hemodynamic instability (systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg) or ongoing hemorrhage (eg, frank blood in the nasogastric tube or rectum) - Peritonitis (eg, rigidity, rebound tenderness) - Evisceration (ie, externally exposed intestines) - Impalement (ie, penetrating object still in situ) Impaled objects should not be removed.  Patients should be transported to the operating room for removal because removal of an impaled object may cause massive hemorrhage (object may be tamponading the bleeding). Patients without an indication for immediate laparotomy should undergo further evaluation to determine whether peritoneal penetration occurred (eg, CT scan, local wound exploration for anterior stab wounds) and/or whether other intraabdominal injuries are present.  The presence of either warrants further evaluation and management. ## Liver, kidney, and spleen injuries - **Clinical presentation:**  Liver injuries can present with right upper quadrant pain, abdominal tenderness, and signs of hemorrhagic shock (eg, hypotension, tachycardia, pallor) due to blood loss.  Referred pain to the right shoulder may occur.  Spleen injuries may present with left upper quadrant pain, tenderness, and signs of shock.  Referred pain to the left shoulder (Kehr sign) can also be seen.  Both injuries may lead to peritonitis if blood or bile irritates the peritoneal cavity.  Kidney injuries can present as flank pain and hematuria. - **Imaging:**  Although intraperitoneal free fluid may be evident on FAST exam, CT (preferably with contrast) is the gold standard to identify solid organ injury (eg, liver laceration ((Image 2)), splenic laceration ((Image 3)), renal laceration ((Image 4)) and is the study of choice in patients stable enough to tolerate the examination. - **Management:**  Management is based on the patient's hemodynamic stability, the severity of the injury, and the presence of additional injuries or medical conditions.  A hemodynamically unstable trauma patient with a positive FAST or DPL should have emergency abdominal surgical exploration to determine the source of hemorrhage.  For hemodynamically stable patients, less severe injuries can typically be managed nonoperatively (eg, SPEs, serial laboratory testing) whereas more severe injuries may require angiographic or surgical interventions (particularly splenic injuries). ## Hollow viscus injury - **Clinical presentation:**  Most patients will display abdominal distention, abdominal tenderness, or signs of peritoneal irritation.  The absence of abdominal pain makes the diagnosis unlikely, although the development of symptoms may be delayed by hours to days. - **Imaging:**  CT with intravenous contrast is the preferred diagnostic tool (to visualize pneumoperitoneum); however, injury to bowels (particularly small intestine) is often missed and SPEs are critical.  FAST is not sensitive for diagnosing hollow viscus injury. - **Management:**  Urgent surgical intervention is required in cases of hemodynamic instability, diffuse abdominal pain, signs of peritonitis on physical examination, or imaging findings suggestive of gastrointestinal perforation.  If no obvious injury is detected, SPEs should be performed to detect occult injuries.  Clinically stable patients without evidence of obvious injury should be observed for at least 12 hours for stab wounds and 24 hours for GSWs. ## Vascular injuries - **Clinical presentation:**  Penetrating trauma to the abdomen can affect major vessels ((Figure 2), (Figure 3)) such as the aorta, inferior vena cava, celiac trunk, renal vessels, hepatic vessels, mesenteric arteries and veins, and iliac vessels; smaller vessels are also capable of causing significant bleeding.  Patients may present with back or abdominal pain, depending on the injury site, and often show signs of severe hemorrhagic shock (eg, hypotension, tachycardia). - **Imaging:**  A positive FAST examination (free fluid present in abdomen) is likely in patients with injuries to major vessels.  In stable patients, CT with intravenous contrast can be obtained to evaluate the exact source of bleeding; unstable patients should go to the operating room. - **Management:**  Penetrating injuries to major abdominal vessels often lead to life-threatening hemorrhage.  Immediate intervention (eg, angiography, surgical intervention) is typically required to prevent massive blood loss and death.   Occlusion of the portal triad (hepatic artery, portal vein, and common bile duct) using the Pringle maneuver can be used to distinguish the source of right upper quadrant bleeding:  If the bleeding subsides following occlusion, the source is likely to be the hepatic artery or portal vein; if it persists, the inferior vena cava or hepatic veins are likely to be injured. ## Other considerations Historically, evaluating penetrating wounds to the flank and back was challenging because retroperitoneal injuries ((Table 1)) are difficult to assess using DPL, ultrasonography, or laparoscopy.  However, CT scans of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast have been shown to accurately diagnose retroperitoneal pathology ((Figure 4)) in penetrating trauma and allow for accurate tracking of the path of the projectile. Thoracoabdominal injuries, which involve the upper abdomen and lower chest, are also complex due to the movement of the diaphragm and potential for deflection of projectile or penetrating objects.  In stable patients, a CT scan is recommended, with laparoscopy as a follow-up if the results are inconclusive because it allows for direct inspection of the diaphragm while minimizing nontherapeutic laparotomies. # Complications The complications associated with abdominal trauma are closely linked to the organs and structures involved.  Common complications include: - **Hemorrhagic shock:**  Rapid blood loss from major vessels in the abdomen can result in hemorrhagic shock.  This is more common in penetrating trauma due to direct vessel disruption compared to blunt trauma, where bleeding is more likely to be contained. - **Pulmonary complications:**  Persistent pneumothorax, hemothorax, or empyema can occur following chest trauma, leading to prolonged respiratory compromise and its associated complications.  Widespread inflammation and lung damage from trauma can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome, which can be life-threatening and require intensive care management. - **Infection and sepsis:**  Penetrating trauma introduces external pathogens into sterile body cavities, increasing the risk of infection and abscess formation, especially in the setting of hollow viscus perforation. - **Fistula formation:**  Abnormal connections can develop between organs (eg, aorta and bowel) due to trauma, leading to complications such as gastrointestinal hemorrhage. # Summary Managing penetrating abdominal trauma requires swift, decisive action, particularly when life-threatening conditions are evident.  The ATLS protocol, alongside focused imaging, helps guide the identification of injuries that need urgent surgical intervention.  Penetrating trauma often causes direct damage to vital organs and vessels, which increases the likelihood of requiring operative management compared to blunt trauma.  Whereas blunt trauma is frequently managed nonoperatively in stable patients, penetrating injuries usually demand a more aggressive surgical approach due to the precision of the injury path and potential for severe hemorrhage or organ damage. ​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌

Retroperitoneal abdominal organs

  • Suprarenal (adrenal) glands
  • Aorta & inferior vena cava
  • Duodenum* (except 1st part)
  • Pancreas* (head & body)
  • Ureters
  • Colon* (ascending & descending)
  • Kidneys
  • Esophagus
  • Rectum (middistal)

Mnemonic: SAD PUCKER

*Secondarily retroperitoneal (developed intraperitoneal & migrated retroperitoneal).

# Trauma: Major Extremity Trauma # Introduction Extremity trauma can be either blunt or penetrating, involving injuries that affect bones, muscles, vessels, and nerves.  Complications include as ischemia, infection, nerve damage, and potential loss of limb function.  Blunt trauma can cause fractures, soft tissue injuries, and compartment syndrome, whereas penetrating trauma may result in direct damage to vital structures such as blood vessels and nerves. # Upper extremity anatomy ## Major vascular structures Axillary, brachial, radial, and ulnar arteries ((Figure 1)). ## Major nerves - **Brachial plexus**:  a network of nerves ((Figure 2)) originating from the spinal cord (C5-T1) that provides motor and sensory innervation to the shoulder, arm, and hand.  It divides into 5 major peripheral nerves: the axillary, musculocutaneous, radial, median, and ulnar nerves. - **Axillary nerve** ((Figure 3)):  innervates the deltoid and teres minor muscles, allowing shoulder abduction and external rotation.  Provides sensation to the skin over the lateral shoulder ((Figure 4)). - **Musculocutaneous nerve** ((Figure 5)):  controls elbow flexion by innervating the biceps brachii, brachialis, and coracobrachialis muscles.  Provides sensation to the lateral forearm ((Figure 6)). - **Radial nerve** ((Figure 7)):  controls extension of the elbow (triceps), wrist, and fingers, and assists in forearm supination.  Provides sensation to the posterior arm, forearm, and back of the hand, including the thumb, index, and middle fingers ((Figure 8)). - **Median nerve** ((Figure 9)):  controls most of the muscles responsible for flexing the wrist and fingers (flexor muscles), as well as thumb opposition (thenar muscles).  Supplies sensation to the palmar side of the thumb, index, middle finger, and lateral half of the ring finger ((Figure 10)). - **Ulnar nerve** ((Figure 11)):  innervates muscles that control fine movements in the hand (intrinsic hand muscles), as well as wrist and finger flexion on the ulnar side.  Provides sensation to the palmar and dorsal surfaces of the little finger and medial half of the ring finger ((Figure 12)). ## Skeletal/muscular structures Bony structures in the arm include the humerus, radius, and ulna.  Major muscles include the biceps ((Figure 13)), triceps ( (Figure 14)), forearm flexors, and extensors. # Lower extremity anatomy ## Major vascular structures Femoral, popliteal, tibial, and dorsalis pedis arteries ((Figure 15)). ## Major nerves - **Femoral nerve** ((Figure 16)):  innervates the muscles of the anterior thigh, including the quadriceps femoris (extends the knee joint).  Supplies sensation to the anterior thigh and medial leg. - **Sciatic nerve** ((Figure 17)):  splits into the tibial and common fibular (peroneal) nerves, aids in knee flexion.  Supplies sensation to the posterior thigh, posterior leg, and most of the foot. - **Deep peroneal nerve** ((Figure 18)):  innervates the muscles of the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg, including the tibialis anterior and peroneal muscles (which dorsiflex the ankle and extend the toes).  Supplies sensation to the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot. - **Tibial nerve** ((Figure 19)):  innervates the posterior compartment of the leg, including the gastrocnemius, soleus, and muscles of the foot.  Provides sensation to the sole of the foot and the posterior calf. ## Skeletal/muscular structures Bony structures in the lower extremity include the femur, tibia, fibula, and patella.  Major muscles in the lower extremity include the following ((Figure 20)): - **Quadriceps muscles** (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius) - **Hamstrings** (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus) - **Calf muscles** (gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis anterior and posterior, fibularis longus and brevis, flexor and extensor digitorum longus, flexor and extensor hallucis longus) # Clinical presentation and evaluation Extrema trauma can cause injuries to the vessels, muscles, bones, and nerves.  Clinical presentation and subsequent evaluation will depend on what structures are injured. ## Vascular injuries - **Findings** - "Hard signs": - Observed pulsatile bleeding - Presence of a bruit or thrill over the injury - Expanding hematoma - Signs of distal ischemia (eg, absent pulses, cool extremities) - "Soft signs":  Diminished pulses, history of significant hemorrhage, bony injury, neurologic abnormality - **Implications for further evaluation** - Patients with hard signs should generally be taken for immediate surgical exploration. - Patients without hard signs should have further diagnostic evaluation: - **Injured extremity index (IEI):**  The IEI is analogous to the ankle-brachial index (ABI) ((Figure 21)) but can apply to any extremity.  It is indicated for any patient with suspected vascular injury but without obvious hard signs (eg, diminished but present pulses, small hematomas).  The IEI is the ratio of the highest systolic occlusion pressure in the injured extremity at the level of the dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial (or radial/ulnar arteries) divided by the systolic pressure in a proximal vessel in an uninjured extremity (eg, brachial artery).  An IEI ≤0.9 is abnormal ((Table 1)) and indicates the need for further vascular imaging. - **CT angiography (CTA):**  The gold standard for evaluating vascular injuries.  CTA is indicated when "soft signs" are present, IEI is abnormal (eg, ≤0.9), or there is suspicion of arterial involvement based on examination or history (eg, high-velocity projectile near major vessels).  Conventional arteriography can also be used but is invasive and more time consuming. - **Duplex ultrasonography:**  Can be used to evaluate specific vascular injuries (eg, pseudoaneurysms, arteriovenous fistulas) when CTA is unavailable or contraindicated. ## Musculoskeletal injuries - **Findings** - Obvious deformity, instability, or crepitus may indicate a fracture or dislocation. - Limited range of motion or inability to bear weight can suggest muscle injury, tendon rupture, or fracture. - Open wounds over a fractured bone are concerning for open fractures (occur when bone penetrates the skin, exposing the fracture site to the external environment). - **Implications for further evaluation:**  Any physical examination abnormality suggestive of a fracture, dislocation, or foreign body (eg, bullet) warrants plain x-rays.  X-rays should typically include the joint above and below the suspected injury. ## Neurologic injuries - **Findings** - Motor weakness or complete paralysis in certain muscle groups can indicate nerve injury (eg, wrist drop with radial nerve damage, foot drop with peroneal nerve injury). - Sensory loss in specific dermatomes or loss of reflexes. - **Implications for further evaluation:**  When neurologic deficits are present on physical examination, further evaluation is indicated.  Depending on the specific deficit, this may require imaging (eg, spine imaging), consultation with a specialist (eg, hand surgeon), or monitoring for improvement (particularly true in blunt trauma).  Given that many nerves run with vascular structures, vascular injury should also be considered and carefully evaluated. ## Traumatic amputation - **Findings** - Complete severing of a limb or appendage, often accompanied by severe bleeding. - Surrounding tissue may show signs of crush injury, ischemia, or contamination, increasing the risk of infection or poor healing. - **Implications for further evaluation:**  Imaging of the stump and amputated part (if replantation possible) is typically obtained.  If the patient is a candidate for replantation, transfer to an appropriate institution should occur. ## Compartment syndrome - **Findings** ((Table 2)) - Early signs: - Pain out of proportion to the injury - Pain with passive stretch of muscles - Tense, swollen compartments - Paresthesias - Late signs: - Decreased sensation - Weakness, paralysis - Decreased distal pulses - **Implications for further evaluation:**  Any clinical suspicion of compartment syndrome warrants immediate surgical consultation to evaluate the need for fasciotomies (in unclear cases, compartment pressures may be measured).  Compartment syndrome is discussed in more detail in another article. # Management ## Hemorrhage control - **Direct pressure:**  primary method of controlling active bleeding ((Table 3)).  Apply over the wound immediately. - **Tourniquets:**  should be applied for uncontrolled hemorrhage or exsanguination.  Use proximal to the injury but remove as soon as bleeding is controlled to avoid prolonged ischemia. - **Resuscitation:**  Intravenous fluids or blood products should be administered based on hemodynamic status.  Damage control resuscitation (DCR) is often used in patients with significant hemorrhage.  The goal of DCR is to rapidly control hemorrhage while minimizing the potential for complications associated with massive hemorrhage and coagulopathy (achieved by limiting crystalloid use, transfusing appropriate ratio of blood products early, and managing temperature). ## Vascular injuries - **Unstable patients:**  should be taken immediately to the operating room for repair. - **Hard signs present:**  Immediate surgical exploration ((Table 4)) is required for hard signs of vascular injury (eg, pulsatile hemorrhage, expanding hematoma, absent pulses). - **Soft signs present:**  CTA and IEI should be performed.  If significant vascular injury is confirmed (eg, arterial occlusion, transection), surgical intervention with repair (eg, vascular grafting or ligation) is indicated. ## Musculoskeletal injuries - **Open fractures:**  Immediate (eg, within hours) debridement and irrigation are necessary.  Surgical stabilization (eg, external or internal fixation) is required, and broad-spectrum antibiotics should be initiated to prevent infection. - **Closed fractures:**  Displaced fractures should be reduced (ie, realigned) and immobilized immediately.  When surgery is indicated, the timing of surgical repair will depend on the type and location of the fracture. - **Joint dislocations:**  Dislocations should be reduced as quickly as possible to limit further injury to the skin (eg, tissue necrosis due to pressure can convert a closed injury to an open injury), nerves, and vascular structures.  Dislocations causing neurovascular compromise should be reduced immediately (do not wait for imaging). - **Tendon injuries:**  Tendon repair should be performed if lacerations are identified, with physical therapy initiated postoperatively to restore function. ## Neurologic injuries - **Motor and sensory deficits:**  Management depends on the patient's overall clinical status, severity of the injury, and specific nerve involved.  Complete transection (ie, neurotmesis) of a nerve will require surgical repair.  In general, outcomes are better if the nerve is repaired promptly (eg, within 24-72 hrs).  Patients with neuropraxia (impairment of nerve function without structural damage to the nerve fibers) or axonotmesis (nerve injury that affects the nerve fibers but not the connective tissue), which are more common with blunt than penetrating trauma, may recover spontaneously.  Regular examinations to monitor improvement are recommended followed by delayed repair if symptoms do not resolve. ## Traumatic amputation - **Care of the amputated part:**  The amputated part should be wrapped in sterile, saline-moistened gauze and sealed in a plastic bag.  The bag should be then placed in a container of ice water to be transported with the patient (cooling of the amputated part decreases tissue metabolism and oxygen demand, thereby minimizing ischemic damage and prolonging the window of viability for replantation). - **Replantation:**  When replantation is indicated, it should occur as quickly as possible;  delays reduce the likelihood of success.  Replantation is more common in the upper extremity (particularly the digits) than in the lower extremity. ## Compartment syndrome - **Emergency fasciotomy:**  Surgical release of the involved compartments should be performed immediately to decompress compartments and restore perfusion.  Delays will cause long-term neurovascular injury and may even result in an amputation. # Complications - **Ischemia:**  Vascular injuries that are not addressed in a timely manner can lead to distal ischemia, requiring amputation. - **Compartment syndrome:**  Failure to recognize and treat this condition can result in permanent muscle and nerve damage or loss of limb. - **Infection:**  Open fractures and soft tissue injuries, especially those associated with foreign body contamination, carry a high risk of infection, including osteomyelitis. - **Nerve injury:**  Delayed nerve repair can result in chronic motor or sensory deficits, which may be permanent. - **Deep venous thrombosis:**  a leading cause of mortality in patients with major trauma.  Patients with extremity trauma (particularly lower extremity trauma) are at significantly increased risk.  Thromboprophylaxis should be considered. - **Phantom limb pain:**  occurs when a patient perceives pain in an amputated body part.  The pain can vary in intensity and can be difficult to manage (pain is thought to arise from the brain and spinal cord's continued response to nerve signals from the missing limb). - **Posttraumatic neuromas:**  a painful, tangled mass of unmyelinated nerve endings that develops over weeks to months after amputation.  The diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by temporary pain relief from local anesthetics.  Treatment involves neuroma excision or pain management (eg, tricyclic antidepressants, antiepileptics). # Summary Evaluation of extremity trauma requires a structured, systematic approach to identify and manage vascular, musculoskeletal, and neurologic injuries.  Management of severe extremity trauma focuses on controlling hemorrhage, assessing the neurovascular status, and performing appropriate imaging.  For vascular trauma, the presence of hard signs typically necessitates immediate surgical exploration and repair, whereas soft signs indicate the need for further diagnostic evaluation (eg, CT angiography, injured extremity index).  Fractures and dislocations should be promptly reduced and immobilized to avoid further injury; this should be followed by timely surgical repair (when indicated) to prevent long-term disability.  Early recognition and intervention, supported by diagnostic tools such as x-rays, injured extremity index, and CTA, are required to optimize outcomes and prevent complications such as ischemia, nerve damage, and infection.​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​

Injured extremity index* (IEI)

>0.9

Highly negative predictive value for vascular injury

≤0.9

Indicative of vascular injury; additional vascular imaging is indicated

*Analogous to the ankle-brachial index; IEI is a trauma-specific term that can be applied to any extremity.
IEI = ratio of the systolic occlusion pressure distally in an injured extremity to the occlusion pressure at a proximal site in an uninjured extremity.

Acute compartment syndrome of the extremity

Pathophysiology

  • ↑ Pressure within enclosed fascial space
  • ↓ Blood flow & tissue perfusion

Common causes

  • Crush injury, long bone fracture, rhabdomyolysis
  • Reperfusion after prolonged ischemia
  • Massive fluid resuscitation

Clinical features

  • Early:
    • Progressive, severe pain
    • Rapidly ↑ & tense swelling
    • ↑ Pain with passive stretching
    • Paresthesia
  • Late:
    • ↓ Sensation
    • Weakness (within hours), paralysis (late)
    • Loss of pulses (uncommon)

Management

  • Compartment pressure measurement* can confirm diagnosis
  • Emergency fasciotomy

*Delta pressure (diastolic pressure − compartment pressure) ≤30 mm Hg is consistent with compartment syndrome.

Management of hemorrhage due to trauma

Control
bleeding

  • Control bleeding from any compressible site
  • Early transfer to location (trauma center, operating room, angiography suite) for definitive care & control of hemorrhage

Give blood
products early

  • Transfuse blood products early in resuscitation
  • Massive transfusion protocol*: ratio of 1:1:1 FFP/pRBCs/platelets to minimize risk of coagulopathy

Limit use of crystalloids

  • Limit to ~1 L if patient is hypotensive
  • Switch to blood products as soon as available
  • *Massive transfusion protocol likely required in patients with ≥2 of the following: SBP ≤90 mm Hg, pulse ≥120/min, positive FAST examination, and penetrating mechanism of injury.
  • FAST = Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma; FFP = fresh frozen plasma; pRBCs = packed red blood cells; SBP = systolic blood pressure.

Extremity vascular trauma

Clinical manifestations

Hard signs

  • Observed pulsatile bleeding
  • Presence of bruit/thrill over injury
  • Expanding hematoma
  • Signs of distal ischemia
 

Soft signs

  •  History of hemorrhage
  •  Diminished pulses
  •  Bony injury
  •  Neurologic abnormality

Evaluation

If hard signs or hemodynamic instability

  • Surgical exploration
 

Otherwise

  • Injured extremity index
  • CT scan or conventional angiography
  • Duplex Doppler ultrasonography
