articles.title: Transient Tachypnea Of The Newborn
articles.markdown:
# Transient Tachypnea Of The Newborn # Introduction Transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN) is a benign, self-limited condition that occurs due to delayed reabsorption of fetal alveolar fluid.  It is the most common cause of respiratory distress in late preterm (>34 weeks gestation) and term (>37 weeks gestation) neonates.  Patients typically experience respiratory distress (eg, tachypnea, increased work of breathing) shortly after birth. # Pathophysiology and risk factors In early gestation, fluid is normally secreted into the alveolar space to stretch the parenchyma as it grows and develops.  In late gestation, this fluid is actively reabsorbed through sodium channels on alveolar epithelial cells.  Reabsorption is most pronounced before and during labor due to surges in catecholamines and other hormones that upregulate sodium channel expression. In TTN, there is **delayed alveolar fluid reabsorption**; retained alveolar fluid moves into the interstitial space (not the alveolar epithelium and vascular space) where it accumulates.  Excess fluid in the interstitial space compresses the bronchioles and traps air distal due to the compression.  Ongoing perfusion of the hypoventilated alveoli leads to hypoxemia and, in severe cases, hypercapnia.  In addition, interstitial fluid decreases pulmonary compliance and subsequently increases work of breathing.  Although the exact cause of delayed reabsorption of alveolar fluid in TTN is unknown, proposed mechanisms include surfactant and/or nitric oxide (a potent vasodilator) deficiencies. Therefore, risk factors for TTN include: - **Prematurity**:  In late gestation, pulmonary epithelial cells switch from alveolar fluid secretion to active reabsorption in response to circulating hormones.  Preterm neonates are born before this transition occurs, increasing the risk for TTN. - **Cesarean delivery**:  There is a higher incidence of TTN in neonates born via cesarean delivery, particularly without preceding labor and its associated increase in circulating catecholamines.  In addition, although minor, mechanical pressure on the thoracic wall during vaginal delivery (but not during planned cesarean delivery) likely contributes to alveolar fluid clearance. - **Maternal factors**:  Diabetes mellitus, asthma, and obesity are common risk factors. Antenatal corticosteroids may be protective, likely related to catecholamine-induced fluid reabsorption; however, the risks associated with antenatal corticosteroids (eg, neuropsychiatric disorders due to possible disruption of normal fetal brain development) in late preterm and term neonates may not outweigh the benefits because TTN is a benign, self-limited condition. # Clinical presentation Patients typically develop tachypnea (**respirations >60/min**) **within 2 hours of birth**.  In moderate to severe cases, patients can develop increased work of breathing (eg, subcostal/intercostal retractions, nasal flaring, expiratory grunting) and cyanosis.  Lungs are often clear to auscultation (no rales or rhonchi). # Diagnosis TTN is a clinical diagnosis based on history and physical examination findings.  Characteristic radiographic findings include hyperinflation, perihilar linear streaking, and **fluid in the interlobar fissures** ((Image 1)).  Resolution of symptoms within 12-24 hours for mild to moderate cases or 48-72 hours for severe cases confirms the diagnosis. # Differential diagnosis The differential diagnosis for TTN includes other conditions that cause respiratory distress in the neonatal period, such as the following: - **Respiratory distress syndrome** (RDS):  This condition occurs in preterm (<34 weeks gestation) due to surfactant deficiency.  Distinguishing radiographic findings include widespread alveolar collapse (ground-glass opacities) and air bronchograms ((Image 2)). - **Neonatal pneumonia**:  Chest radiograph reveals focal alveolar densities or consolidations, unlike the perihilar streaking seen in TTN. - **Congenital heart disease**:  Depending on the underlying cardiac lesion, patients can have respiratory distress that is often worse with feeding.  The diagnosis can be distinguished from TTN via physical examination (eg, heart murmur, central cyanosis), chest radiography (eg, cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema), or pre- and postductal pulse oximetry; postductal oxygen saturation is lower in patients with defects in which right-to-left shunting of deoxygenated blood occurs through the ductus arteriosus. - **Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn**:  This condition occurs due to persistently elevated pulmonary vascular resistance after birth.  Right-to-left shunting across the ductus arteriosus can cause cyanosis and respiratory distress; however, chest radiography is often normal, and preductal oxygenation saturation is higher than postductal oxygen saturation. # Management Management of TTN is primarily supportive, as follows: - **Supplemental oxygen** - Nutrition:  Orogastric tube feedings or intravenous fluids should be considered to avoid aspiration in patients with respirations >60/min. If respiratory distress persists beyond 72 hours or worsens despite supportive care, then alternate diagnoses (eg, RDS, neonatal pneumonia) should be considered while escalating respiratory support to continuous positive airway pressure. # Prognosis The prognosis for patients with TTN is excellent.  In general, TTN is a **benign, self-limited condition**, and complications (eg, persistent oxygen requirement, pulmonary hypertension) are uncommon. # Summary Transient tachypnea of the newborn ((Table 1)) is a benign, self-limited condition that occurs in neonates due to delayed reabsorption of retained fetal alveolar fluid.  Patients typically experience respiratory distress (eg, tachypnea, increased work of breathing) shortly after birth.  Treatment is supportive (eg, oxygen) until symptoms resolve within 72 hours of birth. ​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​

Transient tachypnea of the newborn

Pathophysiology

  • Retained fetal lung fluid

Risk factors

  • Cesarean birth
  • Prematurity
  • Maternal diabetes mellitus

Clinical findings

  • Tachypnea, increased work of breathing
  • Clear breath sounds
  • Chest x-ray: hyperinflation, fluid in fissures

Management

  • Supportive care (eg, oxygen, nutrition)
  • Self-resolution in 1-3 days

articles.title: Surgical Airway: Tracheostomy And Cricothyrotomy
articles.markdown: # Surgical Airway: Tracheostomy And Cricothyrotomy # Introduction Standard airway intubation can be performed through the mouth (orotracheally) or through the nose (nasotracheally).  When standard intubation is impossible or unsafe (eg, due to airway obstruction or trauma), a surgical airway can be lifesaving.  The 2 most common surgical airway procedures are cricothyrotomy and tracheostomy: - A cricothyrotomy provides rapid but temporary airway access through the cricothyroid membrane.  It is performed emergently when patients are in a CICV (**C**an't **I**ntubate, **C**an't **V**entilate) scenario. - A tracheostomy provides more definitive long-term access through the tracheal rings.  It is performed under more controlled settings, often when prolonged mechanical ventilation is anticipated. This article discusses surgical anatomy, indications, techniques, complications, and aftercare of these procedures. # Surgical anatomy ## Cricothyrotomy In emergencies, the target is the **cricothyroid membrane** ((Figure 1)), located below the skin and fascia.  It can be palpated as a soft, slightly depressed gap (~2 cm × 0.5 cm in adults) in the midline just below the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple). The main advantage of cricothyrotomy is rapid access; the membrane is a thin, avascular layer of connective tissue that can be cut quickly.  Compared with tracheostomy, it carries a lower risk of hitting major vessels because the entry site is higher in the neck.  It requires incision through the following:  Skin → superficial cervical fascia (including subcutaneous fat and platysma muscle) → investing and pretracheal layers of the deep cervical fascia → cricothyroid membrane.  Disadvantages include its temporary nature and smaller opening (which may limit ventilation). ## Tracheostomy For less urgent situations, a tracheostomy provides more definitive access ((Figure 2)).  The target is the **second to fourth tracheal cartilage rings** at the midline.  The relevant area is identified by palpating from the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple) to the cricoid cartilage, then locating the rings just below ((Figure 3)). The main advantage of tracheostomy is its stability for long-term ventilation.  The larger opening allows easier suctioning and secretion clearance and reduces airway resistance.  Disadvantages include slower access (eg, tissue dissection may be required) and higher potential to injure nearby blood vessels (eg, high-riding innominate \[brachiocephalic\] artery). # Indications and contraindications ## Cricothyrotomy A cricothyrotomy is performed in emergencies, such as: - CICV scenario. - Severe upper airway obstruction or distortion (eg, angioedema, head and neck trauma, foreign body aspiration). - Failed endotracheal intubation. The main contraindication is age <12 because cutting the developing cricothyroid membrane risks severe subglottic injury and fixed stenosis.  Instead, a needle (vs incisional) cricothyrotomy, in which a small catheter is inserted in the cricothyroid membrane to allow jet ventilation with short, pressurized oxygen bursts, is preferred. ## Tracheostomy A tracheostomy is performed less urgently, for example when there is: - An anticipated need for prolonged mechanical ventilation (>10 days) (eg, due to neuromuscular weakness or severe lung damage). - Upper airway obstruction (eg, tumor, trauma) at or above the glottis that blocks orotracheal or nasotracheal intubation. There are no absolute contraindications.  Relative contraindications include uncorrected coagulopathy, infection overlying the incision site, and a high-riding innominate (brachiocephalic) artery ((Figure 4)) (often screened with preprocedural bedside ultrasonography). # Procedure ## Cricothyrotomy The patient is placed supine with the neck extended (if possible).  The cricothyroid membrane is palpated as a soft gap just below the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple).  In patients with trauma or a thick neck, a vertical skin incision over the larynx can improve exposure ((Figure 5)).  A horizontal stab incision is created through the cricothyroid membrane, and the opening is dilated with a blunt instrument.  A small tracheostomy tube is inserted and sutured in place.  Its placement is confirmed with capnography. ## Tracheostomy The patient is positioned supine with the neck extended (if possible).  Preprocedural ultrasonography can identify the tracheal rings and vascular anomalies (eg, high-riding innominate artery).  A skin incision is made over the second to fourth tracheal rings, and dissection is carried through the subcutaneous tissue.  A tracheal incision is made through the rings, and a cuffed tracheostomy tube is inserted and sutured in place ((Figure 6)).  The tracheostomy **cuff is inflated** to seal the trachea, which allows for positive pressure from the ventilator to expand the lungs.  Correct placement is usually confirmed by bronchoscopy.  During placement, an obturator—a rigid introducer rod inserted into the tracheostomy—facilitates smooth insertion by providing shape and stiffness but must be removed immediately after insertion because it completely obstructs airflow.  Most tracheostomy tubes also have an inner cannula, which sits inside the outer cannula and can be removed and replaced independently of the outer tube if necessary ((Figure 7)). In the intensive care unit, a percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy is commonly performed at the bedside.  The trachea is punctured with a needle and the tract is serially dilated over a guidewire before inserting the tracheostomy tube.  Concurrent bronchoscopy is commonly used to check positioning and minimize the risk of posterior wall injury. # Complications ## Early complications Early complications occur within the first several hours to days. **Hemorrhage** from superficial veins (eg, anterior jugular, thyroid veins) is relatively common but is usually not serious.  Rarely, massive hemorrhage results from injury to the **innominate (brachiocephalic) artery**, producing brisk bleeding that quickly floods the airway.  Such bleeding is managed by immediate digital compression by pinching the innominate (brachiocephalic) artery against the sternum through the tracheostomy stoma and performing emergency intubation (if possible) and emergency surgery to ligate the vessel. **Accidental decannulation** (dislodgment/removal of the tube) is most dangerous in the first 7 days, before the tract has matured.  Blindly reinserting the tube should never be attempted because it risks creating a false passage, resulting in hypoxemia and subcutaneous emphysema.  Instead, the patient should be reintubated (eg, orotracheally) while preparing for a redo tracheostomy.  After 7-10 days, reinsertion is safer but still best done under bronchoscopic guidance. **Site infection** (local cellulitis around the stoma) is relatively common in the early period because the upper airway is naturally unsterile (due to skin and respiratory flora).  It presents with erythema, tenderness, and purulent drainage.  Most cases are mild and respond to local wound care and antibiotics, but deeper infection can track along the tracheostomy tract, leading to mediastinitis or sepsis if not promptly recognized. ## Late complications Late complications occur weeks to months after tracheostomy placement. **Tracheal damage** can occur if the cuff pressure is set too high (eg, >30 cm H2O), which can cause mucosal ischemia within hours.  Sequelae include subglottic stenosis (fibrotic narrowing) or tracheomalacia (thinning and collapse of cartilage).  Patients may be asymptomatic while the tracheostomy is in place.  Manifestations are often discovered during weaning or after decannulation and include respiratory difficulty, stridor, or wheezing.  Flow-volume loop can show fixed obstruction (stenosis) ((Figure 8)) or variable intrathoracic obstruction (tracheomalacia) ((Figure 9)).  Diagnosis is confirmed with bronchoscopy. **Airway granulation** involves exaggerated tissue growth at the stoma that can obstruct the tracheostomy tube.  It presents with dyspnea, increased peak pressure (if on ventilator), and difficulty passing a suction catheter.  The granulation tissue may be internal, requiring visualization with bronchoscopy.  Management includes excision (eg, surgical, laser). **Tracheal fistulas** include late tracheoinnominate fistula (TIF) and tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF).  TIF is a rare but catastrophic erosion between the anterior tracheal wall and innominate (brachiocephalic) artery.  Risk factors include prolonged tube contact with the tracheal wall (eg, extra-long tube), low tracheostomy (eg, below the fourth ring), and cuff overinflation (pressure necrosis).  It often presents with a small herald bleed, followed by massive hemorrhage if untreated.  TEF occurs due to erosion between the posterior tracheal wall and esophagus, most often due to cuff overinflation.  It presents with recurrent aspiration pneumonia, copious secretions, and gastric distension with air. ## Mucus plugging Thick secretions can obstruct the tracheostomy tube at any time.  Mucus plugging is the **most common cause** of acute respiratory deterioration.  It presents with sudden respiratory distress and high-pressure ventilator alarms.  Exchanging the inner cannula often resolves the plugging.  Additional management includes suctioning, humidified oxygen, or hypertonic saline to loosen secretions.  If obstruction persists, the entire tracheostomy tube needs to be exchanged urgently. # Aftercare ## Routine care Ongoing care focuses on preventing mucus plugging and infections ((Figure 10)).  The inner cannula is typically cleaned or replaced daily to avoid buildup of mucus.  The stoma is inspected and redressed.  Cuff pressures are checked regularly and maintained below approximately 25 cm H2O to minimize tracheal injury.  Tracheostomy tubes are generally exchanged every 1-3 months. # Weaning The first step in tracheostomy weaning is reducing and ultimately discontinuing ventilator support: - Patients undergo a **spontaneous breathing trial (SBT)**, monitoring respiratory effort when the ventilator is disconnected for several hours.  The cuff remains inflated, and all airflow passes through the tracheostomy. - If the patient passes the SBT, **tracheostomy collar** trials, in which the patient breathes humidified oxygen through the tracheostomy with the cuff still inflated, can proceed.  The duration of the tracheostomy collar trials is  gradually lengthened, often alternating with ventilator support until endurance improves. - Once long periods (eg, 48 hr) can be sustained on tracheostomy collar, a **cuff deflation trial** is performed to assess whether patients can ventilate through their upper airway and protect against aspiration.  Finally, a **capping trial** occludes the tracheostomy, and patients breathe entirely through their upper airway. If patients tolerate deflation and capping, removal (decannulation) may be possible.  However, recovery may be slow (eg, after major critical illness or surgery).  During this period, speech and swallowing rehabilitation typically proceed while the tracheostomy remains in place. ## Phonation With the cuff inflated, airflow passes through the tracheostomy tube instead of the larynx.  Therefore, patients cannot vocalize.  One-way speaking valves (eg, **Passy-Muir**) allow inspiration through the tracheostomy but exhalation through the larynx.  Temporarily occluding the tracheostomy (eg, with a finger) during exhalation achieves the same effect, although this is less practical and hygienic.  Fenestrated tubes are another option, with openings that permit some airflow through the larynx.  In general, patients are ready for a speaking valve trial once they can tolerate cuff deflation. ## Swallowing While the tracheostomy is in place, oral intake may be possible in patients with intact cognitive, nerve, and muscle function.  However, the tracheostomy can impair swallowing due to cuff inflation, which eliminates subglottic airflow needed for normal laryngeal sensation and elevation.  (A common misconception is that cuff inflation compresses the esophagus posteriorly, but this does not occur.) All patients should undergo a swallowing assessment (eg, fiberoptic, colored food dye) before advancing oral intake.  Importantly, cuff inflation reduces, but does not eliminate, the risk of aspiration pneumonia; however, it does substantially reduce the risk of massive fatal aspiration.  During meals, the **cuff is deflated**, which improves swallowing mechanics.  Speaking valves concurrently improve swallowing function by restoring subglottic pressure. ## Decannulation Decannulation is possible once the initial indication for a tracheostomy has resolved and the patient can breathe spontaneously through their native upper airway (eg, after successful cuff deflation and capping).  Often, the tube is downsized before removal.  After removal, the stoma is covered with a sterile dressing and typically closes on its own. # Summary Surgical airways can be lifesaving when standard intubation is not possible.  Cricothyrotomy provides rapid but temporary access during an airway crisis (can't intubate, can't ventilate).  Tracheostomy is preferred for stable long-term airway management.  Early complications include accidental decannulation (the cannula should never be replaced while the tract is immature) and hemorrhage (eg, from innominate artery erosion).  Late complications include tracheal stenosis, tracheomalacia, and obstruction with granulation tissue.  Mucus plugging is the most common cause of acute deterioration and can occur at any time.  Weaning involves a stepwise process of spontaneous breathing trials, cuff deflation, and capping until decannulation is possible. ​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​

articles.title: Smoking Cessation
articles.markdown:
# Smoking Cessation # Introduction Cigarette smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease, disability, and death among adults worldwide.  Smoking cessation is an evidence-based suite of behavioral support and pharmacotherapy approaches that need to be individualized to each patient. # Pathophysiology ## Nicotine dependency Problematic (chronic) tobacco use (eg, tobacco use disorder) involves complex physiological and psychosocial mechanisms: - **Physiological** (ie, dependency):  Nicotine strongly binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), primarily in the mesolimbic dopamine pathway.  Tolerance (higher concentrations of nicotine needed to achieve similar levels of dopamine release) gradually develops.  Sudden nicotine cessation leads to acute withdrawal (irritability, cravings), which is the hallmark of dependency. - **Psychosocial** (ie, addiction):  Patients with longtime smoking habits may develop distorted perceptions about their smoking behavior.  For example, they may overestimate potential benefits (eg, weight control) while underestimating risks (eg, asthma flare-ups).  Habits may contribute.  For example, smoking is often linked to daily routines (eg, first cigarette with morning coffee), and oral fixation (satisfaction from the ritual of lighting up a cigarette, holding it, and exhaling smoke) can become a conditioned response to stress. ## Predictors of continued smoking Among patients trying to quit, unsuccessful smoking cessation correlates with the following factors: - High nicotine dependency:  **Time to first cigarette** (TTFC) upon waking is the single most powerful indicator of nicotine dependency.  A short TTFC (<30 min) or smoking in bed indicates greater physiological dependency.  Heavy smoking (eg, >30 cigarettes/day) is important but not as predictive as TTFC. - Comorbid psychiatric disorders:  Over one-third of patients who smoke have a serious concurrent psychiatric illness.  Smoking cessation is least likely to succeed in patients with schizophrenia and substance (eg, alcohol) use disorders. - Cohabitation with an individual who smokes (lack of social support, constant exposure to environmental smoking cues):  Cessation is typically difficult unless the entire household is committed as a team. - Other factors: - Younger onset of smoking (ie, during adolescence) is associated with a lower quitting rate, possibly due to higher expression and sensitivity of dopaminergic receptors in youth. - Low motivation or confidence (<7 on a 10-point scale) in ability to quit - Brief periods of abstinence following past cessation attempts (ie, frequent relapses).  Notably, the number of previous quit attempts is *not* necessarily a negative predictor (eg, patients often learn through prior experiences). # Core principles ## The 5As The universal principles of smoking cessation are summarized with the 5As ((Table 1)): - **Ask** about tobacco use:  All patients should be asked about tobacco use at each clinic visit.  The screening question is constructed to have the highest sensitivity possible (eg, "Do you *ever* smoke cigarettes?"). - **Advise** against smoking:  Patients who are currently smoking should be advised to quit immediately (eg, "Now is a great time to quit smoking.  I will help you.").  Every minute counts (eg, 5 min of advice = 5% increase in quit success rate). - **Assess** readiness to quit:  The most direct way is to ask for a firm quit date (eg, "When are you going to quit smoking?  Let me mark it on my calendar.").  For patients who do not answer right away, the urge to propose a date for them should be resisted.  Often, resolutions solidify in the period of hesitation. - **Assist** with quitting:  When a firm quit date is established, a cessation plan should be developed with the patient.  The plan typically includes individual interventions (eg, behavioral therapy plus pharmacotherapy), trigger anticipation, and external resources (eg, quit hotline). - **Arrange** follow-up:  Proactive (eg, clinical calls to patients 3 days before their planned quit date) contact is more effective than waiting for the next office visit. ## Three major interventions Based on the 5As, smoking cessation consists of 3 major interventions: - Motivational interviewing - Behavioral counseling - Pharmacotherapy These interventions (used alone or together) are tailored to the patient's stage of change ((Table 2)).  Motivational interviewing is traditionally viewed as the main tool for advancing from precontemplation to preparation.  However, it is relevant at all stages of change ((Table 3)). # Not ready to quit The stage of being not ready to quit is also referred to as the **precontemplation** stage of change.  For patients in the precontemplation stage (eg, those unwilling to give a firm quit date), the goal is to help unlock their internal motivation. ## Motivational interviewing At the heart of motivational interviewing is the notion that all individuals in the precontemplation stage harbor some **ambivalence** about their behavior (despite not acknowledging negative consequences of their behavior).  At this stage of motivational interviewing, there are 2 goals: - Explore ambivalence:  The key components are open-ended questions (eg, "What are some things you like and dislike about smoking as part of your daily routine?") and reflective listening (eg, asking clarifying questions, paraphrasing). - Develop **discrepancies**:  The next phase of motivational interviewing is to help patients recognize a gap between their current smoking and deeper personal values.  This can be accomplished through provocative prompts (eg, "Tell me about a time when smoking got in the way of something important to you"). Although recommending action is premature during this stage, it is helpful to provide education on short- and long-term benefits of smoking cessation.  Some **motivational nuggets** are provided below: - Major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) - One week after smoking cessation:  The risk for acute myocardial infarction and stroke begins to decrease measurably. - One year after smoking cessation:  The risk for MACE is reduced to 50% compared to a person who continues to smoke. - Cancer risk - One year after smoking cessation:  The risk for being diagnosed with any cancer (primarily lung) decreases measurably. - Ten years after smoking cessation:  The risk for dying from cancer is reduced to 50% compared to a person who continues to smoke. - Mortality (smoking cessation improves survival at all ages) - Quitting by age 30 eliminates 100% of future attributable risk and adds 11 years to the patient's life expectancy. - Quitting by age 50 eliminates 50% of future attributable risk and adds 7 years to the patient's life expectancy. Certain conditions may resonate more personally with patients based on their fears and experiences (eg, friend recently diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). ## Precontemplation pharmacotherapy For patients in the precontemplation stage, it is reasonable to offer proactive treatment with **varenicline** while continuing general motivational interviewing.  This strategy results in a 2-fold improvement for 1-year complete smoking cessation.  Varenicline is a partial agonist of nAChR that simultaneously activates (prevents nicotine withdrawal) and inhibits (reduces cravings) the receptor.  Patients successfully treated report becoming apathetic towards smoking ("I just kind of lost interest").  Varenicline is generally continued for 12 weeks after the last cigarette. # Ready to quit The stage of being ready to quit is also referred to as the **preparation and action** stage of change and is signaled by committing to a firm quit date.  To capitalize on momentum, the quit date should be within 2 weeks from the current date.  In some cases, some patients are motivated by dates carrying special significance (eg, anniversaries, birthdays).  The goal of complete cessation (ie, zero cigarettes) should be stated explicitly (eg, "Cutting down is not enough.  You only get the benefits by quitting completely."). ## Motivational interviewing During the preparation and action phase, the 2 goals of motivational interviewing are the following: - Promote **self-confidence**:  High confidence (≥7 on a 10-point scale) in one's ability to quit enhances the likelihood for success.  Confidence can be built with strategic questions to create positive bias (eg, "You mentioned that your confidence level is 6 out of 10.  Why didn't you say 4?") and nudge patients to recognize their own internal strength. - Enact **small steps** (precessation):  Prior to the quit date, it is important to enact a set of concrete changes, including: - Consolidating smoking paraphernalia (eg, ashtrays, lighters) to be discarded on the quit date - Broadcasting their quit date to social supports (eg, family, friends, colleagues) - Identifying and replacing triggers (eg, drink morning tea instead of coffee) - Rehearsing action plans during cravings (eg, chew gum and call a friend) Advanced preparation yields better outcomes.  Ideally, patients should feel relaxed (and potentially excited) about stopping smoking on their quit date. ## Combination therapy Behavioral counseling and pharmacotherapy have synergistic effects when combined.  Compared to patients who use neither behavioral counseling nor pharmacotherapy, those who use either alone have a 40% higher likelihood of smoking cessation, and those who use both have a 170% higher likelihood of smoking cessation. **Behavioral counseling** ((Table 4)) includes motivational interviewing and other forms of behavioral counseling: - Synchronous interaction (eg, telephone calls or telemedicine visits) - Asynchronous interaction (eg, secure text messaging) - Smartphone applications - Generative artificial intelligence chatbots **Pharmacotherapy** ((Table 5)) includes nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), bupropion, and varenicline: - **NRT:**  A basal + bolus (eg, patch + gum) approach is recommended.  The basal component prevents nicotine withdrawal and is dosed based on average daily cigarettes (eg, 21-mg patch if >10 cigarettes/day).  The bolus component simulates plasma nicotine peaks during smoking and is dosed based on TTFC (eg, 4-mg gum if <30 min).  The bolus product type (eg, inhaler, lozenge, spray) can also combat oral fixation. - **Bupropion:**  In addition to being a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor, bupropion is also a nAChR agonist.  Its anorectic properties can reduce postcessation weight gain, and it may be a good choice for patients who smoke and have comorbid depression. - **Varenicline:**  This is the most effective single agent (vs NRT or bupropion alone).  A partial nAChR agonist, varenicline prevents withdrawal (agonist effect) and reduces cravings (antagonist effect).  Common adverse effects include insomnia and bizarre dreams, but these symptoms are mitigated by taking the second dose several hours before bedtime.  Despite a previous black box warning (reversed in 2016), varenicline can be safely used in patients with stable mood disorders. Bupropion and varenicline are typically started a week prior to the quit date and continued for 12 weeks after the last cigarette. Combined behavioral therapy and pharmacotherapy are recommended for most adults who smoke.  However, initial behavioral therapy alone may be appropriate for selected patients ((Figure 1)) (eg, those who smoke little or occasionally, adolescents, pregnant women). # Struggling to quit Smoking cessation is an iterative process in which relapses are common.  However, the epidemiology of cessation reveals an optimistic picture overall: - Of patients who attempt to quit, >50% eventually stop smoking permanently. - It takes an average of approximately 5 sincere quit attempts before durable cessation. - The prevalence of smoking is declining steadily. ## Motivational interviewing For patients who are struggling to quit (or facing a recent relapse), the 2 goals of motivational interviewing are to: - **Reinforce partial achievements:**  Forward-looking statements can reinspire hope in patients who may be feeling discouraged (eg, "Given your success in reducing your smoking so far, I believe in your goal of quitting completely").  Although progress should be praised, it is important to avoid settling for the lesser goal of partial cessation. - **Unlink triggers:**  Patients should list triggers and habits that prompt them to smoke (eg, morning coffee, stressful commute, bowel movement).  Next, they should propose alternate behaviors (eg, walking 500 steps, practicing deep breathing) that can distract from the urge to smoke.  It is helpful to reassure patients that most strong urges only last 5-10 minutes.  Focusing on the first cigarette of the day makes the challenge more manageable.  Postponing the first cigarette develops skills that immediately translate to the broader cessation effort. ## Managing cessation's "side effects" A range of bothersome symptoms ((Table 6)) occur after smoking cessation.  They usually resolve with supportive care and determination.  Patients should be prepared to experience: - Nicotine withdrawal:  Despite pharmacotherapy, some amount of dysphoria, restlessness, and cravings should be expected. - Weight gain:  Increased appetite postcessation leads to a 2-4 kg (5-8 lb) weight gain on average.  The benefits of smoking cessation far exceed the slight increase in BMI. - Productive cough:  Bronchial cilia are paralyzed by cigarette smoke.  As they reawaken, excessive mucus production and bronchospasm can occur.  These symptoms resolve after 2-4 weeks. # Summary Cigarette smoking is the leading cause of preventable death globally.  Tobacco use disorder is a complex process involving physiological dependency (nicotine tolerance and withdrawal) as well as psychological addiction (based on habits and social structures).  A patient's inability to delay the first cigarette upon waking is the strongest predictor of dependency.  Comorbid psychiatric disorders and cohabitation with an individual who smokes also hinder cessation efforts.  The 3 key interventions for smoking cessation are: - Motivational interviewing - Behavioral counseling (eg, proactive telephone support) - Pharmacotherapy (eg, nicotine replacement therapy, bupropion, varenicline) Motivational interviewing is appropriate during every stage of change but is most relevant for patients who are not ready to quit.  Combined behavioral therapy and pharmacotherapy are recommended for most patients who smoke and are ready to quit.  Relapse is common, but >50% of those attempting to quit eventually succeed. ​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​

The 5As of smoking cessation

Ask

Ask about tobacco use at every visit

Advise

Provide clear, personalized advice to quit

Assess

  • If willing, assist (see below)
  • If unwilling, provide motivational intervention

Assist

  • Recommend medications to reduce nicotine withdrawal symptoms

  • Repeat at every visit
  • Prescribe varenicline* to facilitate reduce-to-quit strategy

Ready to quit

  • Set a firm quit date & discard smoking paraphernalia
  • Provide behavioral counseling & engage support systems
  • Prescribe pharmacotherapy (eg, varenicline, bupropion, NRT)

Struggling to quit

  • Reinforce partial achievements
  • Identify triggers & link them to other (distracting) activities
  • Use biofeedback loops (eg, exhaled CO monitoring, gamification using mobile app)

Recently quit

  • Congratulate & offer continued support
  • Continue pharmacotherapy for 12 weeks
  • Encourage active reflection (anticipated problems, "how has your life changed?")

# Sleep Apnea

# Introduction

Apnea refers to cessation of airflow and is classified as obstructive ("can't breathe") or central ("won't breathe").  Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects approximately 1 in 5 adults.  It can have multiple complications, from workplace accidents and motor vehicle collisions to cardiometabolic disease.

# Pathophysiology

## Obstructive sleep apnea

In OSA ("can't breathe"), airflow is absent or reduced, but respiratory effort (thoracic/abdominal) is increased ((Figure 1)).  The mechanism involves intermittent collapse of the upper airway during sleep, leading to hypoxemia and sleep disruption.  Patients with OSA have risk factors that cause the airway to excessively narrow.  These include:

-   Structural abnormalities (eg, retrognathia, macroglossia).
-   Obesity and large neck circumference.
-   Older age (associated with increased tissue laxity).
-   Male sex (possibly due to differences in upper airway fat distribution, muscle activity, and hormonal factors).

These factors exacerbate physiologic pharyngeal relaxation during sleep (which normally does not cause airflow obstruction).

Preexisting OSA can be exacerbated by substances that further relax muscle tone (eg, alcohol, other central depressants, antispasmodic drugs) or conditions that increase upper airway resistance (eg, adenoid hypertrophy during respiratory infections, allergic rhinitis, nasal polyps).

## Central sleep apnea

In central sleep apnea (CSA) ("won't breathe"), airflow is absent or reduced due to a lack of respiratory effort, reflecting diminished respiratory drive ((Figure 2)).

Risk factors include:

-   Central depressants (eg, alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines).
-   Congenital hypoventilation (ie, Ondine curse).
-   Respiratory center damage (eg, prior brainstem stroke).
-   Global brain hypoperfusion (eg, severe heart failure).
-   Metabolic encephalopathy (eg, uremia).

Central depressants and congenital hypoventilation result in pure hypoventilation.  In contrast, other causes of CSA (eg, heart failure) involve abnormalities in carbon dioxide chemoreceptor sensitivity that result in a delayed response and overcorrection, causing swings between hyperventilation and hypoventilation (ie, Cheyne-Stokes breathing) ((Figure 3)).

Preexisting CSA can be exacerbated by additional insults that further destabilize ventilation patterns (eg, metabolic alkalosis, high altitude, excessive supplemental oxygen).

# Clinical features

OSA produces a range of signs and symptoms during sleep and waking hours ((Table 1)).

## Awake symptoms

OSA involves repeated respiratory interruptions, producing microarousals and frequent semiawakenings.  Patients may never achieve restorative sleep ((Table 2)), resulting in prominent daytime symptoms.

-   **Excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS)**:  EDS is the cardinal symptom of sleep apnea, present in approximately 80% of patients.  Sleepiness (inability to remain awake when required) is distinct from fatigue (subjectively low mental or physical energy).  The sleepiness is not relieved by daytime napping or a longer sleep duration.  EDS is measured using standard questionnaires such as the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, which assesses the likelihood of falling asleep during passive or sedentary activities (eg, reading, watching television, driving).
-   **Affective-cognitive symptoms**:  Many patients with sleep apnea experience mood disturbances, which can resemble major depression (eg, dysphoria, irritability).  Concentration difficulties and slowed mental processing are common, often leading to poor job or school performance.
-   **Morning headache**:  Approximately one-third of patients with significant sleep apnea have morning headaches, which may reflect cerebral vasodilation from hypoxemia and hypercapnia.  The quality resembles that of a tension headache (ie, bilateral, frontal or circumferential, dull or squeezing).

## Sleep symptoms

-   **Interrupted airflow**:  The primary nocturnal symptom is **snoring**, which can be so loud that it disturbs bedmates.  Sleep partners may also report **witnessed apneic episodes**, obvious pauses in airflow often described as alarming periods of silence between snoring.  The apneic periods may be followed by **resuscitative gasping**, a dramatic bout of snorting and heavy breathing, as the airway reopens following prolonged obstructive apnea.  This gasping alleviates acidosis and hypoxemia that accumulate during the apneic episode.
-   **Nocturia**:  Patients may report frequent awakenings to urinate, likely due to their lighter arousal threshold.  Urine production is also increased due to afferent glomerular vasoconstriction from renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation, as well as the release of increased natriuretic peptide (atrial natriuretic peptide and brain natriuretic peptide).
-   **Sleep maintenance insomnia**:  Approximately 50% of patients with OSA experience insomnia despite their EDS.  Respiratory-related arousals can awaken patients, causing stimulation that prevents them from falling asleep again.  Comorbid mood and anxiety disorders also contribute.

# Complications and comorbidities

## Chronic cardiovascular disease

OSA is associated with recurrent sympathetic surges, intermittent hypoxemia, low-grade systemic inflammation, and generalized endothelial dysfunction.  Chronic cardiometabolic and vascular manifestations include:

-   **Hypertension**:  OSA is the leading cause of secondary hypertension and is present in >75% of patients with resistant hypertension (ie, requiring ≥3 medication classes, including a diuretic).
-   **Left-sided heart failure**:  Hypertensive heart disease with diastolic dysfunction is very common and increases proportionally with OSA severity.  Untreated (or undertreated) OSA is a major precipitant of heart failure exacerbations.
-   **Atherosclerosis**:  OSA-induced vascular inflammation and stress lead to accelerated atherosclerosis, particularly carotid stenosis and coronary ischemic heart disease.
-   **Insulin resistance**:  Untreated OSA is a major driver of poor glycemic control in patients with preexisting diabetes mellitus.
-   **Erectile dysfunction**:  Penile tissue is especially susceptible to generalized endothelial dysfunction (ie, decreased nitric oxide bioavailability).  In contrast to psychogenic erectile dysfunction, patients typically report loss of nonsexual (eg, early morning) erections.

## Acute cardiovascular events

OSA is associated with neurohormonal and hemodynamic stress that can trigger acute cardiovascular events:

-   **Nocturnal arrhythmias**:  OSA provokes bradyarrhythmias, which typically occur during apnea due to high vagal tone.  It also provokes tachyarrhythmias, which typically occur during postapneic recovery periods due to high sympathetic tone and include premature atrial or ventricular contractions, atrial fibrillation/flutter, and even ventricular tachycardia.
-   **Nocturnal angina**:  In patients with preexisting coronary artery disease, OSA can induce myocardial ischemia due to increased cardiovascular stress during apnea episodes.  Angina pectoris can sometimes awaken patients from sleep.  In some cases, demand-induced non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction can occur.
-   **Heart failure exacerbations**:  Untreated (or undertreated) OSA is an important precipitant of exacerbations of left-sided heart failure.
-   **Acute ischemic stroke**:  OSA can lead to acute ischemic stroke from carotid atheroma rupture, cerebral watershed infarction (eg, hypoxemia), or cardioembolism from atrial fibrillation.

## Pulmonary hypertension

Both OSA and CSA result in periods of alveolar hypoventilation during sleep, leading to recurrent episodes of hypoxemia.  Untreated, chronic nocturnal hypoxemia can induce pulmonary vasoconstriction, which can eventually lead to pulmonary hypertension (PH) and right ventricular hypertrophy.  Manifestations include daytime exertional dyspnea, peripheral edema, and digital clubbing.

## Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) ((Table 3)) is defined by daytime hypercapnia (PaCO<sub>2</sub> >45 mm Hg) in a patient with obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m<sup>2</sup>) and no other cause of hypoventilation.  There is close overlap between OSA (present in ~90% of patients with OHS) and OHS (present in ~20% of patients with OSA).  OHS symptoms mirror those of OSA (eg, daytime somnolence, morning headaches), but signs of right-sided heart failure (eg, jugular venous distension, pedal edema) are typically more pronounced because hypercapnia-induced pulmonary vasoconstriction increases right ventricular afterload.  OHS is also associated with more significant fluid retention due to renal bicarbonate retention as metabolic compensation for hypercapnia.

## Other conditions

Other conditions that are frequently comorbid with OSA include:

-   **Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)**:  Large intrathoracic pressure swings (during obstructive apnea), especially in the supine position, encourage esophageal reflux of gastric acid.
-   **Aspiration**:  OSA increases the risk of aspiration pneumonitis (sterile inflammation) or pneumonia (bacterial contamination), especially in the setting of severe gastroesophageal reflux.
-   **Asthma**:  OSA-related systemic inflammation worsens airway edema and immune cell activation, and OSA-exacerbated acid reflux can further irritate the bronchi, resulting in worsening asthma control.
-   **Sickle cell anemia**:  Nocturnal hypoxemia can exacerbate red blood cell sickling, potentially triggering vasoocclusive pain crises or priapism.
-   **Seizure disorders**:  Sleep fragmentation lowers the seizure threshold, contributing to breakthrough seizures (especially during sleep) in patients with underlying epilepsy.

# Diagnosis

## Suspecting OSA

The most common presentations of potential OSA are EDS (reported by the patient) and snoring (reported by the patient's bedmate).  OSA is also frequently considered during work-up for resistant hypertension and PH.  Additional laboratory findings include polycythemia (eg, hematocrit >50%) from chronic nocturnal hypoxemia and metabolic alkalemia (eg, serum bicarbonate ≥28 mEq/L) from chronic respiratory acidosis in patients with concurrent OHS.

OSA pretest probability can be assessed with screening tools such as the **STOP-Bang** score ((Table 4)).  This score is applied to patients with potential symptoms of OSA.  It assigns 1 point each for **S**noring, daytime sleepiness (**T**iredness), **O**bserved apneic breathing, high blood **P**ressure, **B**MI, **A**ge, **N**eck circumference (>40 cm), and male **G**ender.  As a sensitive tool, it screens out OSA in patients with a low score (ie, ≤2 points).

## Indications for OSA testing

Sleep apnea testing is most strongly indicated for patients at risk for OSA (eg, STOP-Bang score ≥3) and either a classic presentation (eg, snoring with or without EDS) or severe unexplained cardiopulmonary disease (eg, unexplained recurrent heart failure exacerbations despite good medical adherence).

## Types of OSA testing

There are 2 forms of sleep testing:  home sleep apnea study (HSAT) and formal supervised polysomnography (PSG) performed in the laboratory.

-   **HSAT**:  In most patients, the diagnosis of OSA begins with an HSAT.  The take-home kit contains sensors that patients attach to themselves, such as a nasal airflow meter, chest and abdominal straps (to measure respiratory effort), and a continuous pulse oximeter.  HSATs can confirm OSA (ie, good specificity) but not rule it out (ie, poor sensitivity).  Because of low sensitivity, a negative HSAT requires further testing with formal PSG.
-   **PSG**:  This more comprehensive study has the benefit of direct observation for accurate determination of respiratory events.  PSG (rather than HSAT) is the preferred initial test for **mission-critical workers** (eg, airline pilots, railroad controllers).  In addition, PSG is much better at discriminating between obstructive and central events; therefore, it is also preferred for patients with suspected hypoventilation (eg, neuromuscular disease) or CSA (eg, prior stroke).

## Sleep apnea severity

The severity of sleep apnea is determined by the duration and number of apneic and hypopneic episodes detected on HSAT or PSG.

-   Apnea is a more severe event, involving complete cessation of airflow (≥10 sec). 
-   Hypopnea is a milder event, involving a partial reduction of airflow (≥10 sec) accompanied by desaturation.

The **apnea-hypopnea index (AHI)** is the average combined apneic and hypopneic episodes per hour, with an AHI ≥5 events/hr of sleep suggesting sleep apnea.  Patients may have predominant OSA (~65%), predominant CSA (~10%), or mixed sleep apnea (~25%).  Patients with severe (AHI >30 events/hr) sleep apnea are at greatest risk of complications such as cardiovascular disease and PH. 

Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) is an umbrella term encompassing OSA, CSA, upper airway resistance syndrome, and other respiratory disturbances.

# Differential diagnosis

Sleep apnea (and other SDBs) is a major cause of EDS.  However, several other disorders affecting sleep are on the differential diagnosis.

## Other medical conditions

Nocturnal asthma, GERD, and upper airway cough syndrome ((Table 5)) can cause respiratory difficulties during sleep and are sometimes bothersome enough to repeatedly awaken patients, leading to EDS.  In addition, the paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (eg, sudden awakening with a drowning or suffocating sensation) seen in left-sided heart failure can mimic gasping arousals due to obstructive apnea.

## Sleep restriction

Sleep restriction is defined as insufficient sleep (ie, <6 hr/night) due to insomnia (difficulty falling or staying asleep) or voluntary restriction (choosing to sleep less \[eg, to study\] or limited sleep opportunity \[eg, new parents\]).  These are diagnosed using the sleep history and diary, the search for precipitating factors such as life stressors, and, in the case of insomnia, underlying conditions ((Table 6)) or medications ((Table 7)).

## Sleep-related movement disorders

Repetitive and persistent nocturnal movements may disturb sleep quality and produce daytime impairment.  These disorders include restless legs syndrome (RLS) ((Table 8)), periodic limb movement disorder, and bruxism.  RLS involves unpleasant sensations of the legs (usually) or arms (rarely), such as crawling, cramping, or tingling ((Figure 4)); these can cause sleep deprivation and EDS.  RLS is associated with iron deficiency anemia, uremia, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, and certain medications (eg, dopamine antagonists, antihistamines).  RLS is diagnosed clinically based on a history of characteristic symptoms, and the diagnosis is supported with iron studies (eg, serum ferritin <75 ng/mL).

## Circadian rhythm disorders

Circadian rhythm disorders involve a mismatch between the internal circadian clock (ie, chronotype) and external schedule.  They include:

-   Shift work and jet lag disorders:  Patients have a normal chronotype but are forced into unnatural sleep schedules.
-   Advanced, delayed, or non–24-hour sleep-wake phase disorders:  Patients have an abnormal chronotype but are trying to align with conventional sleep schedules.

EDS is due to secondary insomnia caused by efforts to adapt to a normal schedule (eg, forcing an early bedtime).  Diagnosis is made by the patient's use of a sleep diary, with specific attention to differences in sleep and wake times between unstructured days (eg, weekends) versus structured days (eg, school and work days), as well as actigraphy (wrist-worn activity sensor) for objective assessment of sleep schedule.

## Disorders of wakefulness

Disorders of wakefulness are also known as central disorders of hypersomnolence and refer to EDS without an underlying sleep, circadian, or medical disorder.  They include narcolepsy (rare) and primary idiopathic hypersomnia (even rarer).

-   **Narcolepsy**:  Patients with narcolepsy ((Table 9)) have profound EDS and frequently fall asleep at inopportune times despite adequate sleep.  Features include low sleep latency, REM at sleep onset (inset of normal progression), and awake REM intrusion such as cataplexy (eg, sudden muscle atonia, often triggered by emotional stimuli such as surprise or laughter), sleep paralysis, or vivid hypnagogic hallucinations.  Diagnosis involves a Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT), which measures the time to sleep onset using electroencephalography.  Other sleep disorders causing EDS, such as sleep restriction or sleep apnea, must be ruled out first.  Sometimes, narcolepsy is diagnosed based on a low hypocretin-1 (orexin-A) level in cerebrospinal fluid.
-   Primary idiopathic hypersomnia is a rare disorder of constant sleepiness that can be diagnosed only when every other condition has been ruled out.

# Management

## General measures

Several basic interventions should be advised for all patients with OSA:

-   **Avoiding sedatives** or neuromuscular relaxants:  Alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, and antispasmodic agents (eg, cyclobenzaprine, baclofen) can contribute to OSA and should be discontinued or minimized.
-   **Reducing nasal resistance**:  Nasal obstruction increases the effort required to breathe, creating the high negative intrathoracic pressure required during inhalation that pulls on the collapsible structures of the upper airway.  Sinus irrigation and intranasal corticosteroids (eg, fluticasone) can reduce turbinate hypertrophy.  Nasal widening strips can help maintain patency.  Some patients (eg, those with severe septal deviation or nasal polyps) may require surgery.
-   **Sleep repositioning**:  Apneic breathing is most pronounced in the supine position.  If possible, patients should be encouraged to try sleeping at an incline (eg, bed wedge), laterally, or prone.
-   **Weight loss**:  Achieving a 10% weight loss correlates with a 50% reduction in AHI in obese patients with OSA.  Weight loss must be significant enough to reduce neck circumference.
-   **Smoking cessation**:  All individuals should be assisted with smoking cessation.  Compared to the general population, the benefit is larger in patients with OSA due to their elevated baseline cardiovascular risk.

## Positive airway pressure

Most patients with sleep apnea require some degree of positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy.  This can be delivered in 2 forms: continuous (CPAP) and bilevel (BPAP).

-   **CPAP**:  Supplies a constant set pressure (typically 5-15 cm H<sub>2</sub>O) throughout the respiratory cycle.  All breaths are spontaneous (ie, patient triggered).  It is most strongly indicated for most OSA and the OSA components of OHS.
-   **BPAP**:  Supplies a basal level of positive end-expiratory pressure, as well as additional inspiratory pressure support.  Breaths can be spontaneous (ie, patient triggered) or mandated (ie, backup rate).  BPAP is strongly indicated for most patients with CSA, especially those with peripheral hypoventilation (eg, neuromuscular disease, severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) or depressed respiratory drive.

Obstruction worsens during REM sleep due to muscle atonia and, in the supine position, due to gravity.  Therefore, to fully suppress AHI, the CPAP level is titrated to REM sleep in the supine position (ie, worst obstruction).  Home autotitrating CPAP devices are widely used, allowing dynamic adaptation as patient parameters (eg, weight) change.

A variety of PAP interfaces ((Figure 5)) are available (eg, full face, nasal), and the treatment response is usually immediate and dramatic.  The PAP interface is a major determinant of adherence (eg, ≥4hr/night, ≥70% nights) and should be chosen carefully.  In patients experiencing difficulty, behavioral techniques (eg, gentle positive encouragement, bedmate as ally) are usually successful.  Monitoring adherence is critical and can be performed remotely; insurance-sponsored rental machines can be repossessed if adherence is low.

## Adjunctive treatment

Some patients are unable to acclimate to PAP despite their best efforts.  Second-line treatment options include wakefulness-promoting agents (eg, modafinil, pitolisant) to enable safe daytime functioning, upper airway surgery (eg, maxillomandibular advancement, uvulopalatopharyngoplasty), and hypoglossal nerve stimulation (which causes the tongue to move forward slightly, increasing the anteroposterior diameter of the airway).

## Special populations

OSA in children ((Table 10)) is usually due to adenotonsillar hypertrophy rather than large neck circumference and obesity, which are the predominant causes in adolescents and adults.  Additional risk factors include craniofacial abnormalities (eg, retrognathia in Pierre Robin sequence) or neuromuscular laxity (eg, pharyngeal weakness in Down syndrome).  In addition to snoring and EDS, pediatric OSA can present with **atypical symptoms** such as parasomnias (eg, night terrors), enuresis, growth retardation, cognitive and behavioral indications (eg, aggression, poor scholastic performance), and hypertension.  First-line treatment is tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy (rather than CPAP).

OSA in pregnant patients presents similarly to that in nonpregnant patients.  However, management differs in two key aspects.  First, weight loss is not recommended (due to risk of fetal growth restriction).  Instead, controlling weight gain is safer.  Second, CPAP is recommended (vs lifestyle change alone) for even mild (ie, AHI <15 events/hr) or minimally symptomatic OSA because AHI tends to worsen throughout pregnancy and fetuses are particularly susceptible to hypoxemia (ie, maternal SpO<sub>2</sub> ≤90).

# Summary

Sleep apnea is common and has a significant public health impact (eg, motor vehicle collisions, cardiometabolic disease).  Obstructive sleep apnea involves repetitive pharyngeal collapse due to relaxed upper airway muscles during sleep; risk factors include obesity, older age, male gender, and large neck circumference.  Central sleep apnea involves fluctuating or depressed respiratory drive and is associated with decreased brain perfusion (eg, heart failure), central sedatives, or damage to respiratory nuclei (eg, stroke).  Both forms lead to sleep fragmentation and excessive daytime sleepiness, the cardinal symptom.  Cardiometabolic sequelae (eg, due to high sympathetic tone, systemic inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction) include hypertension and accelerated atherosclerosis.  Diagnosis requires a sleep study.  The differential diagnosis of excessive daytime sleepiness includes medical illnesses, sleep restriction disorders (eg, insomnia), sleep-related movement disorders, circadian rhythm disorders, and central disorders of hypersomnolence (eg, narcolepsy).  Treatment usually involves positive airway pressure therapy.  General measures include losing weight and avoiding central sedatives (eg, alcohol).
