articles.title: Sarcoidosis
articles.markdown:
# Sarcoidosis # Introduction Sarcoidosis is an idiopathic condition featuring granulomatous inflammation that affects multiple organ systems, with prominent involvement of the lungs and lymphatics ((Figure 1)).  Because granulomas can affect virtually any organ, sarcoidosis is a "great masquerader" in medicine. # Pathogenesis The molecular basis of sarcoidosis is not entirely clear but may reflect dysregulated cell-mediated immune response.  Although granulomas are typically a response to failed clearance of known antigens (eg, chronic fungal infection, hypersensitivity pneumonitis), no trigger has yet been identified in sarcoidosis.  Speculative antigens include beryllium, mycobacteria, and *Propionibacterium*, but no direct causation has been established. Sarcoidosis clusters among first-degree relatives, especially among individuals of African, Scandinavian, and Puerto Rican descent, supporting a genetic component.  Several human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles (eg, HLA-DRB1 variants) are common in patients with sarcoidosis.  When bound to speculative antigens (eg, beryllium), these HLA-encoded major histocompatibility complexes appear to strongly engage T-cell receptors.  Sustained coactivation of CD4+ T lymphocytes and macrophages ((Figure 2)) form compact immune cell collections known as noncaseating granulomas ((Image 1)).  Specifically, cell-mediated immunity is stimulated by production of IL-12 from activated antigen-presenting cells.  IL-12 stimulates CD4+ helper T cells to differentiate into the Th1 subtype.  Th1 cells then secrete IL-2 and interferon-γ (IFN-γ).  IL-2 stimulates the autocrine proliferation of Th1 cells and furthers Th1 recruitment.  IFN-γ activates macrophages and promotes granuloma formation.  Activated macrophages and T cells also produce tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), further assisting in leukocyte recruitment and granuloma maintenance. # Clinical presentation and diagnosis Sarcoidosis affects multiple organs, leading to protean manifestations ((Table 1)). # Pulmonary sarcoidosis Most (~90%) patients with sarcoidosis have lung involvement at diagnosis.  Pulmonary sarcoidosis has a center outwards progression, starting in the hilar lymph nodes and spreading into the parenchyma.  As the parenchymal disease worsens, the adenopathy recedes.  The typical presentation is slowly progressive dyspnea and constitutional symptoms (eg, fatigue and low-grade fever). ## Chest imaging Chest x-ray typically shows mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy ((Image 2)) and varying degrees of parenchymal infiltrations (eg, reticular opacities, nodules, consolidations, ground-glass opacities) ((Table 2)).  The parenchymal opacities usually affect the mid and upper lung zones, and they usually follow the pulmonary lymphatic network (bronchovascular bundles, interlobular septa). ## Pulmonary function tests Parenchymal infiltration can produce a restrictive pattern (ie, decreased lung volumes) with reduced diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO).  An obstructive pattern can be seen when granulomas form within or around the airways.  Mixed obstruction and restriction are also regularly observed. A subset of patients (~10%) can develop progressive fibrotic lung disease, with dense reticulation and confluent scarring and progressive restriction leading to respiratory failure. # Extrapulmonary sarcoidosis ## Cardiac Inflammation of the heart causes the majority of deaths from sarcoidosis. - **Conduction system disease:**  Granulomas can form anywhere along the conduction system, leading to atrioventricular block and bundle branch blocks. - **Cardiomyopathy:**  Granulomatous infiltration of the ventricular muscle can lead to depressed left ventricular ejection fraction, restrictive physiology (eg, fibrosis), and ventricular tachyarrhythmias with sudden cardiac death.  Specialized imaging (eg, cardiac MRI) often reveals midwall enhancement in a noncoronary distribution (reflecting patchy inflammation). ## Cutaneous - **Lupus pernio:**  a reddish violaceous induration affecting the nares and midline face, often resistant to treatment and causing disfigurement ((Image 3)). - **Erythema nodosum:**  panniculitis (immune complex deposition and inflammation of subcutaneous fat), manifesting with tender red macules, usually affecting the shins and forelegs ((Image 4)). - **Papules, nodules, and plaques:** on the shoulders, backs, arms, and buttocks. ## Ophthalmologic - **Uveitis:**  anterior (eg, iris: painful red eye) ((Table 3)) or posterior (eg, retina: painless vision loss and hazy vitreous fluid due to suspended inflammatory cells). - **Keratoconjunctivitis sicca:**  dry eyes and mouth (granulomatous destruction of tear ducts and salivary glands). ## Gastrointestinal - **Hepatomegaly:** asymptomatic liver involvement (eg, abnormal LFTs, hepatomegaly) is common and can cause cholestatic (eg, mild alkaline phosphatase elevation) followed by hepatocellular (eg, mild amniotransferase elevation) changes.  - **Splenomegaly** ## Other - **Neurologic:**  cranial nerve palsies (particularly the facial nerve \[CN VII\], can be bilateral), hypopituitarism (particularly central arginine vasopressin deficiency \[diabetes insipidus\]), and leptomeningeal spread (eg, chronic aseptic meningitis).. - **Endocrinologic:  hypercalcemia** (due to ectopic vitamin D production from granulomas), which can be accompanied by renal stones ((Figure 3)). - **Constitutional:** fever, fatigue, and malaise. - **Parotid and salivary glands:** painless swelling of the salivary and parotid glands; severe parotid gland swelling can lead to facial nerve palsy. ## Acute sarcoidosis Sarcoidosis can present acutely in 2 major febrile variants: - **Löfgren syndrome:**  fever, polyarthralgias (especially of medium-sized joints such as ankles and knees), erythema nodosum, and hilar lymphadenopathy - **Heerfordt syndrome (uveoparotid fever):**  fever, anterior uveitis (can be unilateral), bilateral parotitis and enlargement, and CN VII palsy # Diagnostic strategy A biopsy demonstrating noncaseating granulomas is generally necessary to prove sarcoidosis, but biopsy can be avoided in patients with certain pathognomonic presentations: - Asymptomatic symmetrical hilar lymphadenopathy - Acute sarcoidosis (ie, Löfgren syndrome, Heerfordt syndrome) - Lupus pernio - Imaging-suspected cardiac sarcoidosis (eg, patchy wall enhancement) In these cases, the specificity of clinical findings alone is >95% (ie, biopsy detects an alternative diagnosis in <5% of cases).  Biopsy can also be deferred for patients with overwhelming clinical suspicion based on multiple compatible findings (eg, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, hypercalcemia, erythematous skin nodules). When a biopsy is needed, the most accessible site (eg, peripheral lymph node) is sampled.  Most patients with suspected pulmonary sarcoidosis undergo bronchoscopy with fine-needle biopsy of hilar lymph nodes.  Erythema nodosum should not be biopsied because granulomas are not involved in the lesion. # Differential diagnosis ## Granulomatous lung disease When limited to the lungs, granulomas could also indicate: - **Hypersensitivity pneumonitis:**  Granulomas form in response to known inhaled organic antigens (eg, bird feather proteins, mold antigens), resulting in a mid to upper lung zone nodular infiltrates, akin to sarcoidosis.  However, in contrast to the center outward progression of sarcoidosis, thoracic lymph nodes are usually not involved (the immune response starts and stays in the alveoli). - **Silicosis:**  Granulomas form in response to known inhaled inorganic antigens (eg, talc and mineral dusts).  Patients have an obvious occupational exposure (eg, miners and quarry workers).  Similar to sarcoidosis, mediastinal adenopathy and mid to upper lung opacities are common in silicosis and pneumoconiosis.  However, the lymph nodes tend to peripherally calcify ("eggshell"), and the lung opacities coalesce into fibrotic masses. ## Granulomatous systemic disease When present in the lungs and/or extrapulmonary sites, granulomas could indicate: - **Infections:**  These include mycobacterial (eg, *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, *Mycobacterium avium* complex), fungal (eg, *Histoplasma*, *Coccidioides*), and bacterial (eg, *Nocardia*) infections.  They are usually limited to the lungs but can occasionally disseminate (eg, *Nocardia* brain abscess).  In contrast to sarcoidosis, these infections tend to produce necrotizing/caseating (eg, tuberculosis) or calcified (eg, fungal) granulomas. - **Malignancy:**  Lymphomas produce bulky lymphadenopathy, which can induce a secondary granulomatous reaction.  Unlike sarcoidosis, clonal expansion of lymphocytes is observed within the nodes. - Other conditions: - **Primary immunodeficiencies** (eg, common variable immunodeficiency, chronic granulomatous disease), which feature granulomas due to nonresolving infection and inflammation - **Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) small vessel vasculitis** (eg, granulomatosis with polyangiitis), which feature granuloma formation within the vessel wall - Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease) and other **autoimmune conditions** (eg, Sjögren syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis) ## Nongranulomatous disease Other nongranulomatous conditions are included in the differential diagnosis: - Pulmonary:  **Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis** can also cause restrictive lung disease with constitutional systems (eg, fatigue), but it does not cause lymphadenopathy, inflammation, or multiorgan system manifestations and has different findings on imaging (eg, basilar-predominant and subpleural fibrosis). - Systemic:  **Infiltrative conditions** (eg, AA amyloidosis, hemochromatosis) can cause restrictive cardiomyopathy and neurologic manifestations, but lung involvement is rare and some findings (eg, cardiac midwall enhancement) are more characteristic of sarcoidosis. These conditions are discussed in separate articles. # Management and prognosis Treatment of sarcoidosis involves various levels of immunosuppression, which are determined based on whether organ-threatening disease  is present ((Table 4)). ## Organ-threatening disease Organ-threatening disease is defined as functionally significant involvement of the skin (eg, disfigurement), lungs (eg, reduced pulmonary function), heart (eg, conduction block, cardiomyopathy), eyes (eg, uveitis), or musculoskeletal system (eg, destructive arthritis, weakness from myopathy). **Cardiac sarcoidosis** can be asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic, but it is still treated as organ threatening because it is the leading cause of sarcoidosis-related death (usually due to sudden heart block or ventricular tachyarrhythmia).  Therefore, initial screening followed by serial ECG is recommended for all patients with known sarcoidosis.  Even seemingly innocuous findings (eg, first-degree atrioventricular block, mild intraventricular conduction delay) require ongoing monitoring and possible treatment. Treatment involves systemic **corticosteroids** (eg, prednisone), usually administered for several months (often up to a year).  Refractory disease requires additional immunosuppression ranging from antimetabolites (eg, methotrexate, mycophenolate) to biologic agents (eg, anti–TNF-α monoclonal antibodies \[eg, infliximab\]) or B cell depletion (eg, rituximab). ## Non-organ-threatening disease Milder disease (eg, isolated erythema nodosum, general polyarthralgias) can be treated without systemic corticosteroids.  Most symptoms respond favorably to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or watchful waiting. # Prognosis Most patients with sarcoidosis have a favorable outcome, with approximately two-thirds experiencing spontaneous remission or a mild stable disease course that resolves with minimal therapy (eg, a course of systemic corticosteroids that is tapered off).  However, approximately one-third of patients have a chronic or progressive disease course that leads to irreversible organ damage (eg, pulmonary fibrosis, heart failure) with increased mortality. # Summary Sarcoidosis is a multisystem organ disease with protean manifestations.  Most (~90%) patients have lung involvement at diagnosis, with reticular opacities and hilar lymphadenopathy being the primary radiologic findings.  Cardiac involvement (eg, conduction system disease, cardiomyopathy) causes the majority of deaths from sarcoidosis.  In addition to other granulomatous diseases, the differential diagnosis for sarcoidosis includes nongranulomatous pulmonary (eg, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) and systemic (eg, infiltrative) conditions. ​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌

articles.title: Routine Newborn Care
articles.markdown:
# Routine Newborn Care # Introduction Routine newborn care supports a safe transition to extrauterine life, allows for early detection and treatment of serious medical conditions, and provides the family with education before being discharged home.  From delivery to discharge, the components of routine newborn care include delivery room care, prophylactic interventions, a comprehensive physical examination, nursery care, screening tests, and discharge education. # Delivery room care The first step in the evaluation of a term newborn is the assessment of the transition to extrauterine life.  This is typically performed via an Apgar score, which is a quick assessment performed at 1 and 5 minutes after birth.  Apgar is an acronym for the components that are assessed, including ((Table 1)): - Appearance (color). - Pulse (heart rate). - Grimace (reflex irritability). - Activity (muscle tone). - Respiration (rate and effort). Each component is assigned a score of 0, 1, or 2, with a total score ranging from 0 to 10.  A higher score suggests a more successful transition to extrauterine life, and scores below 7 warrant close monitoring and likely intervention (eg, placed on radiant warmer for stimulation, possible neonatal resuscitation). In general, newborns who are breathing comfortably (or crying) and have vigorous movement do not require resuscitation (ie, stimulation, clearing of secretions).  Instead, these newborns can be placed directly on the mother's chest for at least the first hour of life ("the golden hour").  This is preferred because it: - Provides warmth:  Because newborns have an underdeveloped thermoregulatory center, they are at risk for hypothermia.  Skin-to-skin contact prevents heat loss during the first hour of life. - Promotes early initiation of breastfeeding (if desired):  While on the mother's chest, newborns explore through innate reflexes (eg, rooting) and often latch to the breast spontaneously.  This practice has been shown to help prevent breastfeeding complications (eg, cracked nipples), hypoglycemia, and hyperbilirubinemia. Routine suctioning of the mouth and nose is not recommended unless obstruction is suspected. # Prophylactic interventions Prophylactic interventions help prevent potentially life-threatening conditions that may not be obvious at the time of birth.  These interventions are performed after the first hour of skin-to-skin contact and include: - Ophthalmic erythromycin:  Reduces the risk of gonococcal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) but does not prevent chlamydial conjunctivitis, both of which can be acquired via vertical transmission during delivery. - Vitamin K intramuscular injection:  Helps prevent vitamin K deficiency and subsequent bleeding (hemorrhagic disease of the newborn).  Oral vitamin K is poorly absorbed in the newborn gut and is therefore less effective than intramuscular vitamin K. - Hepatitis B vaccination:  Recommended to prevent vertical transmission.  If the mother's hepatitis B surface antigen status is positive or unknown, hepatitis B immunoglobulin is also administered. - Respiratory syncytial virus protection:  A monoclonal antibody (nirsevimab) is available to protect newborns when the prevalence of infection is high.  Alternatively, the newborn is considered adequately protected if the mother received a vaccine at least 14 days prior to delivery. # Physical examination A newborn physical examination is a systematic, head-to-toe assessment that occurs in the first 24 hours of life and can detect congenital anomalies and other medical conditions, allowing for early intervention.  Because the newborn undergoes physiologic changes during the transition to extrauterine life, there are unique physical examination findings, such as: - Vital signs:  Normal ranges for newborns include temperature 36.5-37.5 C (97.7-99.5 F), pulse 120-160/min, and respirations 40-60/min. - Head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat (HEENT):  Unique findings in newborns include open anterior and posterior fontanelles ((Figure 1)).  Cranial molding and overriding sutures are common, especially after vaginal deliveries.  Caput succedaneum ((Figure 2)) is scalp edema that crosses suture lines and can occur after difficult vaginal deliveries (eg, vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery). - Pulmonary:  Periodic breathing is a pattern of rapid breathing alternating with brief pauses (ie, 5-10 sec) in breathing.  Although concerning for caregivers, this is normal in newborns due to immature CNS respiratory centers. - Cardiac:  A transient, soft murmur is often heard due to turbulent flow through the pulmonary vasculature and/or ductus arteriosus during circulatory transition. - Abdominal:  Shows a 3-vessel umbilical cord with 2 umbilical arteries and 1 umbilical vein ((Figure 3)). - Genitourinary:  Labial or scrotal swelling is common.  In addition, withdrawal from maternal hormones can cause mild vaginal discharge or bleeding in female infants. - Chest:  Breast hypertrophy can occur in males or females due to maternal hormones. - Back:  A shallow sacral dimple without overlying hair or skin changes can be a normal finding. - Musculoskeletal:  Positional talipes (flexible clubfoot) ((Figure 4)) can occur due to restricted positioning in the uterus prior to delivery, especially in infants who are large for gestational age or have breech presentation. - Neurologic:  The arms and legs appear flexed.  In addition, Moro ((Figure 5)), rooting, extensor plantar (Babinski), and sucking reflexes are also present. - Skin:  Common findings include vernix caseosa, a natural moisturizer that protects the skin and helps with thermoregulation, and acrocyanosis ((Figure 6)), blue discoloration of the distal extremities due to vasomotor instability.  Benign neonatal rashes are common and include erythema toxicum ((Image 1)), nevus simplex, and congenital dermal melanocytosis ((Image 2)). # Nursery care ## Cardiovascular monitoring Physiologic cardiovascular and pulmonary changes that occur during the first 4-6 hours of life include: - Decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance and increase in pulmonary blood flow. - Expansion of the lungs and improved oxygenation with clearance of alveolar fluid. - Closure of fetal shunts (eg, ductus arteriosus, foramen ovale, ductus venosus) ((Figure 7)). - Increase in systemic vascular resistance. Frequent vital sign assessments ensure a successful transition and provide an opportunity to intervene, if necessary.  After this time, vital signs may be assessed less frequently. ## Feeding and weight change monitoring Breastfeeding is generally preferred because of its benefits for the infant and mother.  In the first few days after birth, mothers produce colostrum, a nutrient-dense fluid that is low in volume.  Milk production typically increases around day 3 or 4 postpartum, but may take longer.  Healthy, full-term babies can lose as much as 10% of their birth weight in the first few days of life, but they generally regain this weight within 10-14 days. Newborns are fed based on their feeding cues (eg, rooting, sucking on fingers, crying) but should be fed at least every 2-3 hours to avoid dehydration and hypoglycemia.  Breastfed newborns typically nurse for at least 15 minutes on each breast.  For bottle-fed newborns, the volume of pumped breast milk or formula per feeding gradually increases as the stomach expands.  Volumes typically start at 15-30 mL per feed and increase to 60-90 mL per feed by the end of the first week. ## Glucose monitoring Glucose measurements using a heel prick and point-of-care glucometer are obtained on newborns who show clinical signs of hypoglycemia (eg, jitteriness, poor feeding) or who are at risk for hypoglycemia (eg, preterm, infant of a diabetic mother).  Hypoglycemia screening is typically performed after the first feed and before any subsequent feeds until the infant is stable, asymptomatic, and outside the window of highest risk (typically 12-24 hours of life). ## Bathing The first bath is typically delayed until 6-24 hours after birth to prioritize breastfeeding and temperature stability. ## Urine and stool monitoring Newborns should pass urine and stool within the first 24 hours of life.  The urine is initially concentrated, resulting in pink or orange-colored stains in the diaper.  These stains represent urate crystals and are normal during the first few days.  The initial stool, known as meconium, is a thick, sticky, and black mixture of sloughed cells and mucus. ## Male circumcision Surgical removal of the penile foreskin is an elective procedure that is typically performed due to religious, cultural, and medical reasons.  Intramuscular vitamin K should be administered prior to the procedure. ## Group B *Streptococcus* monitoring Women are routinely screened for group B *Streptococcus* infection during the third trimester.  If the screening test is positive or unknown at delivery, prophylactic antibiotics are administered ≥4 hours before delivery to prevent group B streptococcal infections (eg, pneumonia, sepsis, meningitis).  If the antibiotics are administered too late or not at all, the newborn is closely monitored for signs of infection (eg, vital sign instability) for the first 36-48 hours of life. # Newborn screening tests ## Hearing screening Otoacoustic emissions or auditory brainstem response testing is performed before discharge to detect hearing loss and allow for early intervention. ## Critical congenital heart disease screening Screening may identify a defect (eg, severe aortic coarctation) that can be initially asymptomatic due to blood flow through the open ductus arteriosus but detected by a difference in preductal and postductal pulse oximetry readings as the ductus constricts after 24 hours of life.  To perform the screening, a pulse oximeter is placed on the right hand (preductal) and foot (postductal).  An oxygen saturation <95% in either region warrants further evaluation (eg, echocardiography). ## Metabolic screening Blood is collected between 24 and 48 hours after birth (ie, after feeding has been initiated) to screen for serious diseases that can have improved outcomes with early intervention (eg, phenylketonuria, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease). ## Hyperbilirubinemia screening Transcutaneous or serum bilirubin is routinely measured at 24-48 hours of life to identify those who are at risk for severe hyperbilirubinemia.  Levels may be measured sooner for those who develop jaundice in the first 24 hours of life or have risk factors (eg, hemolytic disease of the newborn).  Phototherapy ((Figure 8)) may be necessary to prevent complications of severe hyperbilirubinemia (eg, encephalopathy). # Discharge Discharge education improves newborn safety and reduces hospital readmissions because it provides parents with the necessary knowledge and skills to care for their newborn.  Discharge education topics include: - Safe sleep:  The newborn should sleep in their own crib (near parents), on their back, and without loose bedding. - Car seat:  The car seat should be rear facing until age 2. - Umbilical cord care:  The umbilical cord should be kept clean and dry; additional care (eg, alcohol, topical antibiotics) is not needed to prevent omphalitis. - Feeding:  Should be based on feeding cues and offered at least every 2-3 hours.  The newborn may initially need to be woken from sleep (eg, by changing the diaper or rubbing the feet or back) to feed. - Stool and urine:  Production gradually increases over the first few days of life, and an average of 6 voids and 3-8 stools per day is expected by the end of the first week.  Stools typically transition from meconium to a yellow, seedy consistency by the end of the first week. - Signs of illness:  These can vary but include fever, lethargy, and respiratory distress.  If these signs are present, parents should be advised to seek immediate medical evaluation. - Follow-up visit:  Should be scheduled with the newborn's primary care provider within 72 hours of discharge or sooner, depending on risk factors (eg, prematurity, excessive weight loss, hyperbilirubinemia). Newborns are typically discharged 24-48 hours after birth.  Discharge criteria include hemodynamic stability, adequate urine and stool production, multiple successful feedings by parents, completion of newborn screening tests and parental education, and scheduled newborn follow-up appointments. # Summary Routine newborn care ((Table 2)) lays the foundation for healthy growth and development.  Newborn screening and prophylactic interventions help prevent potentially severe, life-threatening conditions.  Patients are eligible for discharge after thorough evaluation, parent education, and adequate follow-up planning. ​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​

Routine newborn care

Preventive

articles.title: Respiratory Viruses
articles.markdown:
# Respiratory Viruses # Introduction Human respiratory viruses are a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, causing infection of the upper respiratory tract (eg, rhinopharyngitis) with potential lower respiratory tract (eg, bronchiolitis, pneumonia) or systemic involvement as well.  Their transmission through respiratory droplets and continuous antigenic changes make them the most concerning class of pathogens for future pandemics. # Major respiratory viruses ## Classification There are 8 categories of major human respiratory viruses: - Influenza viruses (A and B) - Coronaviruses (CoV) - Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) - Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) - Parainfluenza viruses (PIV 1,2, 3, and 4) - Rhinoviruses (RV) - Enteroviruses (EV D68 and A71) including Coxsackie viruses  - Adenoviruses (AdV) There is no standard classification system for these viruses.  Clinically, it is customary to group the winter respiratory viruses (influenza, CoV, RSV) together.  These 3 viruses cause the majority of severe complications (eg, hospitalization) and have vaccines and antiviral therapies against key strains. ## Antigenic diversity Respiratory viruses undergo constant genetic change through 2 mechanisms: - Antigenic **drift**:  Continuous accumulation of mutations causing progressive change in viral proteins.  All viruses slowly drift, gradually escaping adaptive immune recognition and making long-lasting immunization impossible (ie, "there is no cure for the common cold"). - Antigenic **shift**:  Discrete events in which viral genomes undergo reassortment ((Figure 1)) or recombination ((Figure 2)) when 2 viral strains infect the same cell.  This is particularly important for influenza A where the hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) proteins reassort, producing new virulent strains such as swine flu (H1N1) and bird flu (H5N1). # Pathogenesis All of these viruses have the common features of transmission primarily via respiratory droplets (>100 microns, fall with gravity) and aerosols (<10 microns, stay suspended).  Fomites (eg, contaminated surfaces such as door handles) are a secondary source.  On entry, the viruses fuse to and enter upper respiratory epithelial cells (eg, nasopharyngeal mucosa) via specific surface receptors (eg, influenza hemagglutinin binds to sialic acid; RSV F protein binds to nAChR). Once the virus is intracellular, a cytotoxic immune response is activated (eg, interferons, interleukins, CD8+ and NK cells, apoptosis).  Some viruses also induce direct cytopathic effects (eg, RSV creates intercellular syncytia, influenza budding causes membrane lysis) resulting in cell death.  The resulting tissue damage and inflammation coincide with onset of clinical symptoms (eg, congestion, pharyngitis) and generally correspond to PCR positivity. # Specific manifestations All major respiratory viruses produce a similar upper respiratory syndrome (eg, congestion, coryza, cough, varying systemic symptoms).  In addition to these nonspecific aspects, certain clinical features distinguish the viruses: ## Influenza virus Influenza (ie, flu) typically features a milder upper respiratory component (eg, less cough and rhinitis) but more severe systemic symptoms such as high fever, headache, intense malaise, and pronounced myalgias.  Certain populations (eg, elderly, pregnant, chronic medical conditions, nursing home residents) are at high risk of morbidity and mortality.  Death is usually not due to primary influenza infection itself but from secondary bacterial pneumonia (eg, initial improvement followed by sudden worsening). ## Coronaviruses These are divided into 2 categories.  The pandemic severe acute respiratory syndrome viruses (SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV2, and MERS-CoV) are more likely to cause severe viral pneumonia, which can progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and multiorgan failure.  The endemic coronaviruses (eg, CoV2 OC43, 229E, and NL63) mainly cause a milder illness (ie, common cold). ## RSV This is the main cause of bronchiolitis in infants and children (age <2) and a major risk factor for later development of asthma.  RSV bronchiolitis ((Table 1)) involves an upper respiratory prodrome followed by small airway obstruction (eg, wheezing, hyperinflation, retractions).  RSV is also a major cause of severe morbidity in adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (eg, acute exacerbation). ## Human metapneumovirus This is taxonomically related to RSV and is an emerging cause of severe bronchiolitis and pneumonia in high-risk populations (especially elderly, immunocompromised, and chronic lung disease).  Because its prevalence is rising, human metapneumovirus is increasingly recognized as the fourth winter respiratory virus (together with influenza, RSV, and CoV). ## Parainfluenza This is the main cause of croup ((Table 2)) (ie, laryngotracheitis) in infants and children (6 months-3 years).  Parainfluenza infection causes glottic edema, producing inspiratory stridor, a hoarse barking ("croupy") cough ((Audio 1)), and potentially severe narrowing of the upper airway (eg, steeple sign ((Figure 3))) on neck x-ray). ## Rhinoviruses These are the most common cause of the common cold overall (~40%).  RV tends to produce mild symptoms but is a frequent cause of acute exacerbations of asthma and COPD. ## Enteroviruses The nonpolio enteroviruses (mainly EV-D68 and A71) typically cause a common cold syndrome, but rarely produce neurologic infection (eg, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, acute flaccid myelitis).  Contrary to their name, fecal-oral spread and gastroenteritis are minor secondary features.  Coxsackieviruses are a subgroup of EV that cause herpangina (posterior oropharyngeal vesicles), hand-foot-mouth disease (herpangina + palm and sole lesions), pleuritis, and myopericarditis. ## Adenoviruses These viruses cause common cold with conjunctivitis (ie, pink eye), sometimes called pharyngoconjunctival fever.  Other potential manifestations include pneumonia (eg, immunocompromised) and gastroenteritis (eg, fecal-oral transmission and tropism to Peye's patches). # Diagnosis and management For rapid diagnosis, multiplex PCR testing (ie, respiratory viral panel) is now widely available at point of care, detecting all major respiratory viruses with excellent sensitivity and specificity.  Home antigen-based testing is available for influenza and SARS-CoV2 (lower sensitivity than PCR). In practice, the main decision is whether to provide antiviral treatment. - **Influenza**:  **Oseltamivir** and zanamivir are neuraminidase inhibitors ((Figure 4)) that prevent viral release.  They are indicated for high-risk populations ((Table 3)) and can be given prophylactically (ie, within 48 hours of exposure, 10-day course) or therapeutically (ie, within 48 hours of symptom onset, 5-day course).  - **SARS-CoV2**:  Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir is a boosted protease inhibitor that prevents proviral peptide cleavage.  It is indicated for mild-to-moderate (ie, outpatient) COVID-19 in patients with risk factors for progression to severe disease (eg, age ≥65, obesity, chronic medical conditions, immunosuppressed).  - **RSV**:  Nirsevimab is a monoclonal antibody against the fusion protein, preventing cell entry.  Because it is an immune globulin that neutralizes the virus extracellularly, it is also considered a form of passive immunization.  It is indicated for neonates and infants with risk factors for severe RSV bronchiolitis (eg, preterm birth, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease). All viral respiratory infections are managed with supportive care (eg, hydration, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, sinus rinses).  Acute exacerbations of underlying asthma or COPD require standard interventions (eg, bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids).  Severe croup (eg, stridor at rest) is treated with humidified air, systemic corticosteroids, and nebulized epinephrine. Prevention involves social distancing and self-quarantine, hygiene practices (eg, hand washing >20 seconds with soap and water, avoiding hand-to-face contact), personal protective equipment (eg, face masks), and vaccination (influenza ((Table 4)), RSV, SARS-CoV2). # Differential diagnosis ## Bacterial upper respiratory tract infections Viral upper respiratory tract infections involve pharyngitis due to direct infection and postnasal drainage.  However, serious bacterial upper airway infections can have a similar picture, typically with severe throat pain as their central feature: - Epiglottitis:  Mainly caused *Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Haemophilus influenzae* (type B) (now uncommon with HiB vaccine).  Epiglottitis causes inspiratory stridor akin to viral croup.  However, unlike croup, patients appear acutely toxic (eg, very high fever), have severe throat pain, and have very rapid worsening of upper airway obstruction.  Specific features of epiglottitis include drooling, muffled voice, respiratory distress, and thumb (or thumbprint) sign ((Figure 5)) on lateral neck x-ray. - Streptococcal pharyngitis:  Caused by *Streptococcus pyogenes*.  Patients typically present with pharyngitis as the dominant symptom in the background of an influenza-like illness (headache, myalgias, malaise).  Like influenza, cough is relatively absent.  However, purulent pharyngeal exudates and prominent cervical adenopathy are typically present. - Diphtheria:  Caused by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae.*  Patients have severe throat pain and a grayish, thick, fibrinous pseudomembrane adherent to the posterior pharynx and tonsils.  The pseudomembrane can cause airway obstruction and asphyxiation.  ## Bacterial community-acquired pneumonia Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is defined as an new pulmonary infiltrate in the setting of compatible lower respiratory symptoms (eg, fever, chest pain, purulent sputum).  Roughly 70% of CAP cases are bacterial and 30% are viral (mainly influenza, hMPV, and adenovirus). Distinguishing viral from bacterial CAP is important as part of the effort to promote appropriate antibiotic use ((Table 5)) and prevent bacterial resistance.  This is very difficult (and usually impossible) on initial presentation based on clinical data alone.  Although viral pneumonia classically produces diffuse interstitial infiltrates, it can also cause dense focal consolidation (like typical bacterial lobar pneumonia).  The host systemic inflammatory response (eg, fever, neutrophilic leukocytosis) is also similar, although fever and leukocytosis are generally higher with bacterial infection.  A true secondary bacterial pneumonia can develop in ~20% of patients with influenza (eg, initial improvement followed by recurrence of fever and development of productive cough) or COVID-19, further complicating the picture. **Procalcitonin** (PCT) is an acute phase reactant selectively released during bacterial (eg, induced by tumor necrosis factor-ɑ) more so than viral (eg, not induced by interferon-ɑ/ꞵ) infections.  Serum PCT effectively discriminates between bacterial (eg, PCT >0.5 ng/mL) and viral (eg, PCT <0.1 ng/mL) lower respiratory tract infections.  It is increasingly used in hospital settings but typically takes some time to result.  It is used to guide early discontinuation of empiric antibiotics for CAP, rather than the decision to start or withhold them. # Other respiratory viruses Several rarer viruses can cause potentially severe lower respiratory and multisystem involvement: ## Hantavirus  Spread by particulates from rodent feces, particularly in rural areas of the southwestern United States, hantavirus infection begins with a gastrointestinal prodrome (eg, abdominal pain, nausea) with relatively minimal upper respiratory symptoms except for cough.  However, it can rapidly progress to ARDS, circulatory failure, and hemorrhagic fever.  Florid capillary leak (eg, marked hemoconcentration), thrombocytopenia, and copious bronchorrhea are distinctive characteristics.  Diagnosis involves IgM serology.  Treatment is supportive, and patients should be referred to a tertiary extracorporeal membrane oxygenation-enabled care center if possible. ## Rubeola (measles) Spread by respiratory droplets (extremely contagious) among children in congregate settings (eg, daycare), measles typically presents with an upper respiratory prodrome consisting of "3Cs":  coryza, cough, and conjunctivitis.  Koplik spots (small, grainlike, white buccal pustules) are a specific sign.  Later, a diffuse exanthem (morbilliform eruption) appears.  Complications include encephalitis and pneumonia.  Diagnosis involves IgM serology.  Treatment is supportive, with vitamin A given in severe cases (helps to maintain mucosal integrity). ## Parvovirus B19 Spread by respiratory droplet (and vertical) transmission, parvovirus (fifth disease or erythema infectiosum) presents with a nonspecific upper respiratory prodrome and "slapped-cheek" appearance of facial erythema.  In children, it can potentially cause aplastic anemia in patients with chronic hemolysis (eg, thalassemia).  It is the most closely linked virus to seronegative reactive arthritis. # Summary Human respiratory viruses affect the upper and possibly lower respiratory tract, potentially leading to serious complications such as pneumonia and exacerbations of chronic heart and lung conditions (eg, asthma).  There are 8 major categories, with the winter respiratory viruses (influenza, coronaviruses, and RSV) constituting the bulk of morbidity and mortality.  Clinical manifestations often overlap, presenting with upper respiratory symptoms (ie, rhinopharyngitis); however, specific viruses can lead to distinct severe conditions (eg, croup with parainfluenza, bronchiolitis with RSV). Rapid diagnosis with multiplex PCR testing (ie, respiratory viral panel) is widely used.  Antiviral treatments are available for some viruses (influenza, SARS-CoV2, and RSV), while supportive care is the cornerstone of management.  Preventive measures such as vaccination, hygiene practices, and social distancing are vital to reduce transmission risks. ​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​

Bronchiolitis

Pathophysiology

  • Viral-induced inflammation of small, distal airways
  • Bronchiolar obstruction from sloughed epithelial cells, leukocytes & mucus
  • RSV most common cause

Clinical presentation

  • Age <2
  • Antecedent nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, cough
  • Wheezing & crackles, tachypnea, retractions (peak severity days 3-5)
  • ± Hypoxia, fever

Radiographic findings

  • Bilateral hyperinflation, increased interstitial markings & peribronchial cuffing

Treatment

  • Supportive (eg, nasal suctioning, hydration, supplemental oxygen)

Complications

  • Apnea (age <2 months)
  • Respiratory failure

Prevention

  • Nirsevimab for all children age <8 months

RSV = respiratory syncytial virus.

Croup (laryngotracheitis)

Pathogenesis

  • Parainfluenza virus most common
  • Transmitted via direct contact or droplet inhalation of infected respiratory secretions
  • Causes inflammation of larynx & proximal trachea

Clinical features

  • Age 6 months to 3 years
  • Viral prodrome (eg, fever, rhinorrhea)
  • Barking cough, hoarseness
  • Inspiratory stridor

Diagnosis

  • Clinical*

Treatment

  • Mild (no stridor at rest): corticosteroids
  • Moderate/severe (stridor at rest): corticosteroids + nebulized epinephrine

*Radiographs are not required for diagnosis but may show subglottic narrowing (steeple sign).

Adults at high risk for influenza complications

  • Age ≥65
  • Women who are pregnant & up to 2 weeks postpartum
  • Underlying chronic medical illness (eg, chronic pulmonary, cardiovascular, renal, hepatic)
  • Immunosuppressed
  • Morbidly obese
  • Residents of nursing homes or long-term care facilities

Indications & contraindications for influenza vaccination

Live attenuated intranasal vaccine

Indications

  • Healthy individuals age 2-49 

Contraindications

  • Age <2 or ≥50
  • Immunosuppressed patients (eg, HIV with CD4+ cell count <200/mm3) & close contacts
  • Chronic cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurologic, neuromuscular, or metabolic (eg, diabetes, renal insufficiency) diseases
  • History of Guillain-Barré syndrome following previous influenza immunization
  • Pregnant women
  • Children/adolescents receiving long-term aspirin therapy
  • Severe allergy to vaccine or its components 

Inactivated vaccine

Indications

  • Individuals age ≥6 months

Contraindications

  • Severe allergy to vaccine or its components 

Reducing antibiotic use in URI & acute bronchitis

Patient
assessment

  • Careful history & examination to rule out pneumonia & other serious illnesses
  • Patient's understanding of causes & natural history of illness

Patient
education

  • Explain expected duration & self-limited course of illness
  • Explain potential harm & lack of efficacy of antibiotics
  • Refer to infection as a "cold" or "chest cold"

Management

  • Symptomatic treatment: OTC (eg, guaifenesin, tea with honey) & prescription (eg, benzonatate) options
  • Consider delayed antibiotic prescription (ie, prescription to be filled only if no improvement occurs after predetermined time)

OTC = over-the-counter; URI = upper respiratory infection.

articles.title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)
articles.markdown:
# Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) # Introduction Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of lower respiratory tract infections across all age groups worldwide.  Nearly all children experience an RSV infection by their second birthday.  Older adults (eg, age >60), individuals who are immunocompromised, and individuals with chronic cardiac and pulmonary conditions are also particularly susceptible. # Virology ## Transmission RSV spreads through respiratory droplets (eg, via coughing, sneezing) and direct contact with contaminated surfaces followed by self-inoculation of the mucous membranes.  The virus can remain viable on surfaces for several hours.  The incubation period ranges from 2-8 days. ## Life cycle The RSV infection cycle begins when the virus attaches to the ciliated epithelial cells of the host airway using 2 surface glycoproteins: - The **F (fusion) glycoprotein** facilitates viral entry by promoting fusion of the viral lipid envelope with host cell membranes. - The **G (attachment) glycoprotein** facilitates viral entry by allowing the virus to covalently link to chemokine receptors on the cell surface. RSV replicates for several days in the bronchial epithelium.  In the cytoplasm, its RNA is transcribed into messenger RNA (mRNA) by an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.  Host ribosomes then translate the mRNA into viral proteins.  New viral particles assemble in the cytoplasm and bud from the cell, taking a portion of the lipid membrane as their envelope.  During this process, the F glycoprotein causes neighboring epithelial cells to fuse, forming large **multinucleated syncytia**. Syncytia formation disrupts cellular functions (eg, ion homeostasis) and causes apoptotic cell death and **epithelial sloughing**.  The sloughed bronchial cells land in progressively smaller airways, allowing the infection to spread into the respiratory **bronchioles**.  The obstruction and inflammation of these small airways result in characteristic wheezing and hyperinflation seen in **respiratory bronchiolitis**. # Risk factors RSV circulates endemically in communities worldwide.  There are 2 major subtypes: RSV-A and RSV-B.  The RSV-A subtype causes the majority of infections and is associated with a more severe disease course.  Like influenza, RSV infection rates peak in the winter.  Patient groups at particularly elevated risk include: - Infants age <6 months, born prematurely (<35 weeks), or with low birth weight. - Children with congenital heart disease or chronic lung conditions. - Adults age >65 or with chronic cardiopulmonary conditions (eg, heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease \[COPD\]). - Individuals who are immunocompromised (especially stem cell and lung transplant recipients). # Clinical presentation ## Viral upper respiratory infection In **older children** and **healthy adults**, RSV presents mainly as an upper respiratory tract infection.  Symptoms resemble the common cold and include nasopharyngitis, coryza, sneezing, mild cough, and occasional low-grade fever.  Infections are usually self-limiting, resolving within a week with supportive care such as hydration and rest. ## Viral bronchiolitis In **infants** and **young children** (age <2), RSV is the leading cause of **bronchiolitis** ((Table 1)), which occurs when the infection spreads to the terminal bronchioles, leading to diffuse expiratory airflow obstruction.  Manifestations include expiratory wheezing, tachypnea, and poor feeding.  In severe cases, nasal flaring and intercostal retractions can be seen; these signs indicate a high work of breathing and impending respiratory failure.  Occasionally, very young infants can present with **apnea** or sudden death.  Chest imaging can show bronchial cuffing (edema of airway walls), **hyperinflation** (eg, enlarged intercostal spaces), and small nodular tree-in-bud opacities ((Image 1)). ## Viral pneumonia In individuals who are **elderly** or **immunocompromised**, RSV may lead to community-acquired pneumonia, which occurs when the virus reaches the alveolar tissue, causing inflammation and impaired gas exchange.  Symptoms include fever, labored breathing, lethargy, and cyanosis.  Chest imaging typically shows patchy interstitial and alveolar opacities ((Image 2)). Secondary bacterial pneumonia is a potential complication following respiratory viral infections (eg, influenza, RSV) due to severe damage to the respiratory epithelium.  Signs of secondary bacterial pneumonia include new fever after initial defervescence, purulent sputum, and increasing respiratory distress.  Common bacterial pathogens involved in these superinfections include *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Staphylococcus aureus*. ## Exacerbations of chronic disease RSV is an important infectious trigger for acute decompensation of chronic pulmonary and cardiac conditions, especially in older adults. - Pulmonary complications include acute exacerbations of asthma or COPD. - Cardiac complications include acutely decompensated heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, and atrial tachyarrhythmias. During the winter respiratory virus season, RSV accounts for approximately 10% of hospitalizations for COPD or heart failure. # Management ## Diagnosis RSV infection is usually confirmed by PCR testing.  PCR has high sensitivity and specificity, and PCR testing for RSV is typically included as part of a multiplex respiratory viral panel that can detect other viruses (eg, influenza, rhinoviruses).  In many settings, multiplex PCR is routinely performed in adults hospitalized with lower respiratory tract infections.  Confirming RSV is always recommended for immunocompromised patients (particularly stem cell or lung transplant recipients) because they are likely to benefit from antiviral therapy (eg, ribavirin).  In severe cases, a negative upper respiratory sample (eg, nasal swab) should be followed by lower respiratory sampling (eg, bronchoscopy fluid). RSV antigen tests (for detection of the F glycoprotein) are also available but are only validated for younger patients (age <20), who tend to have a high nasal viral load.  Viral serology (eg, RSV IgM) and culture are not clinically useful. ## Supportive care Most **immunocompetent** patients recover spontaneously with supportive care such as adequate hydration and, as needed, short-acting bronchodilators (eg, albuterol) for wheezing.  Adjunctive treatments are administered to patients with respiratory or cardiac comorbidities: - Obstructive lung disease:  Systemic glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone) are indicated for patients with acute exacerbations of asthma or COPD.  In patients with otherwise intact immunity, glucocorticoids can reduce airway inflammation without significantly compromising the defense against viral replication.  Inhaled glucocorticoids are also often added; either beclomethasone or ciclesonide is particularly effective because their microfine particle size (diameter <2 microns) allows them to settle into the terminal bronchioles (eg, to alleviate bronchiolitis). - Heart failure:  Diuretics and afterload-reducing agents may be used for patients with acutely decompensated heart failure.  RSV-exacerbated heart failure is usually due to increased cardiac demand from systemic inflammation, hypoxemia, and work of breathing.  However, less common precipitants include RSV-induced myocarditis or acute ischemic events (eg, myocardial infarction). ## Antiviral therapy Antiviral therapy with **ribavirin** is effective against RSV.  Ribavirin is a nucleoside analogue that inhibits the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase of RSV.  Treatment is most strongly indicated for patients who are **immunocompromised**, particularly hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) or lung transplant recipients.  In addition to ribavirin: - HSCT recipients typically receive pooled intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) to transfer passive humoral immunity.  Specific hyperimmune RSV immunoglobulin is used in some cases. - Lung transplant recipients typically receive systemic corticosteroids to empirically treat acute rejection, which is difficult to differentiate from (and often precipitated by) the underlying viral infection. Oral and intravenous ribavirin are most commonly used.  Its major toxicity is dose-dependent hemolytic anemia (likely caused by the accumulation of ribavirin triphosphate, which causes oxidative stress in red blood cells).  Nebulized ribavirin is also available and offers maximal pulmonary drug concentrations; however, it carries a risk of bronchial irritation and bronchospasm due to drug crystallization in the airways. # Complications RSV bronchiolitis can lead to acute and long-term complications: - Acute:  Infants age <2 months and those born prematurely or with cardiopulmonary disease are at greatest risk for apnea and/or respiratory failure during peak symptoms.  Older, full-term, healthy infants and young toddlers typically recover without acute complications. - Long-term:  RSV bronchiolitis that requires hopsitalization is associated with the development of recurrent wheezing in early childhood in up to 30% of patients.  Additionally, there may be an increased risk of asthma in later childhood and adulthood in children hospitalized with RSV bronchiolitis; however, the causality is unclear.  The increased risk of recurrent wheezing likely reflects direct airway damage or inflammation from the virus, whereas the association with asthma may instead reflect a shared genetic or environmental predisposition.  # Prevention ## Immunoprophylaxis (passive immunization) **Nirsevimab** is a monoclonal antibody that neutralizes the F glycoprotein of RSV, thereby preventing viral entry into host cells.  Nersevimab is indicated for: - **All infants age <8 months** entering their first RSV season (unless the mother received the RSV vaccine ≥14 days before delivery, allowing transplacental passage of maternal antibodies). - High-risk infants age ≥8 months entering their second RSV season.  High-risk conditions include congenital heart disease, cystic fibrosis, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia (ie, lung disease of prematurity). The half-life of nirsevimab is approximately 6 months, covering the infant's first RSV season.  Most infants have developed natural protective titers by their second RSV season, so a second dose is only recommended for patients with high-risk conditions.  Palivizumab is an older-generation monoclonal antibody that can be substituted if nirsevimab is not available. ## Vaccination The F glycoprotein is the primary target for vaccine development.  Antigenic drift, particularly in the G glycoprotein, contributes to the virus's ability to evade host immunity and reinfect individuals. There are currently 3 approved RSV vaccines (2 antigen-based vaccines against the F glycoprotein and 1 mRNA-based vaccine).  Vaccination is indicated for: - All adults age ≥75. - Adults age ≥60 at risk for severe RSV (eg, asthma, COPD, heart failure, ischemic heart disease). - Adults age ≤59 on an individual basis. A small excess risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome has been identified with these antigen-based vaccines (number needed to harm ≈ 125,000). ## Infection control Infection control measures include standard precautions for winter respiratory viruses (eg, frequent handwashing, physical distancing, masking).  In the hospital, infection control measures include droplet isolation precautions (eg, private room, standard surgical mask, gowns, gloves) ((Table 2)). # Summary Respiratory syncytial virus is a major cause of lower respiratory tract infections, particularly affecting infants, older adults, and individuals who are immunocompromised.  Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets or contact with contaminated surfaces, with symptoms ranging from a mild common cold in healthy adults, respiratory bronchiolitis (eg, wheezing, hyperinflation) in infants and young children, and viral pneumonia in elderly patients and in patients who are immunocompromised.  Respiratory syncytial virus infections are an important trigger for acute exacerbations in chronic cardiopulmonary conditions (eg, asthma, chronic obstructive disease, heart failure, and ischemic heart disease).  Diagnosis is typically confirmed via PCR testing, and treatment is largely supportive.  Antiviral therapy (eg, ribavirin) is usually reserved for patients who are immunocompromised.  Prevention includes universal immunoprophylaxis with monoclonal antibodies (eg, nirsevimab) for all infants, vaccination for older adults and individuals with underlying conditions, and standard infection control measures during the winter respiratory virus season. ​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​

Bronchiolitis

Pathophysiology

  • Viral-induced inflammation of small, distal airways
  • Bronchiolar obstruction from sloughed epithelial cells, leukocytes & mucus
  • RSV most common cause

Clinical presentation

  • Age <2
  • Antecedent nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, cough
  • Wheezing & crackles, tachypnea, retractions (peak severity days 3-5)
  • ± Hypoxia, fever

Radiographic findings

  • Bilateral hyperinflation, increased interstitial markings & peribronchial cuffing

Treatment

  • Supportive (eg, nasal suctioning, hydration, supplemental oxygen)

Complications

  • Apnea (age <2 months)
  • Respiratory failure

Prevention

  • Nirsevimab for all children age <8 months

RSV = respiratory syncytial virus.

of droplet precautions

Personal protective
equipment
