articles.title: Pulmonary Vasodilator Therapy
articles.markdown:
# Pulmonary Vasodilator Therapy # Introduction Pulmonary vasodilator therapy plays a central role in management of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), a disorder marked by elevated pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) due to vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling.  Pulmonary vasodilators include nitric oxide potentiators, endothelin receptor antagonists (ERAs), and prostacyclin agonists.  This article reviews the mechanisms of action, clinical indications, adverse effects, and a general treatment framework for these agents. # Relevant physiology ## Normal pulmonary vascular function PVR is determined by the balance between endogenous pulmonary vasodilators and vasoconstrictors: - **Vasodilators**:  Nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin (PGI2). - **Vasoconstrictor**:  Endothelin-1 (ET-1). These mediators are synthesized by the pulmonary artery **endothelial cells** and diffuse from the endothelium (intima) to the adjacent smooth muscle cell layer (media), where they cause dilation or constriction. The pulmonary circulation receives the same cardiac output as the systemic circulation but distributes it through a smaller vascular bed (1/6 the size relative to systemic).  To prevent a rise in pressure within this smaller circulation (ie, pulmonary hypertension \[PH\]), vascular resistance must be inherently low.  This is normally achieved through **constant vasodilation** via NO and PGI2. ## Pulmonary arterial hypertension PAH is characterized by abnormal pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling, which both increase PVR. - **Vasoconstriction**:  Loss of vasodilators (decreased NO and PGI2) and upregulation of vasoconstrictors (increased ET-1) shifts the balance toward vasoconstriction, resulting in elevated pulmonary artery pressure.  This aspect of disease is addressed by **pulmonary vasodilator therapy**. - **Remodeling**:  As PAH progresses over years, the vessels are narrowed and eventually obliterated due to intimal thickening, smooth muscle proliferation, and fibrotic or inflammatory cell infiltration ((Figure 1)).  In these late stages, vasodilators are less effective (because resistance is dominated by structural remodeling).  Therapy with **antiremodeling agents** (eg, transforming growth factor-β \[TGF-β\] modulators, tyrosine kinase inhibitors) becomes more relevant. In addition to PAH (ie, primary PH), PH can also be secondary to other conditions such as left heart disease, lung disease, chronic thromboembolism, or systemic and multifactorial causes ((Table 1)).  Because the pulmonary vasculature is not the primary site of pathology, pulmonary vasodilator therapy is less effective The pulmonary vasodilators discussed in this article are mainly indicated for treatment of primary PAH. # Pulmonary vasodilators Pulmonary vasodilators fall into 3 classes ((Figure 2)): - NO potentiators. - Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) inhibitors. - Soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) stimulators. - ERAs. - Prostacyclin analogues. All these pulmonary vasodilators are **endothelium-dependent** because the mediators they affect (eg, NO, ET-1) are synthesized by endothelial cells. In addition to these 3 classes, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (DHP CCBs)—which are endothelium-independent vasodilators that directly relax smooth muscle—are used in some patients with PAH. These drug classes are discussed in greater detail below. ## Nitric oxide potentiators NO is an endothelium-derived vasodilator that stimulates sGC, resulting in formation of cyclic GMP, which serves as a second messenger for smooth muscle relaxation ((Figure 3)).  This pathway is targeted by: - **PDE5 inhibitors**, which include **sildenafil** and **tadalafil**.  PDE5 inhibitors block degradation of cyclic GMP, increasing the bioactivity of NO.  They are first-line agents for PAH, in conjunction with ERAs.  Although these medications are also used for erectile dysfunction, they are administered at significantly higher doses for PAH. - **sGC stimulators**, which include **riociguat** and **vericiguat**.  They enhance NO-sGC binding and also increase sGC enzyme activity independently of NO, leading to accelerated cyclic GMP production.  They are indicated for PAH and chronic thromboembolic PH (CTEPH). Adverse effects are similar to antianginal nitrates, and include headache, flushing, and potential systemic hypotension.  PDE5 inhibitors and sGC stimulators should never be combined with each other, or with other nitrates, due to risk of precipitating severe systemic vasodilation and **hypotension**.  Other rare but serious side effects of PDE5 inhibitors include priapism and cyanopsia (blue-green visual tint, due to off-target inhibition of retinal PDE6). ## Endothelin receptor antagonists ET-1 is an endothelium-derived vasoactive peptide that binds to the ET-1 receptor on smooth muscle cells.  It promotes vasoconstriction and smooth muscle proliferation.  ERAs block these effects, and include **bosentan**, **ambrisentan**, and **macitentan**.  They are first-line agents for PAH in conjunction with PDE5 inhibitors. ERAs have a wide range of adverse effects including hepatotoxicity (requiring regular liver enzyme monitoring), fluid retention and peripheral edema, and teratogenicity.  The mechanism of these toxicities is unclear but probably reflects the wide distribution of ET-1 receptors in the biliary tree and renal tubules. ## Prostacyclin agonists **PGI****2** is an endothelium-derived metabolite that binds to the prostacyclin (IP) receptor on smooth muscle cells.  Activation of the IP receptor increases intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP), which promotes vasodilation and inhibits smooth muscle proliferation.  This pathway is targeted by: - **Prostacyclin analogs**, which include **epoprostenol**, **treprostinil**, and **iloprost**.  These drugs mimic endogenous PGI2.  They are available in parenteral (intravenous, subcutaneous), oral, and inhaled formulations. - **Selective IP receptor agonists**, such as **selexipag**, which directly activate the prostacyclin receptor without structural similarity to prostacyclin itself. These agents are typically reserved for **advanced PAH** as a third drug class in patients already taking PDE5 inhibitors and ERAs.  Oral prostacyclin agonists (are usually initiated first, with escalation to continuous parenteral therapy in patients who continue to deteriorate despite maximal oral therapy. Common adverse effects are related to systemic vasodilation (eg, headache, flushing, hypotension).  Jaw pain is a distinctive and frequent side effect, thought to reflect masseter muscle vasodilation.  Intravenous prostacyclins are delivered through indwelling vascular catheters, which are susceptible to infection (eg, bacteremia) and thrombosis. ## Calcium channel blockers DHP CCBs antagonize L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle, producing vasodilation.  They include **amlodipine** and **nifedipine**.  In PAH, their use is limited to a small subset (5%-10%) of PAH patients with a **vasoresponder phenotype** identified during right heart catheterization.  The test is used to evaluate for high levels of intrinsic smooth constriction that can be alleviated by calcium blockers.  Patients who exhibit vasodilation in response to calcium blockade are most likely to benefit from CCB therapy.  Most commonly, this includes younger female patients with idiopathic IPAH and primary Raynaud phenomenon. DHP CCBs are administered at significantly higher doses than those used for systemic hypertension (eg, amlodipine 30 mg/day vs typical 10 mg/day).  They should be avoided in nonvasoreactive PAH because they can induce significant **systemic hypotension** without improving PVR. # Antiremodeling agents As PAH progresses, vascular remodeling overtakes vasoconstriction as the main driver of PVR, rendering vasodilators less effective.  Antiremodeling therapies decrease proliferation (or increase apoptosis) of vascular wall cells, which improves the patency of the pulmonary vessels. ## Activin/TGF-β inhibitor **Sotatercept** is a soluble fusion protein that binds to activins and related proteins in the TGF-β superfamily.  This pathway drives pathologic vascular cell proliferation, apoptosis-resistance, and fibrosis seen in PAH.  It is approved for PAH to be used in addition to patients already receiving background triple therapy (ie, PDE5i + ERA + prostacyclin).  In such patients, sotatercept can **reverse** the vascular remodeling and is associated with decreased mortality. ## Other therapeutics Other therapies that have entered clinical stage trials include **receptor tyrosine kinase** inhibitors (eg, imatinib) and **bone morphogenic protein** modulators that affect endothelial and smooth muscle proliferation. # Principles of treatment ## Patient selection Pulmonary vasodilator therapy is: - Most appropriate for patients with **PAH (group 1)** because the primary lesion affects the pulmonary arteries themselves. - Used selectively for certain patients in PH groups 4 (CTEPH) and 5 (eg, sickle cell disease, sarcoidosis) in whom PH may involve microvascular dysfunction or endothelial injury that may be at least partially responsive to vasodilator therapy. - Generally contraindicated in PH groups 2 (left heart) and 3 (lung).  In group 2, they may worsen pulmonary congestion by increasing venous return to a failing left heart.  In group 3, they can exacerbate hypoxemia by increasing perfusion to poorly ventilated lung regions. Despite these risks, pulmonary vasodilators are frequently overprescribed, particularly for group 2 (~70% of PH in the United States). ## Regimens A general framework for PAH pharmacotherapy is as follows: - The small minority of patients (~5%) with a vasoresponder phenotype can be treated with a DHP CCB (eg, amlodipine, nifedipine) alone. - Most patients with PAH are initiated on **dual therapy**, typically with **PDE5i + ERA** (eg, tadalafil and macitentan).  Several large trials confirmed that initial dual therapy is superior to sequential therapy for reducing right ventricular (RV) failure. - Next, a **prostacyclin agonist** is added (ie, **triple therapy**) for patients with high-risk features or with functional decline (eg, resting tachycardia, recurrent hospitalization for RV failure). - Next, **sotatercept** (anti-remodeling agent) is added to existing triple therapy for patients with refractory PAH at high risk of death.  Such patients are typically already evaluated and listed for lung transplantation. Response to therapy is monitored clinically (eg, improved exercise capacity, decreased B-type natriuretic peptide levels). ## Limitations Despite their benefits, pulmonary vasodilators are limited by high cost and treatment complexity. - High cost:  Pulmonary vasodilators are expensive (eg, >$100,000/year), with patients often relying on manufacturer assistance programs, although generic options (eg, sildenafil, treprostinil) have made them more accessible. - Treatment complexity:  Successful therapy requires high patient literacy, strong social support, and close oversight, typically at accredited PH centers.  Use of parenteral prostacyclins is particularly risky because they require refrigeration, manual preparation of each dose, and pump training.  Their short half-life makes them prone to rebound vasoconstriction (eg, rapid and potentially fatal increases in PVR) with even brief treatment interruption. # Summary Pulmonary vasodilator therapy is a cornerstone for management of pulmonary arterial hypertension, a condition marked by pulmonary vasoconstriction and occlusive remodeling.  Pulmonary vasodilator drugs enhance vasodilator pathways (nitric oxide, prostacyclin) or block vasoconstrictor pathways (endothelin).  They include 3 major classes: nitric oxide potentiators (phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators), endothelin receptor antagonists, and prostaglandin agonists.  Most patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension are initiated on dual therapy with a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor and an endothelin receptor antagonist, whereas prostacyclin agonists are typically added for those with high-risk features.  Although vasodilators effectively counteract vasoconstriction, their benefit diminishes in advanced pulmonary arterial hypertension, where irreversible vascular remodeling predominates. ​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌

Classification of pulmonary hypertension

Pulmonary arterial
hypertension
(group 1)

  • Primary change in pulmonary arteries
    • Hereditary (eg, BMPR2 mutation)
    • Connective tissue disease (eg, RA, SS)
    • HIV infection
  • Treatment targeted at endothelial dysfunction

Pulmonary
hypertension
(groups 2-5)

  • Secondary to another disease process
    • Left-sided heart failure (group 2)
    • Chronic lung disease/hypoxia (group 3)
    • Chronic pulmonary thromboembolism (group 4)
    • Other (eg, sarcoidosis) (group 5)
  • Treatment aimed at underlying disease

RA = rheumatoid arthritis; SS = systemic sclerosis.

articles.title: Pulmonary Physiology: Respiratory Neurobiology
articles.markdown:
# Pulmonary Physiology: Respiratory Neurobiology # Introduction Respiratory neurobiology involves the structures and feedback mechanisms that determine breathing patterns and minute ventilation.  Respiratory control can be thought of as a central pattern generator (CPG) (brainstem) with both voluntary inputs (eg, cortical override) and involuntary inputs (eg, chemoreceptors). # Central pattern generator The respiratory CPG is a group of brainstem structures that work together to create a normal, unconscious (automatic) **tidal breathing pattern**.  The CPG consists of the medullary and pontine respiratory centers ((Figure 1)). ## Medullary respiratory center The medullary respiratory center sets the tidal **respiratory rate**.  It contains: - A **pacemaker** nucleus (the pre-Bötzinger complex):  This structure consists of thousands of neurons that spontaneously depolarize (eg, If sodium leak channel), establishing **automaticity**. - A **motor** nucleus (the ventral respiratory group \[VRG\]):  It receives rhythm input from the pacemaker and sends output to the **phrenic motor nucleus** (C3-5) to initiate diaphragm contraction and inspiratory effort; it also projects motor neurons to the accessory muscles of breathing. - A **sensory** nucleus (the dorsal respiratory group \[DRG\]):  It receives **afferent signals** from chemoreceptors (eg, pH, CO2, O2) and mechanoreceptors (eg, pulmonary stretch).  The DRG integrates these signals and accelerates or decelerates the pacemaker nucleus, subsequently quickening or slowing the respiratory rate. ## Pontine respiratory center The pontine respiratory center sets the **inspiratory time**.  It consists of the pneumotaxic and apneustic centers.  They have opposing effects on the VRG, which activates the diaphragm. - The **pneumotaxic center** shortens inspiration (tonic effect). - The **apneustic center** prolongs inspiration. The balance between them determines the transition between inspiration and expiration.  Under normal conditions, inspiration (I) lasts half as long as expiration (E) does (ie, I:E = 1:2) because the pneumotaxic center dominates.  Obstructive conditions are associated with longer expiration (eg, I:E = 1:3), whereas restrictive conditions are associated with longer inspiration (eg, I:E = 1:1). # Modulators of the central pattern generator The unconscious CPG can be modulated by voluntary control (eg, cortex), emotional responses (eg, limbic system), and feedback from chemoreceptors (pH, CO2, O2) and mechanoreceptors. ## Cortical and limbic input - Cortical input (voluntary):  Respiratory patterns can be controlled by the premotor and motor cortices (eg, speech, singing).  However, if pH drops or CO2 levels rise excessively (eg, prolonged breath holding), the medullary respiratory center overrides the cortex, triggering an involuntary breath. - Limbic input (involuntary):  Strong emotions (eg, fear, excitement) can cause involuntary changes in respiration via the **amygdala** and other limbic structures (cingulate cortex, hypothalamus) that project to the respiratory centers. ## Chemoreceptor input Chemoreceptors regulate respiration by detecting changes in pH, CO2, and O2 and adjusting breathing patterns accordingly ((Table 1)).  In order of importance: - **Arterial pH (H****+****)** and **CO****2**:  These are sensed by **peripheral** chemoreceptors (aortic arch, carotid bodies), which send afferents to the DRG via the vagus nerve (CN X) (aortic arch) and the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) (carotid body) ((Figure 2)).  Low pH (acidosis) or high CO2 (hypercapnia) stimulates respiratory rate and depth. - **Low arterial pH** is a **more powerful** stimulus than CO2 and usually causes marked dyspnea.  For example, during diabetic ketoacidosis (eg, pH 7.28), patients continue to hyperventilate (eg, Kussmaul breathing) despite low PaCO2 (eg, 17 mm Hg).  In addition, unlike pH receptors, CO2 chemoreceptors become desensitized with chronic hypercapnia and renal compensation (eg, obesity hypoventilation syndrome). - **Central** chemoreceptors in the medulla sense CO2 **indirectly** by detecting changes in H+ concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).  When CO2 diffuses into the CSF, it creates H+ (ie, CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ **H****+** + HCO3) with the help of carbonic anhydrase. - **Arterial O****2**:  This is also sensed by peripheral chemoreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid bodies.  Low O2 (hypoxemia) stimulates respiratory rate and depth.  Compared to pH and CO2, hypoxemia is a weaker stimulus and generally does not cause significant dyspnea. ## Mechanoreceptor input Breathing patterns can be modulated by afferents from mechanoreceptors in the lungs. - **Pulmonary stretch receptors** are mechanosensitive ion channels located primarily in the airway wall, blood vessels, and pleural surfaces.  The key receptors, **Piezo1** and **Piezo2**, convert mechanical deformation into electrical signals (ie, piezoelectric effect).  When the lungs expand, these receptors send inhibitory signals to the medullary respiratory center, terminating inspiration to **prevent lung overinflation** (Hering-Breuer reflex). - **Alveolar juxtacapillary receptors (C fibers)** are chemosensitive and mechanosensitive sensory nerves located in the alveolar septa near pulmonary capillaries.  They respond to pulmonary congestion (eg, edema), inflammation, and noxious stimuli.  Activation triggers afferent signals via the vagus nerve to the medullary respiratory center, producing a **sensation of dyspnea** and reflex tachypnea. # Abnormal respiratory patterns ## "-pneas" Abnormal breath types are formally referred to by the suffix "-pnea": - Tachypnea refers to an abnormally rapid respiratory rate (eg, >20/min at rest). - Hyperpnea refers to an abnormally deep inspiratory volume. - Bradypnea refers to an abnormally slow respiratory rate (eg, <12/min at rest). - Hypopnea refers to an abnormally shallow inspiratory volume. - Apnea refers to a complete cessation of airflow. In practice, breathing patterns are often described by their gross appearance and tend to have classic associations.  For example, rapid deep breathing (ie, Kussmaul) is associated with metabolic acidosis; slow, shallow breathing is associated with respiratory depression (eg, opioid intoxication). ## Kussmaul Kussmaul respiration is a pattern of rapid, deep breathing associated with acute **metabolic acidosis** (eg, diabetic ketoacidosis, toxic alcohol ingestion).  It represents respiratory compensation through hyperventilation to induce respiratory alkalosis ((Video 1)). ## Cheyne-Stokes Cheyne-Stokes respiration is a periodic breathing pattern that **alternates** between hyperventilation (rapid, deep breathing) followed by hypopnea (shallow, slow breathing) or complete apnea.  The cycle repeats every 30 seconds to 2 minutes.  It is associated with: - Severe **heart failure**. - Stroke or diffuse brain injury. - Metabolic derangements (eg, uremia). Normally, rising arterial CO2 levels immediately signal the medulla to increase minute ventilation to quickly blow CO2 back down to normal ranges.  In Cheyne-Stokes respiration, **delayed feedback** from central chemoreceptors (eg, sluggish circulation in heart failure) causes CO2 to rise excessively.  This is followed by overcorrection via hyperventilation, causing CO2 levels to drop too low.  The low CO2 levels suppress the chemoreceptors, triggering hypoventilation or apnea until CO2 builds up again.  This restarts the cycle of apnea followed by gradually increasing and then decreasing (crescendo-decrescendo) tidal volumes  ((Video 2)). ## Ondine curse Ondine curse refers to central hypoventilation due to congenital (eg, *PHOX2B* mutation) or acquired lesions (eg, tumor) affecting the **medullary** respiratory center.  Automatic involuntary respiration is lost, particularly during sleep.  Sensitivity to acidosis or hypercapnia is also severely blunted or lost entirely.  Constant voluntary effort is required (ie, the patient must always remember to breathe).  It usually requires lifelong mechanical ventilation. ## Apneustic breathing Apneustic breathing is a pattern of prolonged inspiration, a long pause, and a very short expiration, which is associated with **pontine damage** (eg, herniation).  The pons regulates the inspiratory time through its pneumotaxic versus apneustic centers. ## Ataxic (Bitot) breathing Ataxic (Bitot) breathing involves erratic, unpredictable breaths that vary significantly in frequency, duration, and depth.  It is associated with **widespread damage** to multiple areas of the CPG (eg, pons, medulla). ## Agonal breathing Agonal breathing is a disorganized respiratory pattern that occurs in patients **near death**; it is characterized by irregular gasping or guppy-like breaths.  It results from generalized dysfunction of all respiratory control centers and is often accompanied by loss of upper airway tone (eg, gurgling, death-rattle). # Summary The brainstem's central pattern generator, consisting of medullary and pontine centers, establishes an automatic tidal pattern that can be modified by voluntary and involuntary inputs.  The medullary respiratory centers (pre-Bötzinger complex, dorsal and ventral respiratory groups) set the native respiratory rate, whereas the pontine centers (pneumotaxic and apneustic centers) determine inspiratory duration.  Tidal breathing can be modulated by voluntary control (eg, cortex), emotional responses (eg, limbic system), and feedback from chemoreceptors (pH, CO2, O2) and mechanoreceptors (eg, muscle spindles).  Abnormal patterns include Cheyne-Stokes respiration (eg, heart failure), Kussmaul respiration (eg, metabolic acidosis), and apneustic breathing (eg, pontine injury). ​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​

articles.title: Pulmonary Physiology: Respiratory Mechanics
articles.markdown: # Pulmonary Physiology: Respiratory Mechanics # Introduction Respiratory mechanics describe how pressure, volume, and flow are related to each other in the respiratory system.  This article integrates principles of physics and physiology to discuss the interaction between the lungs and chest wall, the process of normal tidal respiration, and the work of breathing. # Lungs and chest wall The respiratory system consists of the **lungs** and **chest wall**, which are considered **independent** elements because they are anatomically separated.  Changes in the lungs do not affect the intrinsic properties of the chest wall, and vice versa.  However, changes in either affect the entire respiratory system in an additive manner. ## Functional residual capacity The lungs and chest wall have opposing natural tendencies: - The lungs have a tendency to recoil inward (collapsing force) due to the elastin content of lung tissue. - The chest wall has a tendency to recoil outward (expanding force) due to the curvature of the ribs and intrinsic tension in the intercostal muscles. The lungs pull the chest wall inward, and the chest wall pulls the lungs outward.  The point where these forces balance each other is the **functional residual capacity (FRC)** ((Figure 1)).  FRC is the natural resting state of the respiratory system in the absence of voluntary effort.  It is equivalently described as the volume of air remaining in the lungs after normal passive exhalation. Tidal breathing begins from FRC because it minimizes energy expenditure.  Maintaining lung volumes above or below FRC requires additional muscular effort, which can be simulated—holding the breath above FRC requires effort to counter inward lung recoil, similar to keeping a spring stretched out.  Holding the breath below FRC requires effort to counter outward chest wall recoil, similar to compressing a spring.  Pathologic conditions can increase or decrease FRC.  FRC decreases when lung recoil increases (eg, interstitial fibrosis) or when chest wall recoil decreases (eg, pectus excavatum).  Conversely, FRC increases when lung recoil decreases (eg, emphysema) or when chest wall recoil increases (eg, pectus carinatum \[rare\]). ## Respiratory system compliance Compliance (C) describes how volume (V) changes in response to pressure (P) (ie, C = ΔV/ΔP).  Noncompliant (stiff) objects experience minimal change in volume when pressure is applied.  Normal respiratory system compliance (CRS) is 100 mL/cm H2O (each additional centimeter of water of pressure should inflate the lungs by 100 mL). Several disease states can alter CRS by affecting the lungs or chest wall: - Lung compliance (CL) decreases with interstitial stiffening (eg, pulmonary fibrosis) or alveolar filling processes (eg, pulmonary edema, pneumonia).  It increases with emphysema. - Chest wall compliance (CCW) decreases with thoracic cage deformities (eg, kyphosis), arthritis (eg, costochondral joints), extreme obesity, restrictive pleural disease (eg, adhesions, fibrothorax), or rare dystonic drug reactions (eg, serotonin syndrome).  It does not increase. The relationship between the 3 compliances is as follows:  1/CRS = 1/CL + 1/CCW. ## Lung hysteresis In a pressure-volume diagram, CL is often shown as a relatively straight line with a slope of ΔV/ΔP ((Figure 2)).  This line represents inspiration only.  When both inspiration and expiration are graphed, the result is a loop—at a given pressure, the lungs hold more volume during expiration than inspiration ((Figure 3)).  This is called **hysteresis**. Hysteresis occurs because surfactant spreads out during inflation, reducing its concentration and requiring more pressure to overcome surface tension.  During expiration, surfactant concentration increases again.  The process of hysteresis is somewhat analogous to how memory foam slowly returns to its original shape after being compressed.  Loss of surfactant (eg, in acute respiratory distress syndrome) reduces hysteresis (resulting in a narrower loop) and lowers CL (resulting in a steeper slope). # Tidal breathing Tidal respiration refers to quiet breathing that occurs under normal conditions.  In adults, normal tidal volume is approximately 500 mL, corresponding to approximately 6 mL/kg of ideal body weight. ## Respiratory muscles - **Inspiration** is an active (effort-dependent) process requiring muscular effort.  The primary muscle of inspiration is the **diaphragm**.  In patients with dyspnea or respiratory distress, accessory muscles of inspiration can be activated; these include the neck strap muscles (eg, sternocleidomastoid, scalenes) and, in extreme cases, additional chest muscles (eg, pectoralis minor, trapezius, latissimus dorsi, serratus anterior). - In contrast, **expiration** is a passive (effort-independent) process that utilizes the natural recoil of the respiratory system.  No muscular effort is typically required.  However, in patients with dyspnea or respiratory distress, accessory muscles of expiration, including the internal **intercostals** and **abdominal wall** muscles (eg, obliques, transversus abdominus), may be used. Greater effort during inspiration shortens inspiratory time.  Conversely, greater effort during expiration does not shorten the expiratory time because the additional force produces dynamic airway collapse, delaying the expiratory airflow.  This can be observed by comparing the time required to exhale all the way to residual volume gently versus forcefully—despite the additional force, the time remains the same. ## Normal pressure swings There are 2 key pressures that govern breathing: the alveolar pressure and the pleural pressure.  These are measured in centimeters of H2O, with atmospheric pressure set to 0 cm H2O by convention. - **Alveolar pressure (Palveolar)**:  The pressure inside the lungs.  Air flows from areas of higher pressure to areas of lower pressure.  Inspiratory airflow occurs when Palveolar is negative (eg, −2 cm H2O), creating a gradient between the atmosphere (ie, mouth and nose) and the lungs; conversely, expiratory airflow occurs when Palveolar is positive (eg, 2 cm H2O) ((Figure 4)). - **Pleural (intrapleural) pressure (Ppleural)**:  The pressure in the pleural cavity (ie, between the lungs and chest wall).  Because the lungs and chest wall are constantly trying to pull apart from each other, Ppleural is always negative (eg, −5 cm H2O).  During inspiration, the diaphragm moves downward, and Ppleural becomes even more negative (eg, to -8 cm H2O), encouraging the lungs to expand. **Transpulmonary (transpleural) pressure (PTP)**:  The difference between alveolar (ie, inside the lungs) and pleural (ie, outside the lungs) pressure.  PTP is always slightly positive because Palveolar is always higher than Ppleural (even when both are negative).  The positive PTP keeps the lungs inflated against the chest wall throughout both inspiration and expiration. # Disrupted mechanics As discussed above, the transpulmonary pressure (PTP) is always slightly positive.  Normal PTP = Palveolar – Ppleural = (–2) – (–8) = 6 cm H2O.  Several situations can disrupt this relationship, resulting in PTP that is excessively positive, zero, or negative. ## High PTP An excessively high PTP occurs if Palveolar becomes too positive (↑↑ Palveolar) or Ppleural becomes too negative (↓↓ Ppleural): - **Palveolar can become too positive** during mechanical ventilation (with inappropriate settings), violent coughing, or severe air trapping (eg, asthma exacerbation). - **Ppleural can become too negative** with fibrotic lung disease, causing the lung to retract away from the chest wall.  It can also become too negative during forceful inhalation against a closed glottis (Müller maneuver), as seen in hanging injuries or severe obstructive sleep apnea. Dangerously elevated PTP (eg, >30 cm H2O) can cause barotrauma such as pleural rupture and pneumothorax, especially if there is underlying weakness of the lung tissue (eg, emphysematous bleb).  Excessive distention of the alveoli can also damage them, causing edema or hemorrhage. ## Zero PTP PTP falls to zero with a **spontaneous pneumothorax** (eg, ruptured bleb).  This occurs because Ppleural equalizes with atmospheric pressure through the lung defect.  Palveolar also remains at zero because the lung cannot retain volume as air escapes through the hole.  Loss of P**TP** causes the lung to collapse under its intrinsic elastic recoil. ## Negative PTP A negative P**TP** occurs when Ppleural exceeds Palveolar.  It occurs in 2 scenarios: - **Tension pneumothorax**:  During standard pneumothorax, Ppleural is zero (ie, atmospheric pressure).  However, in tension pneumothorax, Ppleural becomes positive if air continues to enter the pleural space faster than it can escape.  The high Ppleural compresses the lung and mediastinal structures.  This situation also develops with a sucking chest wound, a type of penetrating chest wall injury that creates a tissue flap allowing air to enter but not escape. - **Flail chest**:  Normally, the ribcage changes position in unison with the lungs, moving outward with inspiration and inward with expiration.  If a section of the chest wall breaks free (eg, ≥3 consecutive ribs are each fractured in ≥2 places), the ribcage paradoxically moves inward with inspiration.  This may cause the Ppleural to become positive with inspiration, limiting the ability of the lungs to fill. # Work of breathing ## Resistive and elastic The work of breathing (WOB) is composed of 2 components, resistive and elastic work. **Resistive work** is the energy required to overcome resistance to airflow.  It depends on: - **Airway resistance**:  Mainly determined by **airway diameter** (resistance ∝ 1/diameter4).  Airway resistance increases in conditions that narrow or obstruct the airway, such as asthmatic bronchospasm and mucus plugging.  Low lung volumes (eg, atelectasis) also increase airway resistance because the airway caliber is reduced. - **Respiratory rate**:  High respiratory rates produce faster airflow velocities, increasing turbulence, fiction against the bronchial tree, and air resistance. **Elastic work** is the energy required to overcome the intrinsic elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall.  Work is required to distend these structures even when flow is absent.  Elastic work depends on: - **Elastance**:  Respiratory system elastance is the inverse of **compliance** (ERS = 1/CRS).  It is elevated in conditions that decrease CL (eg, interstitial fibrosis, pulmonary edema) or CCW (eg, obesity, kyphosis). - **Tidal volume**:  Elastic work is increased with larger tidal volumes due to the additional recoil of the lung tissue and chest wall as they are stretched. ## Optimization of work of breathing Total WOB is the sum of the energy expenditure of the resistive and elastic components of the respiratory system ((Figure 5)). Humans unconsciously minimize the work required to maintain normal minute ventilation (VE), which is defined as the product of respiratory rate (RR) and tidal volume (VT) (VE = RR × VT).  As outlined above, resistive WOB increases with lower lung volume and higher respiratory rate; in contrast, elastic WOB increases with higher lung volume and lower respiratory rate.  Optimal WOB strikes a balance between these extremes, with RR of 12-14/min and VT of 400-600 mL.  This balance changes with obstructive or restrictive conditions: - In obstructive lung diseases (eg, asthma), resistive work is optimized by decreasing airway resistance (eg, bronchodilator therapy) and adopting a slower, deeper breathing pattern to minimize airflow turbulence. - In restrictive lung disease (eg, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis), elastic work is optimized by adopting a rapid, shallow breathing pattern, which trades greater resistive work (eg, faster airflow) for less elastic work (eg, lower tidal volume). Normally, not much work is required for tidal breathing (eg, 2%-5% of total basal energy expenditure).  As resistance or elastance increases, greater muscular effort is required to produce the same tidal volume.  For example, in advanced chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), WOB can increase to as much as 30%-40% of total energy expenditure.  This chronically increased energy demand contributes to **pulmonary cachexia**.  WOB can dramatically increase during acute exacerbations, leading to respiratory failure if patients develop muscle fatigue. # Summary Respiratory mechanics describe how pressure, volume, and flow change during breathing.  The lungs and chest wall are components of the respiratory system with opposing tendencies: The lungs recoil inward due to elastin, whereas the chest wall recoils outward due to rib curvature.  These forces are balanced at functional residual capacity, the natural resting lung volume after passive exhalation.  Normal tidal breathing involves effort-dependent inspiration driven by the diaphragm and effort-independent expiration driven by natural recoil.  The work of breathing consists of resistive and elastic components.  Resistive work overcomes airflow resistance and is determined by airway resistance and respiratory rate; elastic work overcomes lung and chest wall recoil and is determined by respiratory system elastance (the inverse of compliance) and tidal volume. ​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​

articles.title: Pulmonary Physiology: Pulmonary Circulation
articles.markdown: # Pulmonary Physiology: Pulmonary Circulation # Introduction The pulmonary circulation refers to blood flow from the right side of the heart, through the lungs, and to the left side of the heart.  Normal pulmonary circulation is a low-resistance, low-pressure system.  This article discusses the factors that influence pulmonary vascular resistance and the ways that the right ventricle (RV) responds to changes in its afterload. # Properties In anatomic order, the pulmonary circulation includes the RV, RV outflow tract, main pulmonary artery (PA), pulmonary arterial branches, pulmonary arterioles, pulmonary capillaries, pulmonary venules, pulmonary veins, and left atrium (LA). The pulmonary circulation handles the same cardiac output (CO) as the systemic circulation, in keeping with the continuity of flow principle (Qpulmonary = Qsystemic).  To accommodate this same flow within the lungs' smaller volume, the pulmonary circulation has **high compliance**.  Pulmonary arteries have thinner walls with less elastin and smooth muscle, allowing greater distensibility compared to systemic arteries.  Along with its high compliance, the pulmonary circulation is a **low-resistance, low-pressure** system: - Low resistance:  Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is approximately one-sixth of systemic vascular resistance (SVR):  PVR = 30-200 dynes·s/cm5, whereas SVR = 800-1200 dynes·s/cm5. - Low pressure:  Mean PA pressure (mPAP) is approximately one-sixth of mean arterial pressure (MAP):  mPAP = 15 mm Hg, whereas MAP = 90 mm Hg. # Right heart catheterization ## Procedure Right heart catheterization (ie, Swan-Ganz) records pressures at key points in the pulmonary circulation ((Figure 1)).  A catheter is introduced via the internal jugular or femoral veins and advanced into the superior vena cava.  Waveform and pressure readings are captured at the following: - Right atrium:  The classic central venous waveform (a, c, v, x, y) is seen ((Figure 2)).  The average value of all wave heights is the mean right atrial pressure. - RV:  When the catheter enters the RV, a sine waveform appears, ranging from 0-5 mm Hg at the end of diastole to approximately 25 mm Hg during peak systole. - PA:  As the catheter advances from the RV into the main PA, a pressure step-up occurs immediately after the catheter crosses the pulmonic valve.  Unlike the RV, the PA retains pressure during diastole due to vascular resistance and pulmonic valve closure.  This establishes a PA diastolic pressure (dPAP), which is approximately 10 mm Hg.  The PA systolic pressure (sPAP) closely matches the RV systolic pressure, which is approximately 25 mm Hg. - Wedge:  The catheter has a small balloon at its tip that allows it to lodge in a distal pulmonary artery ((Image 1)).  The pressure at this location is known as the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP).  When wedged, the catheter tip is isolated from the proximal PA pressure (due to the balloon) and detects only pressure transmitted backward from the pulmonary veins and LA.  Therefore, PCWP is a surrogate for LA pressure (LAP) ((Figure 3)).  Normally, PCWP is 5-8 mm Hg. Pressures collected during right heart catheterization are used to calculate PVR. ## Calculation of PVR From the Ohm law, the pressure drop across a circuit is equal to the flow multiplied by the resistance of the circuit (ΔP = Q × R).  In the pulmonary circulation: - ΔP is the difference between the main PA and LA.  Therefore, ΔP = mPAP − LAP. - mPAP = ⅓ × sPAP + ⅔ × dPAP = ⅓ × 25 + ⅔ × 10 = 15 mm Hg in healthy adults (because more time is spent in diastole than in systole).  As discussed previously, PAP is measured during right-sided heart catheterization of the main pulmonary artery. - LAP ≈ PCWP = 8 mm Hg in healthy adults.  As discussed previously, PCWP is measured during right-sided heart catheterization by occluding the distal pulmonary artery. - Q is the CO, or the total flow through the lungs.  CO is measured during right-sided heart catheterization using thermodilution (temperature curve after cold bolus injection into the PA) or the Fick method (difference in oxygen saturation between arterial and mixed venous blood).  Under normal conditions, CO ≈ 5 L/min. Therefore, substituting these values into ΔP = Q × R, the equation becomes (mPAP − LAP) = CO × PVR.  Rearranging this equation yields PVR = (mPAP − LAP) / CO ≈ (15 − 8)/5 = 1.4 mm Hg / (L/min) = 1.4 Wood units (wU).  (To convert between wU and dynes·s/cm5, the units of the International System of Units, multiply by 80.) ## Interpretation of PVR Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is defined as elevated mean PAP >20 mm Hg.  PH can occur with elevated or normal PVR: - **PH with elevated PVR** (≥3 wU):  In this scenario, PH is due to remodeling of the PAs and arterioles (the resistance vessels).  Known as **precapillary PH**, this encompasses PA hypertension (PAH, Group 1), PH due to chronic lung disease or hypoxemia (Group 3), and PH due to chronic pulmonary thromboembolism (Group 4). - **PH with normal PVR** (<3 wU):  In this scenario, PH is due to the transmission of venous pressure backward from the left atrium.  Known as **postcapillary PH**, this encompasses PH due to left-sided heart disease (eg, heart failure) or mitral valve disease (Group 2).  This is the most common cause of PH in the United States.  PCWP is expected to be elevated (eg, >15 mm Hg). # Determinants of PVR PVR is determined by vascular tone, compression, recruitment, and remodeling. ## Vascular tone The balance between endogenous vasoconstrictors and vasodilators sets the vascular tone. - The major pulmonary **vasodilators** include nitric oxide and prostacyclin (or prostaglandin I2). - The major pulmonary **vasoconstrictors** include endothelin-1 and catecholamines (eg, epinephrine).  Pulmonary vasoconstriction is also stimulated by hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis, as well as by other vascular mediators such as angiotensin II, serotonin, and leukotrienes. ## Vascular compression Pulmonary capillaries are divided into extraalveolar (interstitial) and intraalveolar vessels. - At low lung volumes (near residual volume), extraalveolar vessels are compressed, but intraalveolar vessels remain open. - Conversely, at high lung volumes (near total lung capacity), extraalveolar vessels are open, whereas intraalveolar vessels are compressed. Both vessel types are maximally open at intermediate lung volumes (near functional residual capacity) ((Figure 4)). Like alveolar volume, alveolar pressure has a direct effect on vascular compression.  High positive airway pressure (eg, mechanical ventilation) can compress all capillaries, raising PVR. ## Vascular recruitment At rest, only around 66% of the pulmonary vessels are open.  The remaining 33%, particularly at the lung apices, are unperfused.  During exertion, increased CO recruits these underperfused vessels while the other vessels distend to accommodate the higher blood volume.  This combination of **recruitment and distension** helps keep PVR stable despite increased blood flow. ## Vascular remodeling Normal PA have a relatively thin wall.  In PH, the arteries can undergo structural changes, including neointimal hyperplasia, smooth muscle thickening, and adventitial fibrosis ((Figure 5)).  The vascular bed can be obliterated by emphysema or obstructed by chronic thromboemboli. Remodeled vessels progressively lose their ability to respond to vasodilators and vasoconstrictors.  In advanced stages, they may become completely unresponsive.  These structural changes are typically irreversible and contribute to elevated PVR. # RV function ## RV versus LV The RV has several key functional differences from the LV: - **Preload tolerance**:  The RV adapts well to sudden increases in preload due to its high compliance; in contrast, the LV adapts poorly due to its low compliance (eg, volume overload can quickly lead to pulmonary congestion and edema). - **Afterload tolerance**:  The LV adapts well to sudden increases in afterload, whereas the RV adapts poorly (eg, a sudden increase in PA pressure, such as acute pulmonary embolism, can quickly lead to RV dilation and failure). - **Contraction**:  RV myocytes are arrayed linearly, so the ventricle contracts lengthwise, and RV ejection fraction is best assessed by **longitudinal shortening**.  In contrast, LV myocytes are arrayed helically, so the ventricle contracts torsionally, and LV ejection fraction is best assessed by circumferential contraction. - **Ventricular interdependence**:  The LV "owns" the septum, whereas the RV "borrows" the septum for contractile efficiency.  RV pressure overload (eg, severe PH) or pericardial constriction (eg, tuberculosis) leads to septal bowing into the LV, compromising its filling and subsequent output (eg, pulsus paradoxus).  Conversely, LV pressure overload does not move the septum to the right and has minimal impact on RV filling. - **Coronary perfusion**:  The LV is perfused only during diastole when intraventricular pressure drops below coronary artery pressure.  In contrast, the RV, with its lower pressure, is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle ((Figure 6)).  Therefore, the RV is more vulnerable to hypotension and ischemia due to its reliance on continuous perfusion. ## RV-PA coupling As discussed, the RV is much more **afterload sensitive** than the LV.  If too sudden, even a small increase in PAP (eg, 20 mm Hg) can cause acute RV dysfunction.  This explains why signs of RV dysfunction (eg, peripheral edema, jugular venous distension) typically appear earlier than signs of low CO (eg, hypotension, cool extremities). Over long periods, the RV hypertrophies to adapt to high afterload.  This maintains **ventriculoarterial (RV-PA) coupling** despite the high PAP.  Patients with chronic PH can often have PAP approaching or even exceeding systemic pressures but appear remarkably well compensated due to RV adaptation.  However, some conditions can induce concurrent myocardial fibrosis (eg, scleroderma, sarcoidosis), impairing RV coupling and leading to earlier failure and more significant symptoms at comparatively lower PAP.  RV coupling is also impaired by factors that depress myocardial contractility (eg, cytokines, ischemia, acidosis, beta blockers).  Coupling can be conceptualized as the ratio of RV contractility to RV afterload. # Summary The pulmonary circulation is a low-resistance, low-pressure, and high-compliance system that transports blood from the right side of the heart, through the lungs, and to the left side of the heart.  Pulmonary vascular resistance is influenced by vascular tone (eg, nitric oxide, endothelin-1), physical compression (eg, high lung volume), vessel recruitment (eg, exercise), and structural remodeling (eg, medial thickening).  The right ventricle is highly sensitive to afterload and can acutely fail, with sudden increases in pulmonary artery pressure. ​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌

articles.title: Pulmonary Physiology: Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve
articles.markdown:
# Pulmonary Physiology: Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve # Introduction Oxygen (O2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) must be transported efficiently between the lungs and tissues through the bloodstream.  Most O2 is transported via the carrier protein hemoglobin, whereas most CO2 is transported in the form of bicarbonate (HCO3−).  Hemoglobin has unique properties that create varying affinity for O2 and help optimize O2 loading in the lungs and unloading in the tissues.  These are reflected in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.  Several factors influence the overall affinity of hemoglobin for O2, allowing the body to adjust O2 loading and unloading as needed. # Gas transport and the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve ## Hemoglobin structure and cooperative binding Hemoglobin is a tetrameric hemeprotein contained within red blood cells (RBCs).  It is usually composed of 2 alpha and 2 beta globin chains, each containing a heme group capable of binding a single O2 molecule; therefore, each hemoglobin molecule can bind up to 4 O2 molecules ((Figure 1)).  Most O2 in the blood (~98%) is carried by hemoglobin, whereas a small percentage is transported dissolved in the plasma. The **oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve** illustrates the relationship between the degree of O2 saturation of hemoglobin and the partial pressure of O2 (PO2) dissolved in the blood.  The curve reflects hemoglobin's varying binding affinity for O2 and its ability to load O2 in the lungs and release O2 in the tissues. O2 binding to hemoglobin is cooperative, meaning that after a single O2 molecule binds, the conformation of hemoglobin changes and the remaining heme groups bind O2 more readily.  This **cooperative binding** interaction between hemoglobin subunits creates a characteristic sigmoidal (S-shaped) hemoglobin dissociation curve ((Figure 2)): - At very low PO2, hemoglobin is largely deoxygenated and its O2 affinity is relatively low, so the first O2 molecule binds poorly, and the curve is flat. - Once the first O2 molecule binds to 1 hemoglobin binding site, increased affinity of the remaining sites creates the steep middle portion of the curve. - With increasing PO2, more binding sites become occupied and hemoglobin approaches full saturation, creating the plateau portion of the curve. ## O2 loading in the lungs and unloading in the tissues The cooperative nature of O2 binding allows hemoglobin to transport O2 efficiently between the lungs and the tissues. In the lungs, alveolar PO2 is typically around 100 mm Hg.  At this high O2 tension, hemoglobin operates on the plateau portion of the dissociation curve and becomes nearly fully saturated.  Because the plateau is relatively flat, moderate reductions in alveolar PO2 lead to only small reductions in hemoglobin saturation.  This acts as a safety mechanism because it helps maintain adequate O2 loading even when some degree of lung hypoxia is present. In the peripheral tissues, PO2 is typically around 40 mm Hg, which corresponds to the steep portion of the curve.  In this region, small reductions in PO2 create relatively large decreases in hemoglobin saturation.  This facilitates O2 release into the tissues. ## CO2 transport and the Bohr and Haldane effects The majority of CO2 is carried in the blood as HCO3− (~70%), whereas some is bound to hemoglobin and an additional small portion is transported dissolved in the plasma ((Figure 3)).  Molecular interactions, namely the Bohr and Haldane effects, contribute to the efficient transfer of O2 and CO2 in the lungs and tissues ((Figure 4)): - In the capillaries of the **peripheral tissues**, high levels of CO2 increase local (ambient) acidity, which decreases overall hemoglobin affinity for O2 (ie, shifts the entire oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right) and facilitates the unloading of O2 (factors that shift the entire dissociation curve are discussed later).  This is known as the **Bohr effect**.  CO2 combines with water (H2O), resulting in a hydrogen (H+) ion and HCO3−.  The H+ ions are carried by hemoglobin, whereas the HCO3− is transferred to the plasma for transport to the lungs. - In the capillaries of the **lungs**, binding of O2 molecules to hemoglobin decreases the affinity of hemoglobin for CO2, which facilitates the unloading of CO2 from hemoglobin.  The binding of O2 also increases the acidity of the hemoglobin molecule and facilitates the release of H+ ions from hemoglobin binding sites.  This is known as the **Haldane effect**.  The H+ ions combine with HCO3− to produce H2O and CO2.  The CO2 then crosses the alveolar capillary-membrane into the lungs and is expired. ## Role of bisphosphoglycerate RBCs do not have mitochondria and therefore use glycolysis, rather than oxidative phosphorylation, as the major pathway to generate energy.  During normal glycolysis, ATP is generated when 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG) is converted to 3-phosphoglycerate by the enzyme phosphoglycerate kinase ((Figure 5)).  However, RBCs can bypass this part of the pathway using an enzyme called BPG mutase to convert 1,3-BPG to 2,3-BPG.  2,3-BPG binds to deoxyhemoglobin in a pocket between the 2 beta globin chains.  Positively charged amino acids within this pocket interact with the negatively charged phosphate groups of 2,3-BPG, allosterically reducing hemoglobin's affinity for O2.  The conversion of 1,3-BPG to 2,3-BPG is increased with hypoxemia or other conditions of low blood O2 content (eg, anemia):  Higher 2,3-BPG levels within RBCs facilitate easier delivery of O2 to the peripheral tissues. # Physiologic factors that shift the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve A commonly used parameter from the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is the P50, which is the PO2 at which 50% of hemoglobin binding sites are occupied by O2 molecules.  The average P50 of hemoglobin under normal conditions is 26 mm Hg, such that >50% of hemoglobin sites are occupied even in venous blood, where PO2 is generally approximately 40 mm Hg. Changes in the P50 reflect changes in the overall O2 affinity of hemoglobin: - **Lower P****50** indicates **higher O****2** **affinity** and manifests as a **left shift** of the entire curve. - **Higher P****50** indicates **lower O****2** **affinity** and manifests as a **right shift** of the entire curve. Several physiologic variables alter the O2 affinity of hemoglobin and shift the position of the dissociation curve ((Figure 6)): ## Rightward shift - A **rightward shift** indicates **decreased O****2** **affinity** and **encourages O****2** **release into the tissues**.  It also somewhat discourages O2 uptake in the lungs, but this effect is minimal because it involves the plateau portion of the dissociation curve.  A rightward shift is driven by conditions that increase O2 need in the tissues (eg, exercising muscle, elevated metabolic rate) and occurs with: - Decreased pH. - Increased temperature. - Increased 2,3-BPG. ## Leftward shift A **leftward shift** indicates **increased O****2** **affinity** and **discourages O****2** **release to the tissues**.  It also somewhat encourages O2 uptake in the lungs, but again, this effect is minimal at the plateau portion of the dissociation curve.  A leftward shift occurs with: - Increased pH. - Decreased temperature. - Decreased 2,3-BPG. # Hemoglobin A and other types of hemoglobin (different chain compositions) Hemoglobin, composed of 2 alpha chains and 2 beta chains, is the normal and most common type of adult hemoglobin.  It is referred to as **hemoglobin A**. ## Abnormal variants of hemoglobin A Genetic mutations (usually point mutations affecting a single amino acid) can create abnormal variants of hemoglobin A that have altered conformation and different O2 affinity than normal hemoglobin A. Increased O2 affinity variants include hemoglobin Chesapeake and hemoglobin Kempsey.  The increased affinity reduces O2 unloading in the tissues, creating tissue hypoxia that stimulates erythropoietin production and erythrocytosis (high RBC count). Decreased O2 affinity variants include hemoglobin C and hemoglobin sickle cell (hemoglobin S): - Hemoglobin C results in a decreased RBC lifespan and usually mild anemia.  Increased O2 unloading in the tissues allows most affected patients to generally remain asymptomatic. - Hemoglobin S allows increased O2 unloading in the tissues, but it creates other substantial disruptions.  Low PO2 encourages polymerization of hemoglobin S, which disrupts RBC shape and can impair blood flow.  RBC lifespan is markedly shortened, which can result in severe anemia. ## Other types of hemoglobin Other types of hemoglobin result from combinations of different types of globin chains ((Table 1)).  Relevant for O2 transport are the following: - **Fetal hemoglobin**:  Fetal hemoglobin (hemoglobin F) is synthesized primarily during fetal development (~8 weeks gestation until term) and consists of 2 alpha chains but with 2 gamma chains instead of beta chains.  The gamma chains do not bind effectively to 2,3-BPG due to the replacement of a histidine residue with serine ((Figure 7)); therefore, fetal hemoglobin has significantly higher O2 affinity than adult hemoglobin ((Figure 8)).  This allows fetal hemoglobin to extract more O2 from the adult hemoglobin in the placenta, providing the developing fetus with an adequate supply of O2. - **Hemoglobin H**:  Hemoglobin H is an abnormal hemoglobin composed of 4 beta chains.  It is dysfunctional and cannot effectively transport O2.  It is seen in adults with alpha thalassemia intermedia (substantially impaired production of alpha chains) ((Table 2)). - **Hemoglobin Bart**:  Hemoglobin Bart is an abnormal hemoglobin composed of 4 gamma chains.  It is dysfunctional and cannot effectively transport O2.  It is seen in fetuses with alpha thalassemia major (absent production of alpha chains), which is incompatible with life and usually results in intrauterine demise. # Other clinically important structural relatives of hemoglobin ## Carboxyhemoglobin Carbon monoxide (CO) has extremely high binding affinity for hemoglobin and is highly toxic (and potentially fatal) in anything other than small quantities.  CO outcompetes O2 for hemoglobin binding sites, and, once bound, creates carboxyhemoglobin, which has a dissociation curve shifted far to the left with an asymptotic (rather than sigmoid) shape ((Figure 9)).  Toxicity results from fewer O2 molecules being able to bind to hemoglobin, and those that do bind cannot be released into the tissues.  Carboxyhemoglobin is normally present in small amounts (eg, <1%-2% of all hemoglobin) but is present in higher quantities in smokers (eg, ~10%).  Higher blood levels, typically due to exposure to high levels of ambient CO (eg, house fire, faulty indoor heating equipment), are considered toxic. ## Myoglobin In contrast to hemoglobin, myoglobin is a monomeric heme protein and is the primary O2\-storage protein in skeletal and cardiac muscle.  Myoglobin has only 1 heme group and does not exhibit cooperative binding interactions; therefore, its O2\-dissociation curve has a hyperbolic shape ((Figure 10)).  The affinity of myoglobin for O2 is far higher than that of hemoglobin, with myoglobin having a P50 of only 1 mm Hg (compared to ~26 mm Hg for hemoglobin), such that myoglobin is highly saturated with O2 even in a low-O2 environment. # Summary Most oxygen is transported in the bloodstream via the carrier protein hemoglobin, whereas most carbon dioxide is transported in the form of bicarbonate (but some is carried by hemoglobin).  The most common type of normal adult hemoglobin (hemoglobin A) is composed of 2 alpha and 2 beta globin chains, and the unique structure allows for cooperative binding properties that help optimize oxygen loading in the lungs and unloading in the tissues.  Factors that decrease the overall affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen (ie, shift the dissociation curve to the right) and facilitate oxygen delivery to the tissues include decreased pH, increased temperature, and increased 2,3- bisphosphoglycerate levels. ​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌
