articles.title: Pulmonary Physiology: Gas Exchange
articles.markdown:
# Pulmonary Physiology: Gas Exchange # Introduction Respiratory gas exchange involves the following processes: - Oxygenation (oxygen extraction in the lungs). - Ventilation (carbon dioxide elimination by the lungs). - Oxygen and carbon dioxide transport in the blood. - Respiratory quotient (carbon dioxide produced per oxygen consumed). This article discusses these processes, how they are regulated at rest, and how they respond during exercise. # Oxygenation Oxygenation refers to the extraction of oxygen in the lungs.  Normal oxygenation requires: - Normal inspired oxygen (ie, PiO2). - Normal alveolar ventilation (ie, PaCO2), which requires normal minute ventilation and dead space. - Normal alveolar-capillary exchange (ie, A-a gradient), which requires: - Proper ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) matching. - Efficient diffusion. ## V/Q matching Ventilation (V) and perfusion (Q) matching can be conceptualized as the **opportunity** for oxygen uptake.  Wherever air (ventilation) is present, there should be corresponding blood flow (perfusion).  When ventilation is wasted on areas with insufficient blood flow (ie, dead space) or when perfusion is wasted on areas with insufficient ventilation (ie, shunt), V/Q mismatching occurs. Ventilation and perfusion both decrease from the lung bases to the lung apices ((Figure 1)): - Ventilation is slightly greater at the lung bases because basal alveoli, compressed by overlying lung weight, start smaller and can expand relatively more during inspiration; conversely, apical alveoli are already stretched open and expand less. - Perfusion is significantly greater at the lung bases due to the effect of gravity.  Gravity increases hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary arteries (PAs), allowing blood to flow continuously (because the PA blood pressure exceeds the alveolar air pressure).  At the apices, PA pressure falls below alveolar pressure; as a result, capillaries are compressed and perfusion is reduced. ## V/Q ratios Based on the relative pressures of the PAs, alveoli, and pulmonary veins, the lung is traditionally divided into 3 zones of West (named after physiologist John West) ((Figure 2)): - **Zone 1 (apices and upper lobes)**:  Ventilation is low at the apices because the already distended alveoli have limited capacity to expand further during inspiration.  Perfusion is even lower because hydrostatic PA pressure is reduced at the apices, allowing alveoli to compress the capillaries and limit blood flow (alveolar pressure > PA pressure).  As a result, the **V/Q is >1** (often >2).  This zone has a **dead space tendency** (ie, wasted ventilation) due to relative underperfusion. - **Zone 2 (midlung)**:  Ventilation is intermediate because the alveoli are moderately compressed and capable of further expansion during inspiration.  Perfusion is also intermediate because the increasing hydrostatic PA pressure toward the lung bases helps keep the capillaries from being compressed by alveolar pressure (PA pressure > alveolar pressure).  As a result, the **V/Q ~1**.  This zone has **ideal V/Q matching**. - **Zone 3 (bases and lower lobes)**:  Ventilation is high at the bases because the basal alveoli expand the most during inspiration.  Perfusion is even higher because the gravitational hydrostatic pressure in the PAs keeps the vessels open.  As a result, the **V/Q is <1**.  This zone has **shunt tendency** due to relative overperfusion. At **rest**, V/Q ratios normally range from 3 at the apices to ~0.6 at the bases, with a global average ratio of ~1 for the entire lung.  The spread of the V/Q ratios is often represented as a histogram centered at 1 ((Figure 3)). ## V/Q with exercise At rest, the V/Q ratio is ~3 at the apices, as described previously.  During exercise, a rise in cardiac output recruits the capillaries in the apices and upper lobes, increasing perfusion in these regions.  As a result, apical perfusion increases, lowering the V/Q ratio toward 1.  This enables V/Q matching to improve **even further** with exercise compared to at rest, optimizing oxygen uptake efficiency.  Consequently, a slight **increase** in PaO2 is considered a normal oxygenation response during exercise.  Desaturation is never normal. ## Diffusion Perfect V/Q matching brings air and blood into close proximity, but oxygenation is not complete unless oxygen effectively crosses the alveolar-capillary membrane, a process known as diffusion.  Normal diffusion is governed by Fick law ((Figure 4)).  The 2 most important variables in Fick laws of diffusion are the following: - Alveolar membrane **surface area (A)** determines the total area available for diffusion, with increased area increasing diffusion.  Membrane surface area is normally 100 m2 in a healthy adult (approximately the size of a tennis court).  It is reduced by conditions such as lung resection (eg, lobectomy) and emphysema. - Alveolar membrane **thickness (T)** determines the distance that oxygen needs to cross, with increased thickness decreasing diffusion.  Membrane thickness is normally 0.5 μm in a healthy adult and comprises 3 layers (epithelium, basement membrane, endothelium).  Thickness is increased by conditions such as interstitial lung disease and pulmonary edema. The other variables include the **diffusion coefficient (D)** (a unique value for each gas representing its solubility \[eg, highest for carbon dioxide\]) and **partial pressure difference (ΔP)** across the membrane (increased by altering the pressure or purity of inhaled gas). ## Diffusion with exercise Oxygen diffuses quickly enough to fully equilibrate between the alveoli and the capillary blood within the first third of the pulmonary capillary.  This rapid diffusion prevents hypoxemia during exercise (eg, even when blood flow triples).  Because diffusion reaches an early ceiling, oxygen uptake can be increased further only by greater perfusion.  As a result, in healthy individuals, oxygen uptake is said to be **perfusion limited**.  However, in individuals with alveolar membrane damage (eg, due to severe emphysema or interstitial lung disease), oxygenation can become diffusion limited ((Figure 5)).  Oxygenation might be marginally normal at rest, but significant desaturation can often be revealed by exertion. # Ventilation Ventilation refers to the elimination of carbon dioxide by the lungs.  It requires normal alveolar ventilation (VA).  Therefore, alveolar hypoventilation and hypercapnia (ie, PaCO2 >45 mm Hg) are synonymous. ## Minute ventilation Minute ventilation (VE) is the total respired volume per minute.  It is calculated as the product of tidal volume (VT) and respiratory rate (RR) (VE = VT · RR).  Normal VT is approximately 500 mL, and normal RR is 12/min, yielding a typical VE of 6 L/min. ## Alveolar ventilation Alveolar ventilation (VA) is the total respired volume that participates in alveolar gas exchange.  It is equal to VE **minus the dead space ventilation (V****D****)**.  Dead space is the fraction of VT that is unavailable for exchange.  There are 2 components of VD ((Figure 6)): - **Anatomic V****D** is created by the conducting airways, such as the trachea and bronchi, where no gas exchange occurs.  In adults, this is a fixed value of roughly 150 mL, so only 350 mL of a normal 500-mL VT ever reaches the alveoli.  As VT decreases, the anatomic dead space fraction increases ((Figure 7)).  For example, with a 300-mL VT, only 150 mL reaches the alveoli. - **Alveolar V****D** is created by alveoli with very high V/Q ratios (eg, extreme lung apices), where perfusion is low compared to ventilation.  Under normal conditions, alveolar dead space is minimal (eg, 5-10 mL), but it can be greatly increased by conditions that reduce perfusion (eg, pulmonary embolism). VA is calculated as VA = (VT − VD) · RR.  Therefore, in normal conditions, VA = (500 − 150) · 12 = 4.2 L/min.  A slower, deeper breathing pattern (eg, VT = 600 mL, RR = 10/min) is preferable to a faster, shallower one (eg, VT = 300 mL, RR = 20/min), even if VE is the same (eg, 6 L/min for both).  The shallow pattern results in a lower VA because more VT is wasted in anatomic dead space. ## PaCO2 PaCO2 is directly proportional to the carbon dioxide production rate (VCO2) and inversely proportional to VA (ie, PaCO2 ∝ VCO2 / VA): - VCO2 (ie, ventilatory load) is determined by metabolic rate.  It increases with exercise, pathologic conditions (eg, fever, hyperthyroidism, sepsis, burns, trauma), and overfeeding (especially with a carbohydrate-rich diet). - VA is determined by VE and dead space, as discussed previously. Normally, a rise in VCO2 is accompanied by a proportional rise in VA.  Peripheral and central chemoreceptors rapidly adjust ventilation to maintain arterial carbon dioxide within a normal range.  If VA fails to keep pace with VCO2, acute hypercapnic respiratory failure results.  This is seen in severe exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, when patients generate more carbon dioxide from their own work of breathing than they can expel through ventilation. ## Ventilation with exercise Exercise leads to increases in both VT and RR.  The respiratory response differs based on the presence of lung disease: - **Healthy**:  With exercise that is low-to-moderate intensity, **V****T** **increases first**.  With higher-intensity exercise, RR increases as VT approaches inspiratory capacity. - **Abnormal**:  In patients with lung disease or neuromuscular weakness, RR increases earlier and more sharply because VT cannot increase sufficiently. In other words, VT is the primary mechanism for increasing ventilation, whereas RR becomes more important as ventilatory load increases.  In clinical practice, persistent tachypnea at rest often signals a serious underlying illness. # Gas transport ## Oxygen transport Oxygen is transported in the blood in 2 forms: - Some 98.5% of oxygen is bound to hemoglobin **(HbO****2****)**.  Each gram of hemoglobin can carry **1.34** mL of oxygen when fully saturated (ie, SaO2 100%). - Some 1.5% of oxygen is carried as a dissolved gas in the plasma **(PaO****2****)**.  Only **0.003** mL of oxygen can dissolve in each deciliter of blood per every 1 mm Hg of increase in partial pressure. Total blood oxygen content (CaO2) is the sum of HbO2 and PaO2:

CaO2 = HbO2 + PaO2\= (1.34 · SaO2 · Hb) + (0.003 · PaO2)

In a healthy patient with normal hemoglobin (eg, Hb = 15 g/dL) and normal oxygenation (eg, SaO2 = 99%, PaO2 = 90 mm Hg), the oxygen carrying capacity is 20.1 mL O2/dL of blood. Carrying capacity is determined **almost entirely** by hemoglobin concentration.  For example, when a patient with severe anemia (eg, Hb = 5 mg/dL) is breathing pure oxygen (ie, SaO2 = 99%, PaO2 = 600 mm Hg), the oxygen-carrying capacity is only 8.43 mL O2/dL of blood (only 42% of normal).  Therefore, the total CaO2 remains very low despite maximizing the dissolved oxygen. ## Carbon dioxide transport Carbon dioxide is transported in the blood in 3 forms: - 70% of carbon dioxide is transported as bicarbonate anion **(HCO****3****−****)**. - 23% of carbon dioxide is transported as carbaminohemoglobin **(HbCO****2****)**. - 7% of carbon dioxide is carried as a dissolved gas in the plasma **(PaCO****2****)**. These 3 states are in an equilibrium mediated by **carbonic anhydrase** in red blood cells ((Figure 8)).  When PaCO2 increases, more HCO3− is formed and subsequently transported out of red blood cells in exchange for chloride anions to maintain electrical neutrality (ie, Hamburger phenomenon).  This phenomenon is one of the reasons that metabolic alkalosis (excess plasma HCO3−) is often accompanied by hypochloremia. Some of the carbon dioxide binds to the terminal amine group of hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin; when exposed to high levels of oxygen in the lungs, the hemoglobin releases carbon dioxide so that it can bind oxygen instead (ie, Haldane and Bohr effects) ((Figure 9)).  This phenomenon contributes to oxygen-induced hypercapnia in patients with marginal VA (sometimes called "chronic carbon dioxide retainers") who receive excessive supplemental oxygen ((Figure 10)). # Respiratory quotient The respiratory quotient (RQ), sometimes referred to as the respiratory exchange ratio, is the ratio between carbon dioxide production and oxygen consumption (RQ = VCO2 / VO2).  The RQ is mainly affected by dietary composition and exercise. ## Effect of dietary composition Carbohydrates, fats, and proteins have differing RQ levels: - The RQ of **carbohydrates** is ~1 because complete oxidation of glucose produces 6 molecules of carbon dioxide and consumes 6 molecules of oxygen (C6H12O6 + **6 O****2** → **6 CO****2** + 6 H2O + 32 ATP). - The RQ of **fats** is ~0.7 because complete oxidation of a long-chain fatty acid (eg, palmitic acid) produces ~16 molecules of carbon dioxide and consumes 23 molecules of oxygen (C16H32O2 + **23 O****2** → **16 CO****2** + 16 H2O + 106 ATP). - The RQ of **proteins** is ~0.85 because complete oxidation of amino acids through intermediate reactions (eg, gluconeogenesis) produces 5 molecules of carbon dioxide and consumes 6 molecules of oxygen (eg, alanine \[C3H7​NO2\] ​+ **6 O****2** → **5 CO****2** + 3 H2O + 15 ATP). For a normal Western diet, the **overall RQ is ~0.8**.  This value is used in the alveolar gas equation (PAO2 = PiO2 − PaCO2 / **RQ** = 150 − PaCO2 / **0.8**). Overfeeding with high-carbohydrate diets can increase RQ and contribute to worsening hypercapnia in patients with underlying respiratory failure.  Therefore, fat- and protein-rich diets are often preferred to help reduce RQ and assist with respiratory recovery (eg, ventilator weaning). ## Effect of exercise The RQ increases during exercise.  At rest or during routine activity, the RQ is approximately 0.8.  With more intense exercise, tissues preferentially use carbohydrates for fuel, causing the RQ to increase toward 1.  With very-high-intensity exercise, the RQ increases further and can exceed 1 as the anaerobic threshold is reached (ie, oxygen is no longer being consumed, but carbon dioxide is still being produced from glycolysis). # Summary Respiratory gas exchange encompasses the processes of oxygenation, ventilation, and gas transport in the blood. Effective oxygenation requires normal alveolar-capillary exchange.  It requires tight ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) matching (ie, opportunity for air to contact blood) and rapid diffusion across the alveolar membrane (ie, speed of oxygen uptake).  V/Q mismatch or diffusion limitation leads to impaired alveolar-capillary exchange and a subsequent fall in PaO2 (ie, hypoxemia).  Blood oxygen content is mainly carried by hemoglobin (98.5%). Effective ventilation requires normal minute ventilation (tidal volume · respiratory rate) and minimal dead space volume.  Insufficient minute ventilation or abnormally increased dead space leads to alveolar hypoventilation and a subsequent rise in PaCO2 (ie, hypercapnia), which can also cause secondary hypoxemia.  Blood carbon dioxide content is mainly carried as intracellular bicarbonate in red blood cells (70%). ​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌

articles.title: Pulmonary Interstitial Emphysema
articles.markdown:
# Pulmonary Interstitial Emphysema

# Introduction

Pulmonary interstitial emphysema (PIE) is a condition in which air leaks into the peribronchovascular (ie, interstitial) space and compresses adjacent structures.

# Pathogenesis

PIE occurs when **air leaks into the peribronchovascular space** due to the rupture of overdistended alveoli.  Air accumulates in the perivascular space and compresses adjacent bronchioles and vessels, resulting in:

-   **increased airway resistance**, which can lead to air trapping and impaired gas exchange.
-   **decreased pulmonary venous return**, which can lead to impaired cardiac output.

In addition, trapped air in the perivascular space leads to decreased pulmonary compliance, further impairing gas exchange.

PIE is a type of **pulmonary air leak disorder**.  Air that leaks into the perivascular space can dissect along the perivascular connective tissue sheath, and the resultant disorder depends on the location of accumulated air.  Other types of pulmonary leak disorders include pneumothorax (ie, air in pleural space), pneumomediastinum (ie, air in mediastinum), and pneumopericardium (ie, air in pericardial space).  Less commonly, air can dissect into the peritoneal space (ie, pneumoperitoneum) or subcutaneous tissue (ie, subcutaneous emphysema).

Therefore, risk factors for PIE include any underlying pulmonary condition that can lead to alveolar overdistension, such as neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnea of the newborn, meconium aspiration syndrome, pulmonary hypoplasia, and pneumonia.  Each of these conditions increases the risk for PIE; in addition, medical management of these conditions with mechanical ventilation further increases the risk for PIE due to high inspiratory pressures and tidal volumes (ie, barotrauma).

# Clinical presentation

PIE can be unilateral or bilateral and most commonly occurs in **mechanically ventilated preterm infants**.  Patients often have worsening hypoxemia and hypercarbia within the first 72-96 hours of life, requiring increased respiratory support (eg, higher tidal volumes) to maintain adequate gas exchange.  Higher ventilator settings also contribute to air accumulation in the peribronchovascular space, resulting in further impaired gas exchange and pulmonary venous return due to compression.  Higher ventilator settings also increase the risk for tissue dissection and air leak into other tissues.

Physical examination may show worsening respiratory distress (eg, tachypnea, retractions) and cyanosis.  Hypotension may occur due to impaired cardiac output.

# Differential diagnosis

The differential diagnosis for PIE includes other types of pulmonary leak disorders (eg, pneumomediastinum, pneumothorax) that present with worsening respiratory distress in a patient with an underlying pulmonary condition often requiring mechanical ventilation.  The location of free air, as visualized on chest radiograph, distinguishes these diagnoses.

# Diagnosis

In cases of suspected PIE, a chest radiograph should be obtained to demonstrate air in the peribronchovascular space, which appears as cyst-like radiolucencies that form irregular, linear streaks in the medial and peripheral lung.  Serial blood gas analyses can show worsening hypoxemia and hypercarbia with escalating respiratory support.

# Management

The management of PIE is **supportive**.  The goal is to maintain adequate gas exchange and cardiac output while minimizing the risk for further air leak (eg, lowest possible ventilator settings).  In addition, the patient should be positioned in the lateral decubitus position with the affected lung down to promote aeration of the unaffected lung.  In severe cases, bronchial intubation of the unaffected lung (ie, extending the endotracheal tube into a main bronchus to aerate only one lung) may be performed to prevent further air leak and allow healing.

# Prognosis

The prognosis of PIE depends on the severity and the underlying pulmonary condition.  Mild cases (eg, mild hypoxemia and hypercarbia that require noninvasive respiratory support) often resolve with supportive care while minimizing ventilatory settings.  However, in severe cases (eg, severe hypoxemia and hypercarbia that require invasive respiratory support), patients are at increased risk for bronchopulmonary dysplasia, or chronic lung disease characterized by prolonged (eg, >28 days) oxygen requirement in a preterm infant, due to chronic inflammation.

# Prevention

Preventative strategies for PIE include:

-   Using the least invasive mode of respiratory support (eg, continuous positive airway pressure) while maintaining adequate gas exchange
-   Minimizing ventilator settings (ie, inspiratory pressures, tidal volumes) to prevent overdistension of alveoli
-   Administering exogenous surfactant in cases of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome to improve pulmonary compliance and avoid using high ventilator settings

# Summary

Pulmonary interstitial emphysema (PIE) is a condition in which air leaks into the peribronchovascular (ie, interstitial) space and compresses adjacent structures.  Patients with underlying pulmonary conditions are at increased risk and often present with worsening respiratory distress, hypoxemia, and hypercarbia within the first 72-96 hours of life.  Treatment is supportive while maintaining adequate gas exchange.

​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​

articles.title: Pulmonary Hypertension
articles.markdown:
# Pulmonary Hypertension # Introduction  Pulmonary hypertension (PH) refers to approximately 50 conditions that increase pulmonary artery pressure (PAP), with a common final pathway of progressive right ventricular failure, carrying high morbidity and mortality.  The formal definition of PH (which has evolved over time) is a mean PAP ≥20 mm Hg. # Pathophysiology Normally, the pulmonary circulation (ie, vessels from the pulmonic valve to the left atrium) is a low-pressure system, flowing at ~1/6th of systemic pressures.  The low pressure is made possible by highly compliant, distensible pulmonary vessels.  PH involves several mechanisms: - Vasoconstriction:  Pulmonary endothelial dysfunction leads to imbalance between endogenous vasoconstrictors (↑ endothelin-1) and vasodilators (↓ nitric oxide and prostacyclin) - Vascular remodeling:  Smooth muscle cell proliferation, neointimal hyperplasia, extracellular matrix deposition, inflammatory cell infiltration, and microthrombosis *in situ* These changes lead to narrowing and obliteration of the vascular bed ((Figure 1)). As the pulmonary vascular remodeling worsens, pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) gradually increases.  At first, the right ventricle (RV) is able to pump against this increased afterload.  To help it adapt, the RV hypertrophies but also may eventually dilate and fail in the face of PH.  Clinical signs of RV failure can develop. # WHO classification PH is classified into 5 groups based on underlying etiology, with group 1 considered primary and all other groups considered secondary. ## Group 1:  (Primary) pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) Direct injury to the pulmonary arteries themselves ((Figure 2)), due to unknown mechanisms (idiopathic), inherited mutations (eg, *BMPR2*), drugs or toxins (eg, methamphetamine), infections (eg, HIV, schistosomiasis), autoimmune conditions (eg, scleroderma), and others (eg, congenital heart disease). ## Group 2:  (Secondary) PH due to left heart disease Retrograde transmission of elevated left-sided filling pressure ((Figure 3)) due to left-sided heart failure or mitral valve disease.  This is the most common form of PH in the US. ## Group 3:  (Secondary) PH due to lung disease and/or chronic hypoxemia (aka, cor pulmonale) Destruction of pulmonary vascular bed due to parenchymal lung disease (eg, cystic fibrosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease \[COPD\]), and sustained pulmonary vasoconstriction due to chronic alveolar hypoxemia (eg, sleep apnea, obesity-hypoventilation, living at high altitude). ## Group 4:  (Secondary) PH due to chronic thromboembolism (CTEPH) Obstruction of pulmonary arteries due to recurrent (or unresolved) pulmonary emboli, particularly with large acute emboli, underlying hypercoagulability, and indwelling venous catheters. ## Group 5:  (Secondary) PH due to unclear or multifactorial mechanisms Wastebasket category for pulmonary vascular remodeling in the setting of complex multisystem conditions such as sarcoidosis, endstage renal disease and hemodialysis, sickle cell disease, and rare metabolic disorders (eg, Gaucher). # Precapillary vs postcapillary PH PH grouping can also be viewed in terms of which side of the pulmonary capillaries the lesion is located.  Precapillary PH (ie, lesions from the pulmonary arteries to arterioles) and postcapillary PH (ie, lesions of the pulmonary veins) can be differentiated based on the PVR and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCPW), measured during right heart catheterization ((Figure 4)): - Precapillary PH (increased PVR): - Groups 1, 3, and 4 - Hemodynamics:  ↑ PAP, ↑ PVR, normal PCWP - Postcapillary PH (normal PVR): - Group 2 - Hemodynamics:  ↑ PAP, normal PVR, ↑ PCWP In many cases, there is a combination of pre- and postcapillary PH due to multiple comorbidities.  The most common combination is group 2 + 3 (eg, heart failure + COPD). # Clinical presentation Patients with PH have general (all groups) signs and symptoms of right ventricular dysfunction, as well as specific manifestations related to underlying etiology (specific groups). ## General findings (all groups) - Related to high PA pressure:  chest pressure and dyspnea, exertional angina (right ventricular \[RV\]  ischemia), cough or hemoptysis, loud P2, right-sided S4, parasternal heave - Related to venous congestion:  peripheral edema, bowel edema (early satiety), abdominal fullness and ascites, jugovenous distension - Related to low cardiac output:  fatigue, presyncope or syncope (especially with coughing and valsalva), systemic hypotension - Chest imaging:  bilateral mainstem pulmonary artery enlargement and prominent right heart border - Pulmonary function testing (PFT):  gas transfer (as measured by the diffusion capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide \[DLCO\]) reduced out of proportion to mechanical lung function (spirometry and lung volume) - ECG:  right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH; tall R wave in V1), right axis deviation, right bundle branch block, right atrial enlargement (P-pulmonale), right ventricular strain patterns (precordial ST-T depression/inversion, S1Q3T3) - Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE):  elevated pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP; aka right ventricular systolic pressure \[RVSP\]); RV hypertrophy, dilation, and systolic dysfunction; septal flattening (D-shaped RV) and bowing into the left ventricle; tricuspid regurgitation; coronary sinus dilatation ## Group 1 (PAH) specific findings - Presentation:  young adult female, little or no medical history, progressive exertional dyspnea often misdiagnosed as asthma for several years - TTE:  isolated RV dysfunction (ie, normal left heart) - Chest imaging:  clear lungs - PFT:  isolated reduction in DLCO (normal spirometry and lung volumes) - Supportive studies:  autoimmune serology (eg, ANA, scl-70), toxicology (eg, amphetamine), HIV testing, and others ## Group 2 (left heart) specific findings - Presentation:  older patient, cardiac risk factors, wet lungs (eg, orthopnea, effusions) - TTE:  left ventricular diastolic or systolic dysfunction, left ventricular hypetrophy, or mitral valvulopathy - Chest imaging:  pulmonary vascular congestion and septal B lines - PFT:  possible restrictive defect and reduced DLCO ## Group 3 (lung) specific findings - Presentation:  older patient, pulmonary exposures (eg, smoking), hypoxemia out of proportion to lung function (indicates an additional vascular component) - Chest imaging:  underlying lung disease (eg, emphysema, bronchiectasis, fibrosis) - PFT:  abnormal spirometry, lung volumes, and reduced DLCO - Supportive studies:  arterial blood gas showing chronic hypercapnia or hypoxemia, polysomnography with apneas/hypopneas and desaturation, blood count with elevated hematocrit ## Group 4 (CTEPH) specific findings - Presentation:  older patient, history of recurrent venous thromboembolism, persistent dyspnea months to years after acute embolic event - PFT:  isolated reduction in DLCO (normal spirometry and lung volumes) - Supportive studies:  ventilation/perfusion (VQ) scan; CT angiography ## Group 5 (multifactorial) specific findings - Presentation:  highly variable, but usually a history of a major multisystem disease (eg, sarcoidosis) - Supportive studies:  chronic intravascular hemolysis (sickle cell), noncaseating granulomas (sarcoidosis), blood polycythemias or cytopenias (myeloproliferative disorders) # Diagnostic workflow Diagnosis of PH is often delayed by several years because obvious signs of right heart failure (eg, edema)  appear late into the disease course.  There is often a slow buildup of vague complaints (eg, chest discomfort, fatigue) and exertional symptoms that are often misdiagnosed as asthma, anxiety, or physical deconditioning.  Young adult females, at greatest risk of (idiopathic) PAH, are also most likely to have the diagnosis overlooked. PH is never diagnosed by biopsy due to the risk of hemorrhage in the setting of high arterial pressure.  Instead, diagnosis of PH is largely noninvasive, gathered from many clinical data points.  The diagnostic approach to PH begins by estimating the PASP (aka RVSP) with **TTE** performed at rest ((Figure 5)). If the TTE shows **evidence of PH** at rest (ie, elevated PASP, RV dysfunction or enlargement) and if: - **LV dysfunction is present** (group 2), then subsequent workup focuses on reversible causes (eg, ischemia, alcohol, mitral valve disease). - **LV dysfunction is absent**, then workup expands to other forms of PH and includes further studies such as HIV testing and autoimmune serologies (group 1); PFT, high-resolution chest CT,  and polysomnography (group 3); VQ scan (group 4). If the TTE shows **no PH** at rest (ie, normal PASP) and if: - Clinical suspicion for PH remains high (eg, numerous risk factors), then further investigation with right heart catheterization (RHC) or exercise TTE is warranted; these studies are more sensitive for detecting dynamic elevations in PA pressure. - Clinical suspicion for PH is reduced, then workup focuses on alternative explanations for the dyspnea and exercise intolerance (eg, ischemic heart disease). # Differential diagnosis ## Elevated venous pressure and volume overload PH-induced RV failure results in central venous congestion (eg, elevated JVP) and peripheral edema.  However, other conditions are on the differential. - **Constrictive pericarditis** (eg, prior tuberculosis or chest radiation):  Pericardial fibrosis and stiffening limits RV diastolic filling, leading to elevated jugulovenous pressure and hepatic/abdominal congestion (and in severe, untreated cases, cardiogenic cirrhosis with nutmeg liver).  Constrictive pericarditis is a problem of RV filling (vs pulmonary vascular remodeling in PH):  the right ventricular systolic function is normal (vs reduced), PVR is normal (vs elevated), and PAP is normal (vs elevated). - **Primary RV failure** (ie, without PH):  Causes include prior RV myocardial infarction, RV outflow tract obstruction (eg, pulmonic stenosis), severe tricuspid regurgitation, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (very rare).  RV systolic function is reduced and central venous pressure is elevated (similar to PH), but PVR and PAP are normal. ## Unexplained exertional dyspnea PH should be considered in patients without a satisfactory explanation after initial workup (eg, normal initial TTE and PFT).  However, subtle presentations of cardiopulmonary disorders (eg, exercise-induced LV diastolic dysfunction, early interstitial lung disease) are also on the differential, requiring more advanced studies for diagnosis (eg, cardiopulmonary exercise testing). # Management Management of PH ((Table 1)) involves general supportive measures (for all groups) and specific therapies (tailored to group): ## General supportive measures (all groups) - Supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥92% (avoid hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction) - Contraceptive counseling (pregnancy in PAH carries a 50% mortality) - Pulmonary rehabilitation (supervised exercise) - Immunizations (influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, COVID-19, and *Pneumococcus*) - Maintenance of euvolemia (eg, weight monitoring and diuretic plan) - Referral to accredited PH center if possible (superior outcomes) ## Group 1 (PAH) - Pulmonary vasodilator therapy ((Figure 6)):  phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (eg, tadalafil), endothelin receptor antagonists (eg, ambrisentan), prostacyclin (eg, treprostinil), and calcium channel blockers (eg, nifedipine) for some patients - Treatment of underlying conditions (eg, immunosuppression for scleroderma-PAH) ## Group 2 (left heart) - Treatment of reversible causes of heart failure (eg, revascularization for ischemic cardiomyopathy) - Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for heart failure with reduced ((Table 2)) or preserved ((Table 3)) ejection fraction ## Group 3 (lung) - Optimization of underlying lung disease:  bronchodilators (COPD), antifibrotic agents (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) - Treatment of sleep-disordered breathing (eg, positive airway pressure for obstructive sleep apnea) ## Group 4 (CTEPH) - Medical therapy:  anticoagulation ± soluble guanylate cyclase inhibitor (eg, riociguat) - Surgery (potentially curative):  pulmonary artery thromboendarterectomy (stripping away old clots and overlying endothelium) ## Group 5 (multifactorial) - Treatment of underlying conditions (eg, chemotherapy for myeloproliferative disorder) ## Pulmonary vasodilator therapy Pulmonary vasodilator therapy is most effective for group 1 PAH because of the central role of vasoconstriction in these patients.  Analogous to their relaxant effect on pulmonary vessels, they also treat severe Raynaud (eg, digital ischemia) in CREST-associated PAH.  Vasodilators are largely contraindicated in group 2 and 3 PH. - In group 2, pulmonary vasodilation increases flow into the dysfunctional left ventricle, precipitating cardiogenic flash pulmonary edema.  - In group 3, pulmonary vasodilation increases perfusion of the entire lung, including diseased areas; this leads to greater VQ mismatch and worse hypoxemia.  Inhaled (rather than oral or parenteral) pulmonary vasodilators (eg, treprostinil nebulizer) mitigate this problem by directing the drug only to well-ventilated alveoli (preserving VQ matching) and are emerging for the treatment of group 3 PH. The only cure for PH is lung transplantation, which replaces diseased vessels with new ones.  RV failure resolves within hours to days after lung transplantation, supporting the concept of PVR-induced demand ischemia as the core driver of RV failure. # Prognosis The prognosis of PH depends on the group. ## Groups 1 (PAH) and 4 (CTEPH) - Before vasodilators (1995), group 1 (PAH) had the poorest prognosis.  In contrast, drug-treated PAH currently has the best prognosis of all 5 groups (median survival ~5 years), although it remains progressive, lethal, and incurable. - Group 4 (CTEPH) has an excellent prognosis when it can be cured by pulmonary thromboendarterectomy surgery (most effective for proximal large-vessel disease).  ## Groups 5 (multifatorial) and 2 (left heart) - Group 5 (multifactorial) has highly variable prognosis depending on the underlying etiology (eg, favorable for sarcoidosis, worse for sickle cell disease) - Group 2 PH has an intermediate prognosis but continues to improve through advances in pharmacologic treatment.  PH related to heart failure with reduced ejection fraction has a better prognosis than that related to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, reflecting abundant mortality-reducing treatment options for systolic failure but fewer options for diastolic failure. ## Group 3 (lung) - Group 3 PH (lung) has the worst prognosis (median survival ~2.5 years).  This likely reflects a lack of treatment options to reverse underlying advanced lung disease, and the poor functional status of these patients at baseline. ## Poor prognostic indicators - Syncope during coughing, tying shoes, or straining (reduced venous return) - Hospitalization for right heart failure - Severe venous congestion (eg, right atrial pressure >20 mm Hg) - Systolic hypotension (systolic blood pressure \[SBP\] <110 mm Hg) or pressure inversion (SBP ≤ PAP) - Renal dysfunction (eg, cardiorenal syndrome) - Limited exercise capacity (eg, low 6-minute walk distance) - Falling PAP (although high PAP generally indicates worse disease, loss of RV contractility and cardiac output causes PAP to fall in the final stages of PH).  RV function continues to worsen because of primary progression of PH itself (ie, rising PVR).  Ultimately, the RV begins to dilate, setting into motion a vicious spiral in which RV dilation compromises LV filling, inducing RV ischemia and further dilation ((Figure 7)).  Patients with severe PH have very limited reserve.  Even minor insults (eg, atrial fibrillation, low-grade respiratory illness) can trigger catastrophic RV failure and death. # Summary Pulmonary hypertension (PH) ((Table 4)) encompasses approximately 50 conditions that elevate pulmonary artery pressure, leading to progressive right ventricular failure.  Its pathogenesis involves abnormal pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling (eg, neointimal thickening and muscular hyperplasia), increasing pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR).  PH is classified into 5 groups based on underlying causes:  Group 1 involves primary pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), group 2 involves PH due to left heart disease, group 3 is PH due to lung disease and/or chronic hypoxemia, group 4 refers to PH from chronic thromboembolism (CTEPH), and group 5 includes PH from unclear or multifactorial mechanisms.  The clinical presentation of PH is related to high pulmonary artery pressure (eg, dyspnea), venous congestion (eg, peripheral edema, abdominal fullness), and low cardiac output (eg, exercise intolerance).  Diagnosis begins with estimating pulmonary artery systolic pressure with echocardiogram, followed by further investigations as needed to classify the PH (eg, autoimmune serologies, chest imaging).  Treatment is determined by group: pulmonary vasodilator therapy is indicated most strongly for group 1 PAH.  Prognosis differs among groups; PAH has the best prognosis with drug treatment, and group 3 PH has the worst prognosis.  Severe right ventricular failure is the most common cause of death, and lung transplantation is the only definitive cure. ​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌

Management of pulmonary hypertension

Group 1
PAH

  • Evaluate for autoimmune CTD, toxins (eg, amphetamines), HIV, schistosomiasis, etc.
  • Pulmonary vasodilator therapy, treat underlying (eg, autoimmune) cause

Group 2
Left-sided
heart disease

  • Echocardiography (± RHC if diagnosis unclear)
  • Optimize left ventricular function (eg, heart failure therapy), treat significant valve disease

Group 3
Lung disease &/or
chronic hypoxemia

  • Pulmonary function tests, chest imaging, polysomnography
  • Treat underlying respiratory condition (eg, obstructive sleep apnea)

Group 4
CTEPH

  • V/Q scan, pulmonary angiography
  • Pulmonary thromboendarterectomy surgery (curative), anticoagulation

General
measures

  • Refer to accredited PH center
  • Maintain normoxia, euvolemia & sinus rhythm
  • Contraceptive counseling, immunization, cardiac rehabilitation
  • Refractory PH: bilateral lung transplant

CTD = connective tissue disease (eg, scleroderma); CTEPH = chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension; PAH = pulmonary arterial hypertension; PH = pulmonary hypertension; RHC = right-sided heart catheterization; V/Q = ventilation-perfusion.

Pharmacotherapy for chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

Medication

Indication

Notes

Initial optimized therapy

Angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor*

NYHA classes I-IV with LVEF ≤40%

  • Slows disease progression & improves mortality

β blocker

  • Metoprolol succinate, carvedilol, or bisoprolol
  • Reduces hospitalization & improves mortality

Diuretics

NYHA classes II-IV with volume overload

  • Loop diuretic ± metolazone
  • Improves symptoms & reduces hospitalization

Step 2 of optimized therapy

Aldosterone antagonist

NYHA classes II-IV

  • Reduces hospitalization & improves mortality

Step 3 of optimized therapy

SGLT-2 inhibitor

  • Reduces symptoms & improves mortality

Supplementary agents

Isosorbide dinitrate + hydralazine

Angiotensin system blocker intolerance

  • Improves symptoms & may improve mortality

Digoxin

Persistent symptoms despite other therapy

  • Reduces hospitalization but no mortality benefit
  • *Other angiotensin system blockers (ie, ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker) are alternatives.
  • LVEF = left ventricular ejection fraction; NYHA = New York Heart Association; SGLT-2 = sodium-glucose cotransporter-2.

Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

Etiology

  • LV diastolic dysfunction due to impaired relaxation

Risk factors

  • Chronic hypertension (concentric LV hypertrophy)
  • Obesity & sedentary lifestyle (myocardial interstitial fibrosis)
  • CAD & related risk factors (eg, diabetes mellitus)

Management

  • Specific therapies to reduce hospitalization & possibly mortality:
    • SGLT-2 inhibitor (eg, empagliflozin) added first
    • MRA (eg, spironolactone) added secondarily
  • Loop diuretics as needed to treat volume overload
  • Antihypertensives as needed to reduce afterload
  • Treatment of exacerbating conditions (eg, CAD, OSA, A-fib)
  • Exercise training, weight loss & cardiac rehabilitation

A-fib = atrial fibrillation; CAD = coronary artery disease; LV = left ventricular; MRA = mineralocorticoid antagonist; OSA = obstructive sleep apnea; SGLT-2 = sodium-glucose cotransporter-2.

Clinical features of pulmonary hypertension

Classification

  • Pulmonary arterial hypertension (WHO group 1)
  • Due to left heart disease (group 2)
  • Due to chronic lung disease or hypoxemia (eg, COPD, OSA) (group 3)
  • Due to chronic thromboembolic disease (group 4)
  • Due to other causes (eg, sarcoidosis) (group 5)

Symptoms

  • ↓ Cardiac output: exertional syncope/presyncope, fatigue, weakness
  • ↑ PA pressure: chest tightness, hemoptysis (rare)
  • RV demand ischemia: exertional angina/tightness
  • Venous congestion: abdominal distension (bowel edema), early satiety

Signs

  • Precordial heave due to RV hypertrophy
  • Loud P2, right-sided S3 &/or S4
  • Holosystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation
  • JVD, ascites, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly
COPD = chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; JVD = jugular venous distension; OSA = obstructive sleep apnea; PA = pulmonary artery; RV = right ventricular.

articles.title: Pulmonary Function Testing
articles.markdown: # Pulmonary Function Testing # Definitions During pulmonary function testing, patients blow through tubing connected to a flowmeter.  This produces a graph of exhaled volume against time.  The graph is often presented as an idealized spirogram, showing tidal breathing followed by a forced vital maneuver ((Figure 1)).  From the spirogram, 4 lung volumes and 4 capacities can be defined. ## Lung volumes Lung volumes are fundamental units (ie, they cannot be expressed in terms of each other): - **Tidal volume** (TV):  the volume of a normal, quiet breath. - **Inspiratory reserve volume** (IRV):  the volume that can be further inspired after normal tidal inhalation. - **Expiratory reserve volume** (ERV):  the volume that can be further expired after normal tidal exhalation. - **Residual volume** (RV):  the volume remaining in the lungs after maximal expiration.  ## Lung capacities Lung **capacities** are the sum of **≥2 lung volumes:** - **Total lung capacity** (TLC = RV + ERV + TV + IRV):  the maximum amount of air that can be held in the lungs.  It is the sum of all lung volumes. - **Vital capacity** (VC = ERV + TV + IRV):  the maximum amount of air that can be inspired or expired.  It is the sum of all lung volumes, excluding RV.  - **Inspiratory capacity** (IC = TV + IRV):  the amount of air that can be inspired after tidal exhalation. - **Functional residual capacity** (FRC = RV + ERV):  the amount of air that remains in the lungs after tidal exhalation.  This is also the resting, effortless volume of the respiratory system, corresponding to the equilibrium between the elastic collapsing force of the lung tissue and the elastic expanding force of the chest wall. **VC** is considered the **master indicator** of lung function because it represents the total amount of moveable air.  It is helpful to think of VC as the difference between TLC and RV (VC = TLC − RV).  A reduced VC can be caused by: - A decrease in TLC due to restrictive conditions (eg, interstitial lung disease \[ILD\]) - An increase in RV due to obstructive conditions (eg, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease \[COPD\]) Lung volumes reflect these different conditions ((Figure 2)). ## Measuring RV, FRC, and TLC **Spirometry** relies on air movement through a tube, so it only measures volumes that can be actively inhaled or exhaled.  Therefore, spirometry cannot measure RV or the capacities constructed from it (ie, FRC and TLC).  These 3 values (RV, FRC, and TLC) require specialized equipment. There is often confusion between the clinical and technical usage of the term "volume."  In clinical settings, the expression "lung volume testing" is used even when measuring capacities (rather than volumes). # Components of pulmonary function tests Pulmonary function test (PFTs) refer to a group of studies generally consisting of 3 parts: - Air movement (ie, spirometry) - Lung volumes (ie, plethysmography) - Gas transfer (ie, diffusion capacity) An order for "full PFTs" generally refers to all 3 components performed as a set. ## Spirometry (air movement) Spirometry measures air movement through a tube.  Therefore, it captures all volumes and capacities that do not depend on RV.  Clinically, the 3 values of greatest interest are: - **FVC** - **FEV1** - **FEV1/FVC ratio** Healthy individuals empty ~80% of their lungs in the first second (ie, normal FEV1/FVC ≈ 0.8).  Early flow is fastest because fully inflated lungs have the highest elastic recoil (ie, because the tissue is stretched taut) and lowest airway resistance (ie, because the bronchi are expanded to their largest diameter).  Conditions that decrease elastic recoil (eg, emphysema) or increase airway resistance (eg, asthma) selectively impact early airflow, resulting in a low FEV1/FVC ratio (eg, obstruction is defined as FEV1/FVC <0.7). Lung emptying is effort independent because expiratory flow is determined entirely by intrinsic elastic recoil of the respiratory system (eg, decreased in emphysema)—a property cannot be voluntarily altered.  This can be verified firsthand by comparing passive against very forceful exhalation:  The emptying is identical. ## Plethysmography (lung volumes) Plethysmography operates on the Boyle gas law (P1·V1 = P2·V2).  It uses an airtight body box that calculates the absolute volume from the absolute pressure.  Plethysmography captures the 3 quantities that depend on RV (often called ***static* volumes** because air movement is not required): - **TLC** - **FRC** - **RV** Lung volume measurement is always needed to confirm a **restrictive** pattern (defined as **TLC, FRC, or RV <80% predicted**). ## Gas transfer:  Diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO), gas transfer Gas transfer is assessed using the DLCO.  Because CO equilibrates immediately across the alveolar membrane (ie, extremely high hemoglobin affinity), the difference between inhaled (known) versus exhaled (measured) CO reflects the rate of diffusion, indicating the health of the **airspace-capillary interface**. ## Other tests A variety of other studies yield further insight into respiratory system physiology.  These expanded or auxiliary PFTs include: - **Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR):**  Unlike overall lung emptying, instantaneous *peak* flow is effort dependent.  Therefore, PEFR serves as an early indicator of impending respiratory muscle fatigue during obstructive lung disease exacerbations (eg, asthma yellow or red zone).  - **Provocation testing:**  Bronchoconstriction sometimes needs to be provoked (eg, methacholine) in order to diagnose intermittent asthma.  Methacholine is a muscarinic agonist that targets smooth muscle M3 receptors to directly constrict the airways.  A high susceptibility to methacholine (ie, minuscule dose needed to induce ≥20% reduction in FEV1) has a moderate positive predictive value for asthma; conversely, a negative test has strong negative predictive value and reliably excludes asthma. - **6-minute walk distance (6MWD)** (ie, pulmonary stress test):  Patient walks as far as possible in 6 minutes while wearing a pulse oximeter to monitor desaturation and supplemental oxygen needs.  The distance has strong prognostic value across a variety of chronic lung diseases. - **Respiratory muscle strength:**  A variety of tests can assess respiratory muscle function, including negative inspiratory force (which measures instantaneous diaphragm strength) and eucapnic maximal voluntary ventilation (which measures endurance).  # Stepwise approach A standard approach to PFT interpretation is outlined ((Figure 3)).  The study is assumed to be valid (eg, good patient cooperation and reproducibility). ## Step 1:  Examine flow-volume loop During the PFT, air flow and lung volumes are measured simultaneously, allowing a flow-volume loop to be constructed.  The shape of the flow-volume loop can offer quick visual clues toward a diagnosis ((Figure 4)): - Normal shape but shrunken indicates restrictive lung disease (eg, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis). - Expiratory scalloping indicates small airway obstruction (eg, asthma, COPD). - Expiratory flattening indicates variable intrathoracic obstruction (eg, tracheobronchomalacia). - Inspiratory flattening indicates variable extrathoracic obstruction (eg, vocal cord dysfunction). - Biphasic flattening indicates fixed obstruction (eg, tracheal stenosis or tumor). ## Step 2:  Classify pattern Spirometry (and lung volumes) are used to classify lung conditions into an obstructive or restrictive pattern: - **Normal:**  If FEV1 and FVC are normal (ie, ≥80%) and FEV1/FVC ≥0.7, the patient's symptoms may be due to an intermittent respiratory process; methacholine challenge may be needed to provoke asthmatic obstruction. - **Obstructive:**  Obstruction is present when FEV1 and/or FVC are reduced (eg, <80%) and **FEV****1****/FVC <0.7**.  If this is present, the next step is to assess reversibility based on pre- and post-bronchodilator testing (eg, albuterol).  - **Restrictive:**  Restriction is suspected when FEV1 and/or FVC are reduced (eg, <80%) despite FEV1/FVC ≥0.7.  However, confirmation with lung volume plethysmography is required.  Restriction is defined by **low lung volumes** (ie, TLC, FRC, and/or RV <80%).  ## Step 3:  Grade severity Obstructive and restrictive lung diseases are often assigned a grade (not for memorization). - **Obstruction** is graded by FEV1 to best reflect early expiratory flow.  It ranges from mild (ie, ≥80%, GOLD stage 1 COPD) to very severe (ie, <35%, GOLD stage 4 COPD). - **Restriction** is graded by TLC to best reflect lung volume.  It ranges from mild (ie, ≥80%) to severe (ie, <50%). ## Step 4:  Assess gas transfer DLCO can further clarify the etiology of obstructive and restrictive conditions: - **Obstructive:**  DLCO is decreased when the alveolar surface area is destroyed (eg, emphysema), relatively preserved when the alveoli are intact (eg, chronic bronchitis), or sometimes increased when there is bronchial hyperemia (eg, asthma). - **Restrictive:**  DLCO can be low with intrinsic restriction (eg, ILD) or normal with extrinsic restriction (eg, neuromuscular weakness). DLCO also correlates with hypoxemia and supplemental oxygen requirements. # Obstructive pattern ## Definition An obstructive ventilatory defect is defined as spirometry showing FEV1/FVC <0.7 prior to a bronchodilator. ## Reversible versus irreversible Obstruction can be reversible or irreversible.  These 2 are distinguished by the response to a short-acting bronchodilator (eg, albuterol): - **Reversible (ie, asthma):**  FEV1/FVC <0.7 before a bronchodilator but improves to >0.7 afterward. - **Irreversible (eg, COPD):**  FEV1/FVC <0.7 before and after a bronchodilator A "positive bronchodilator response" (defined as an improvement in FEV1 or FVC by ≥10% after administration of albuterol) is a related but distinct concept.  Some patients have a positive bronchodilator response but persistent obstruction (eg, post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC still <0.7).  This situation frequently arises in asthma—COPD overlap, which is characterized by an irreversible obstruction with a bronchospastic component. ## Hyperinflation and air trapping In obstructive conditions, lung volumes can show hyperinflation and/or air trapping ((Figure 5)). - **Hyperinflation** refers to overall alveolar enlargement (eg, due to loss of elastic tissue and septations).  It is reflected by an elevated TLC and/or FRC (>120%).  It correlates with a "barrel chest" appearance and diaphragm flattening on chest x-ray.  - **Air trapping** refers to retention of volume due to expiratory closure of small airways (eg, loss of radial elastic support).  It is reflected by an elevated RV (>120%) and/or an RV/TLC.  An isolated increase in RV, a sensitive indicator of small airway collapse and early air trapping, is possibly the first detectable sign of COPD on PFT. # Restrictive pattern ## Definition A restrictive ventilatory defect is defined as decreased lung volumes (TLC, FRC, or RV <80%). ## Intrinsic versus extrinsic  Restriction can be intrinsic or extrinsic.  They are distinguished by DLCO: - Intrinsic (low DLCO):  Restriction originates from stiff lung parenchyma (eg, fibrotic ILD).  DLCO is reduced due to thickening of the alveolar basement membrane.  Subsequent work-up typically focuses on evaluating the lung interstitium (eg, high resolution CT scan of the chest).  Note that spirometry can show FEV1/FVC ≥0.7 (and often higher) because fibrotic lung disease is associated with increased elastic recoil, which can cause high early airflow. - Extrinsic (normal DLCO):  Restriction originates from extrapulmonary issues such as neuromuscular disease (eg, myasthenia gravis) or chest wall deformity (eg, severe kyphosis).  DLCO is preserved because the alveolar membrane is intact.  Subsequent work-up typically focuses on evaluating for neuromuscular weakness (eg, diaphragm sniff fluoroscopy, maximal voluntary ventilation).  # Isolated DLCO reduction ## Pulmonary vascular pattern An isolated reduction in DLCO (ie, low DLCO but normal spirometry and lung volumes), called pulmonary vascular pattern, reflects a dissociation between gas transfer and respiratory mechanics; it usually indicates a problem with pulmonary blood flow. - Alveolar perfusion is impaired (ie, low DLCO), but - Airway and parenchymal function is intact (ie, normal spirometry and lung volumes).  This situation is analogous to hypoxemia with a clear chest x-ray.  Common etiologies include pulmonary hypertension and pulmonary thromboembolism.  Hepatopulmonary syndrome (diffuse pulmonary capillary vasodilation seen in advanced cirrhosis) also produces a similar picture due to the increased diffusion distance and rapid transit of erythrocytes. ## Other etiologies of isolated low DLCO Other etiologies of an isolated low DLCO include: - Anemia:  DLCO is reduced due to reduced hemoglobin carrying capacity.  DLCO is typically normalized (ie, corrected) for hemoglobin. - Early ILD or left heart failure:  Very minimal amounts of interstitial thickening (eg, fibrosis, pulmonary edema fluid) can impair diffusion before they cause abnormalities in spirometry, lung volumes, or even visible infiltrates on chest imaging. - Mixed obstructive and restrictive disease:  Obstruction (low FEV1/FVC ratio, high lung volumes) and restriction (high FEV1/FVC ratio, low lung volumes) have opposing effects that can result in pseudonormalized spirometry and volumes.  However, DLCO can be greatly reduced by the "double hit." # Normative conditions ## Aging The main impact of aging on PFT is a gradual elevation of RV ((Figure 6)).  Aging is associated with a progressive degradation of lung elastin.  Loss of elastic airway tethering fibers allows for easy expiratory closure and air trapping.  Therefore, RV progressively rises, roughly doubling between age 30 and 70.  This produces a concomitant reduction in VC.  In this way, emphysema is often likened to a highly accelerated form of lung aging.  However, PFT values are normalized (ie, expressed as a percent of predicted) for age and height.  Therefore, even though RV increases (and VC decreases), PFT values remain in the normal range within the aging cohort. ## Obesity The primary impact of obesity on PFT is a reduced FRC due to the weight of adipose tissue around the thorax and abdomen.  If plethysmographic lung volumes are unavailable (ie, only spirometry is available), a low ERV can be a surrogate for decreased FRC.  Despite this low-resting lung volume, the inspiratory muscles can compensate and expand the lungs fully against the excess weigh; therefore, TLC is typically preserved.  A true restrictive pattern (ie, TLC <80%) is usually not seen until obesity becomes extreme (eg, BMI is ≥60 kg/m2), at which point the diaphragm cannot counter the increased load. ## Pregnancy The main impact of pregnancy of PFT is reduced FRC due to upward displacement of the lungs by the gravid uterus.  Progesterone stimulates a respiratory drive to increase RV and respiratory frequency, resulting in a higher minute ventilation and slight respiratory alkalosis.  However, spirometry and other lung volumes are generally unaffected.  DLCO is slightly elevated due to increased circulating blood volume and cardiac output. # Summary Pulmonary function tests typically consist of 3 sections. - Spirometry evaluates air movement and measures key metrics such as FVC and FEV1.  These values define the obstructive pattern (FEV1/FVC <0.7).  Spirometry is often performed before and after an acute bronchodilator, which differentiates between reversible (eg, asthma) and irreversible (eg, emphysema) obstruction. - Plethysmography (and other techniques) measures the lung volumes that cannot be assessed via spirometry, namely total lung capacity (TLC), functional residual capacity (FRC), or residual volume (RV).  These values define the restrictive pattern (TLC, FRC, or RV <80%).  - Diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO) evaluates gas transfer from the alveolar airspace into the capillary blood.  This can differentiate between pathologies in which the alveolar membrane is normal (eg, obstructive:  chronic bronchitis; restrictive:  chest wall deformity) or diseased (eg, obstructive:  emphysema; restrictive:  interstitial lung disease).  ​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​

articles.title: Pneumothorax
articles.markdown:
# Pneumothorax # Introduction  Pneumothorax (PTX) occurs when air enters the pleural space, leading to partial or complete collapse of the affected lung.  PTX can occur spontaneously in individuals without any known lung disease (primary PTX), as a complication of preexisting lung diseases (secondary PTX), or as a result of trauma. # Pathogenesis Normally, pleural pressure is negative relative to alveolar pressure, keeping the lung expanded and held against the chest wall.  If air enters the pleural space through a hole in the lung surface (eg, ruptured bleb from emphysema), airway (eg, bronchopleural fistula from surgery), or chest wall (eg, penetrating chest wound), the pleurae will separate, eliminating the negative pressure gradient and causing the lung to collapse (because of the natural inward elastic recoil of the lungs), resulting in a **simple PTX** ((Figure 1)). If air keeps entering the pleural space without the ability to exit, the PTX continues to expand.  As it expands, the PTX compresses mediastinal structures, including the vena cava and right heart chambers ((Figure 2)).  This is known as **tension PTX** ((Figure 3)).  Positive pressure mechanical ventilation is a risk factor for tension PTX, because additional air is forced in with each breath. # Classification As previously mentioned, PTX can be classified mechanistically into primary spontaneous PTX, secondary spontaneous PTX, and traumatic (provoked) PTX. ## Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) - Definition:  no trauma, no underlying lung disease - Risk factors:  younger adult male, tall and thin body habitus, active smoking - Pathogenesis:  normal mechanical stress during respiration causes rupture of occult subpleural blebs (hypothesized) due to subtle defects in lung connective tissue (eg, elastin, collagen, alpha-1-antitrypsin) or areas of concentrated strain (eg, apical stretch in tall individuals) ## Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP) - Definition:  no trauma, presence of underlying lung or airway disease - Risk factors:  emphysema (eg, rupture of bullae or blebs), pneumonia (eg, friability of inflamed lung tissue), malignancy (eg, erosion through pleura), lung cysts, interstitial lung disease (eg, fibrotic retraction), pleural endometriosis (ie, catamenial PTX) - Pathogenesis:  normal mechanical stress during respiration leads to rupture of alveolar walls due to structural or inflammatory lung disease ## Traumatic (provoked) PTX - Definition:  trauma from internal sources (eg, bronchoscopy) or external sources (eg, rib fracture, stab wound; lung apices extend above the level of the clavicle and first rib) - Risk factors:  chest trauma (blunt or sharp), rib fractures, positive pressure ventilation (ie, barotrauma), and iatrogenesis due to procedures (eg, bronchoscopy, thoracentesis, central venous catheter placement) - Pathogenesis:  abnormal physical forces damage the visceral pleura, regardless of underlying lung disease Although spontaneous pneumothoraces are generally thought of as occurring randomly with no provocation, they often develop after a large spike in intrathoracic pressure (eg, violent coughing, sneezing) or a rapid drop in barometric pressure (eg, decompression from diving, air travel). # Clinical presentation and diagnosis ## Presentation PTX typically presents with sudden onset of sharp (pleuritic), unilateral chest pain and dyspnea.  PSPs usually tend to be smaller, with a more benign clinical course due to the absence of preexisting lung disease.  Conversely, SSPs tend to be larger and are more likely to cause overt respiratory failure. ## Physical examination - Palpation can reveal crepitus due to air in the soft tissues; extensive subcutaneous air can result in a raised "puffy" appearance of the torso, neck, or face.  Auscultation reveals **absent breath sound**s on the affected side ((Table 1)).  Percussion is hyperresonant.  - Patients with **tension PTX** have severe respiratory distress, **hemodynamic instability** (ie, hypotension due to reduced venous return), and contralateral **tracheal deviation**.  The position of the trachea can be quickly assessed by placing the index finger on one sternoclavicular joint, the ring finger in the other, and the middle finger on the thyroid prominence. ## Chest imaging - Chest x-ray (CXR):  CXR shows a pleural line that represents the collapsed lung margin, with no lung markings peripheral to it and a hyperlucent rim of air in the pleural space ((Image 1)).  A deep sulcus sign reflects lucency of the costophrenic angle due to air surrounding the diaphragm ((Image 2)); it might be the only indication of PTX in patients who are supine (ie, air rises up anteriorly, so a pleural line cannot be seen on frontal film).  Subcutaneous emphysema appears as air bubbles in the soft tissues ((Image 3)); large collections can even highlight underlying muscle (eg, pectoralis) fibers.  With tension PTX, CXR shows contralateral mediastinal shift and tracheal deviation ((Image 4)). - CT:  Small pneumothoraces (ie, <15% volume collapse) cannot be seen on CXR, and require CT for confirmation.  CXR underestimates actual PTX size due to 1-dimensional representation of a 3-dimensional volume (eg, a 20% pleural line collapse on CXR \[ie, 80% remaining\] = 49% lung volume collapse in reality \[because (80%)3 = 0.83 = 0.51 = 51%\]).  CT is also preferred for visualizing the underlying causes of SSP (eg, cancer, pneumonia, interstitial lung disease).  - Ultrasound:  Bedside ultrasound is gaining popularity for rapid detection of PTX based on absence of lung sliding (ie, no respiratory movement due to separation of visceral and parietal pleurae) and presence of a "lung point" (where the pleural layers join again) # Differential diagnosis Because PTX typically presents to the emergency department, the differential diagnosis is based around the 6 life-threatening causes of acute chest pain (and dyspnea or respiratory distress) and can often be quickly narrowed with basic studies (ie, physical examination, CXR, ECG).  Distinguishing characteristics of each of these conditions are as follows: ## PTX Breath sounds are absent, CXR shows a pleural line, and there is possible tracheal deviation (if tension physiology is developing). ## Pulmonary embolism Breath sounds are normal, CXR is usually normal (or rarely shows focal oligemia or wedge-shaped infarction), and ECG shows sinus tachycardia ± a right ventricular strain strain pattern (eg, S1Q3T3, precordial \[V1-V4\] T-wave inversions \[TWIs\]). ## Acute coronary syndrome Breath sounds are normal, CXR is usually normal (unless there is concurrent acute heart failure), and ECG shows ischemic changes (eg, ST-segment depression or elevation, TWIs). ## Aortic dissection Breath sounds are normal, there is often severe hypertension ± arm pulse differential, and CXR classically shows mediastinal widening (type A) and possible pleural effusion (hemothorax). ## Cardiac tamponade Breath sounds are normal, there may be components of Beck triad (eg, hypotension, muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins), CXR may show a globular cardiac silhouette (effusion), and ECG may show electrical alternans or evidence of pericarditis (eg, diffuse ST-segment elevation). ## Esophageal rupture Breath sounds are normal, patients have a septic appearance, and CXR may show a pleural effusion (left > right) and pneumomediastinum ((Image 5)).  Esophageal rupture can also be associated with extensive subcutaneous emphysema and Hamman crunch (precordial crackles with each heartbeat). ## Special consideration:  Chest polytrauma In the setting of chest trauma, PTX is usually part of a larger injury complex, which can include: - Rib fractures ((Image 6)):  The jagged edge of the fracture can puncture the lung. - Flail chest ((Image 7)):  ≥3 consecutive ribs, each of which is fractured in ≥2 places, may result in paradoxical movement of a chest wall segment. - Hemothorax:  Bood accumulation (eg, due to laceration of an intercostal artery) can coexist with PTX, resulting in an air-fluid level (ie, flat line rather than meniscus). - Pulmonary contusion:  Lung parenchyma bruising (eg, due to trauma) can present on imaging as irregular (non-lobar) opacification, often affecting peripheral lung tissue immediately subjacent to the chest wall ((Image 8)). - Cardiomediastinal injuries:  Traumatic aortic rupture or dissection, cardiac contusion, and hemopericardium. # Management of tension PTX Tension PTX is fatal (ie, obstructive shock, no preload) unless emergently decompressed.  For hemodynamically unstable patients, **needle thoracostomy** (eg, at 2nd intercostal space and midclavicular line) is performed.  An audible rush of air indicates decompression.  Clinical improvement is immediate (ie, blood pressure stabilizes within a few seconds).  Next, definitive drainage is performed with placement of an indwelling pleural drain (eg, pigtail catheter or **chest tube**). In addition to positive pressure ventilation, another high-risk scenario for tension PTX is an open chest wound.  Air is sucked in during inspiration but cannot exit if the wound flap forms a one-way valve.  Such patients can be temporized in the field with a 3-sided dressing, allowing pleural air to exit during expiration while sealing the wound during inspiration ((Figure 4)). # Management of PTX in the absence of tension physiology ## 100% oxygen therapy (nitrogen washout) and observation Therapy with 100% oxygen is a possibility for small PTX (ie, <15% volume loss, or <1 cm rim of air) in clinically stable patients with minimal symptoms.  The mechanism is increased resorption rate of pleural gas.  Breathing 100% oxygen washes out alveolar nitrogen (~0% N2) whereas the PTX consists of atmospheric air (~78% N2).  This creates a gradient for nitrogen to diffuse from the pleural space back into the alveoli and capillaries, leading to resorption of the PTX. ## Definitive drainage:  Pigtail catheter or chest tube Definitive drainage is required for most moderate-to-large PTX (ie, ≥15% volume loss, or ≥1 cm rim of air) and in patients with respiratory difficulty or hypoxemia. - A small bore drain (eg, pigtail catheter) is preferred for simple spontaneous PTX. - A large bore (surgical) chest tube (which leads to pulmonary reexpansion) is preferred for trauma and concurrent inflammatory effusions (eg, hemopneumothorax) ((Image 9)). Insertion is at the 5th intercostal space and midaxillary line. The tubing system is monitored using a water-sealed chamber ((Video 1)): - Air leak (ie, bubbles) indicates an unresolved PTX or an opening in the system (eg, hole in tubing). - Tidaling (ie, respiratory variation in water level) indicates that the lung has not fully reexpanded. The pressure can be adjusted manually.  Placing the system on wall suction (ie, −20 cm H2O) is usually not necessary unless there is significant effusion fluid as well, and doing so can potentially delay PTX healing (ie, by tugging the pleural defect open).  Instead, the chamber should be placed on a water seal, which allows air to escape but not reenter.  Subsequent CXR (eg, 4-6 hours) is obtained to check for reaccumulation of PTX.  The pleural drain can generally be removed if the lung remains fully expanded.  Removal is usually painful and can result in a sudden gasp that sucks air back into pleural space.  Therefore, it is ideally removed during exhalation (ie, patient humming): pull quickly, and immediately cover with adhesive gauze. While the chest tube is inserted, it should be clamped only very briefly when searching for an air leak (ie, persistent bubbles when clamping at the insertion site indicates a leak in the tubing).  Patients should never be left clamped and unattended (risk of tension).  Longer "clamping trials" are indicated only to check for recurrence of pleural effusion. ## Persistent air leak or recurrent PTX Persistent air leak (ie, continued bubbling from pleural drain after 5-7 days) can be due to an **alveolopleural or bronchopleural fistulas**.  Prolonged leaks most commonly occur in the setting of pulmonary resection (eg, 20% after lobectomy).  There are 4 main treatment pathways: - Bronchoscopic occlusion with endobronchial (1-way) valves or sealant material (eg, fibrin glue) - Pleurodesis with chemical sclerosing agent (eg, talc) or autologous blood patch - Surgical repair for control of larger fistulas (eg, muscle flap, stapling) - Discharge with a unidirectional external chest (Heimlich) valve ((Figure 5)); this is most appropriate for patients with minimal air leak (1+ or 2+ bubbles) and excellent medical literacy ## Air travel and diving Flight is absolutely contraindicated for patients with an active PTX.  It is relatively contraindicated with a history of recurrent spontaneous PTX or known bullous emphysematous lung disease.  As airplane cabin pressure drops, any existing air pockets (eg, pneumothoraces, bullae, cysts) will enlarge proportionally, as dictated by Boyle's law (↓P·↑V = nRT = constant).  At the standard pressurization of 8,000 feet (0.7 atm), volume expands by ~43% relative to sea level. Compared to flight, the risk of barotrauma (eg, PTX) is even greater with diving due to the larger depressurization change (eg, from 10 atm at 30 feet below water, to 1 at at sea level).  Diving is contraindicated in any patient with a history of spontaneous PTX or known cystic, bullous, or emphysematous lung disease. # Summary Pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space, leading to partial or complete collapse of the affected lung.  Pneumothorax can occur spontaneously in individuals (tall, thin, male) without any known lung disease (ie, primary spontaneous), as a complication of underlying lung conditions (ie, secondary spontaneous), or as a result of trauma.  Diagnosis is made primarily through chest imaging, which shows the pleural line of the collapsed lung; CT scanning is usually needed to identify the underlying cause of secondary spontaneous pneumothoraces.  Management ranges from observation and oxygen therapy for small pneumothorax to definitive pleural drainage (eg, pigtail catheter) for larger symptomatic pneumothorax.  Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening situation that occurs when the pneumothorax compresses the mediastinum (eg, contralateral shift), resulting in diminished venous return to the right heart.  It is treated with emergent needle decompression. ​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​
