articles.markdown:
# Pneumonia # Introduction Pneumonia refers to infection and associated inflammation of the lung parenchyma due to a wide range of commensal and foreign pathogens.  In addition to local effects on lung tissue, pneumonia often induces a widespread inflammatory host response.  Pneumonia is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, and it is the leading infectious cause of death worldwide. # Classification, microbiology, and pathogenesis Pneumonia can be classified based on the setting of acquisition (eg, community vs hospital), which correlates closely with the causative microorganism. ## Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) - **Definition**:  onset outside hospital settings (eg, at home) or <48 hours after hospital admission - **Microbiology**:  pathogens, in decreasing order of prevalence, include: - Typical bacteria (*Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Moraxella catarrhalis*) - Respiratory viruses (eg, influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, SARS-CoV-2) - Atypical (ie, lacking a cell wall) bacteria (*Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Chlamydia pneumoniae*, *Legionella pneumophila*) - **Risk factors** ((Table 1)):  age (<2 or >65), aspiration (eg, dementia, dysphagia), impaired secretion clearance (eg, immobility, weak cough, post-surgery), chronic heart and lung disease, immunosuppressed states (eg, due to alcohol use), and long-term proton pump inhibitor use - **Pathogenesis**: - Typical bacteria are commensal (ie, normal flora, present in low numbers) in the upper respiratory mucosa, kept at bay by host mechanisms.  Defective host defense (eg, mucociliary paralysis after viral upper respiratory infection), or aspiration, allows bacteria to reach alveoli and replicate extracellularly.  *Staphylococcus aureus*, *S pneumoniae*, and *Streptococcus pyogenes* are the most common causes of postviral secondary bacterial pneumonia (especially after influenza). - Viruses and atypical bacteria are contracted from the environment (typically through droplets) and infect the respiratory and alveolar epithelium, replicating intracellularly. ## Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) and ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) - **Definitions**: - HAP:  onset ≥48 hours after hospital admission - VAP:  onset ≥48 hours after endotracheal intubation, or occurring in a tracheostomized patient - **Microbiology** ((Table 2)):  Nosocomial gram-negative bacilli (eg, *Enterobacteriaceae* spp., *Klebsiella*, *Pseudomonas*) and gram-positive cocci (eg, *S aureus*).  Drug resistance (eg, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase \[ESBL\]–producing, methicillin-resistant *S aureus* \[MRSA\]) is common. - **Risk factors**:  prolonged hospitalization, mechanical ventilation, intensive care unit (ICU) stay, previous antibiotic usage, and chronic disease (especially chronic kidney disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease \[COPD\], and heart failure) - **Pathogenesis**:  colonization of the oropharynx (eg, biofilm around endotracheal tube) followed by aspiration into the lower respiratory tract ((Figure 1)) ## Other pneumonia designations - **Necrotizing pneumonia** results when pneumonia (CAP, HAP, or VAP) leads to lung tissue destruction, resulting in pulmonary cavitation ((Image 1)), abscesses, and higher risk for pleural extension (empyema).  Necrotizing pneumonia is mainly due to oral anaerobes (eg, *Fusobacterium necrophorum*, *Peptostreptococcus*), polymicrobial infection, or bacterial strains with cytolytic toxins (eg, MRSA-producing Panton-Valentine Leukocidin \[PVL\]; *S pneumoniae*–producing pneumolysin A) - **Zoonotic pneumonia** is transmitted to humans through direct or indirect contact with vertebrates: - **Tularemia** ((Table 3)) (*Francisella tularensis*):  wild rabbit hunting; ulcerating painful adenopathy - **Psittacosis** (*Chlamydia psittaci*):  domestic parrots; often severe atypical (interstitial) pneumonia - **Q fever** (*Coxiella burnetii*):  dairy and livestock workers (bovine placentas); indolent atypical pneumonia, hepatitis, and endocarditis - **Pneumonic plague** ((Table 4)) (*Yersinia pestis*):  contagious droplets (flea bite not required); destructive pneumonia (hemoptysis) - **Anthrax** (*Bacillus anthracis*):  animal hides; toxin-mediated, hemorrhagic mediastinitis ## Aspiration pneumonia vs pneumonitis Aspiration **pneumonia** is an infection of the parenchyma due to inhalation of gastric or oropharyngeal bacteria.  In contrast, aspiration **pneumonitis** is sterile lung inflammation due to inhalation of gastric acid ((Table 5)).  Both conditions occur in individuals with aspiration risk factors (eg, depressed mental status, stroke/dysphagia), and both tend to produce right lower lobe (dependent) infiltrates.  However, pneumonitis has a more rapid onset (hr) after aspiration and spontaneous resolution without the need for antibiotic treatment. # Clinical presentation and diagnosis ## Definition and presentation Pneumonia is **clinically** diagnosed based on the combination of: - New **pulmonary infiltrate** on chest imaging - Compatible **symptoms** (fever, cough, chest pain, dyspnea, purulent sputum) Additional symptoms can be due to the location of infiltrate (eg, upper quadrant abdominal pain referred from lower lobe).  General signs of systemic inflammation (eg, malaise, gastrointestinal distress) are common.  Very young or elderly patients tend to have nonspecific presentations (eg, altered mental status, lethargy). Pneumonia due to **atypical** bacteria can be associated with distinctive clinical syndromes, such as hyponatremia (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion) and febrile gastroenteritis with *Legionella* ((Table 6)), or with subacute hemolytic anemia and other cold agglutinin manifestations (eg, acrocyanosis) with *Mycoplasma* ((Table 7)).  These intracellular pathogens also tend to produce pulse-temperature dissociation (ie, relative bradycardia, or Faget sign). Hypoxemia occurs due to ventilation/perfusion mismatch.  In the acute exudative phase of pneumonia, hypoxemia can be marked because local inflammation increases perfusion (hyperemia) to the infected, nonventilated region.  Later, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is restored, and hypoxemia gradually improves despite persistence of radiographic infiltrate for several weeks. ## Radiology Chest x-ray (less sensitive than CT) may lag behind symptoms by up to 48 hours. - A lobar consolidation pattern is most commonly seen with typical bacteria (eg, pneumococcus), and can be multifocal and bilateral ((Image 2)). - A diffuse interstitial pattern is most commonly seen with atypical bacteria (eg, *Mycoplasma*) or viruses ((Image 3)). ## Respiratory (eg, sputum) microbiology - Gram stain:  Typical bacteria (ie, with a peptidoglycan cell wall, extracellular) can be visualized, but atypical bacteria (no cell wall, intracellular) cannot.  Presence of neutrophils with blank Gram stain raises suspicion for atypical (or viral) pathogens. - Culture:  This is generally not relevant for outpatient CAP, but it is recommended for patients who are hospitalized to assess for antibiotic resistance/susceptibility. - PCR:  This is the test of choice to detect respiratory viruses (eg, multiplex panel) and atypical bacteria. ## Other studies: - Urine *Legionella* antigen and serum pneumococcal antigen have become standardized in the work-up of patients with pneumonia. - A blood culture can detect concurrent bacteremia (most commonly seen with *S pneumoniae*) and is indicated in patients who are hospitalized. - Additional testing for mycobacteria (eg, acid-fast bacillus stain), fungi (eg, urine *Histoplasma* antigen), and opportunistic pathogens (eg, *Pneumocystis*, *Cryptococcus*) is directed by clinical data (eg, social history, HIV status). # Differential diagnosis ## Lobar consolidation In addition to lobar pneumonia (usually bacterial), other conditions are on the differential: - **Pulmonary embolism with infarction:**  Peripheral wedge-shaped opacity (Hampton hump) can resemble a pneumonic infiltrate ((Image 4)).  In addition, systemic inflammation (eg, fever) can be present.  However, sputum is usually bloody (hemoptysis) rather than purulent. - **Atelectasis:**  Alveolar consolidation can also be due to atelectasis ((Image 5)).  In contrast to pneumonia (pus filling the alveolar space), atelectasis results in volume loss (airless alveolar space) and a potential mediastinal shift ipsilaterally.  Signs of systemic inflammation are usually absent or minimal. - **Lung mass:**  Focal consolidation can indicate a mass lesion (eg, carcinoma) ((Image 6)).  These lesions are chronic, expand slowly, usually have irregular/spiculated borders, and are not typically associated with acute infectious symptoms unless they block the airway (ie, post-obstructive pneumonia).  Traditionally, follow-up chest x-ray (eg, in 6-12 weeks) was performed in high-risk patients (eg, those who are older, smoke, or have COPD) to evaluate for infiltrate resolution (vs underlying mass).  However, this practice is being replaced with lung cancer screening using low-dose CT scan. ## Diffuse interstitial infiltrates In addition to interstitial pneumonia (usually atypical or viral), other conditions are on the differential: - **Left ventricular failure:**  Interstitial markings can reflect alveolar septal fluid and lymphatic fullness from left ventricular dysfunction or general volume overload ((Image 7)).  Cardiogenic interstitial fluid is usually accompanied by other signs of congestion such as vascular cephalization (engorgement of upper lobe vessels), pleural effusions, and alveolar edema (ground-glass opacity).  However, infections, including pneumonia, are a common trigger for heart failure decompensation. - **Interstitial lung disease (ILD):**  Reticulation (linear, lacy markings) are a central finding of ILDs such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and sarcoidosis ((Image 8)).  The clinical course of ILD is typically chronic (months to years) rather than subacute, as in atypical pneumonia (weeks). ## Recurrent pneumonia Recurrent (sequential) pneumonia is further categorized based on whether episodes are limited to one anatomic region (same lobe each time) or different locations ((Table 8)): - Same lobe:  usually indicates a local postobstructive issue (eg, endoluminal mass, foreign body) or recurrent aspiration (usually in the right lower lobe) (eg, dysphagia, CNS depression) - Different lobes:  usually indicates diffuse/systemic issue such as immunodeficiency with or without bronchiectasis (eg, common variable immunodeficiency, hypogammaglobulinemia) or issues with mucociliary function (eg, Kartagener syndrome, cystic fibrosis) # Management ## Triage The first step in treating patients with CAP is deciding the site of care; a standardized tool (eg, CURB-65) can be helpful ((Figure 2)): - Patients who are stable (ie, CURB-65 score 0-1) can be treated with oral antibiotics on an outpatient basis ((Figure 3)). - Patients who are less stable (ie, CURB-65 score ≥2) require hospital admission of intravenous (IV) antibiotics and closer monitoring. - Patients who are acutely unstable with septic organ dysfunction ((Table 9)) require ICU admission for IV antibiotics and intensive support (eg, mechanical ventilation). All patients with HAP or VAP require inpatient treatment with IV antibiotics. ## Antibiotic therapy Antibiotics are begun empirically based on the class of pneumonia (CAP vs HAP/VAP). For patients with **CAP** ((Table 10)): - Empiric regimen:  Typical bacterial coverage with beta-lactam (eg, amoxicillin, cefpodoxime) PLUS atypical bacterial coverage with macrolide (eg, azithromycin) or doxycycline.  Respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy (eg, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) is also a viable option but is reserved for higher-risk patients with beta lactam intolerance. - Special considerations:  Antipseudomonal and/or anti-MRSA coverage are added for patients who are hospitalized and have risk factors such as structural lung disease (eg, bronchiectasis, advanced COPD), recent IV antibiotic exposure, or clinical clues (eg, MRSA suspected with cavitation, sputum Gram-positive cocci in clusters, positive nasal swab). - Duration:  5-7 days for uncomplicated CAP, but longer courses if complications arise (eg, parapneumonic effusion \[PPE\]) For patients with **HAP or VAP** ((Table 11)): - Empiric regimen:  Broad spectrum gram-positive and gram-negative coverage with antipseudomonal activity (eg, cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam) - Special considerations:  Anti-MRSA coverage added for patients with risk factors (eg, local antibiogram resistance >20%).  Multidrug resistant gram-negative bacteria (eg, long-term nursing home residents, frequent hospitalization) require carbapenems (eg, meropenem) for ESBL-producing organisms, or ultrabroad beta lactamase inhibitors (eg, ceftazidime-avibactam) for carbapenemase-producing organisms. - Duration:  7 days Special populations: - **Childhood:**  Empiric antibiotics are usually guided by clinical features and radiology.  Children with abrupt onset, focal crackles, and lobar infiltrates (ie, mostly due to *S pneumoniae*) are treated with amoxicillin.  Those with subacute onset, bilateral crackles, and interstitial infiltrates (ie, mostly due to atypical bacteria) are treated with a macrolide.  Tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones are generally avoided (eg, due to risk for bone and cartilage damage). - **Pregnancy:**  Tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones are generally avoided due to teratogenicity (eg, skeletal malformations).  There is a lower threshold for hospital admission to prevent fetal complications such as hypoxemia (ie, goal maternal SpO2 ≥95%). In all cases, the empiric regimen is later narrowed based on available microbiology data, or it is potentially discontinued based on negative procalcitonin assay.  Management of viral pneumonia is discussed in detail in a separate article. ## Prevention - CAP is prevented through public health measures such as smoking cessation, hand hygiene, and vaccinations (specifically, influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations).  The pneumococcal immunization schedule is complex due to multiple vaccine brands ((Table 12)).  In general, the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20) is indicated for all adults age ≥65 and selected adults age <65 with risk factors for invasive pneumococcal disease (eg, asplenia, diabetes mellitus, COPD). - HAP and VAP are prevented through hospital checklists targeting aspiration (ie, care bundles), including head of bed elevation, screening for dysphagia, early mobilization (to prevent atelectasis and increase cough strength), and oropharyngeal decontamination (eg, subglottic suctioning, chlorhexidine mouth washes) in patients who are intubated ((Table 13)). # Complications Patients with pneumonia are at risk for local and systemic complications: ## Local complications - **Lung abscess**:  mostly due to anaerobes (eg, poor dentition) or pyogenic bacteria (eg, *S aureus*) creating a suppurative pocket within the parenchyma.  Most (~90%) lung abscesses resolve with prolonged (3-6 weeks) antibiotic therapy alone; large abscess sometimes require percutaneous drainage.  Postinfectious cysts (pneumatoceles) can form but typically cause no long-term problems. - **PPE** ((Table 14)):  results from localized inflammation that allows lung interstitial fluid to move across the visceral pleural membrane into the pleural space.  The fluid is characteristically exudative (eg, based on Light criteria) ((Table 15)). - **Uncomplicated PPE**:  Uncomplicated PPE consists of sterile exudative fluid due to reactive inflammation and typically resolves with antibiotics for the adjacent pneumonia. - **Complicated PPEs and empyema**:  Lack of clinical improvement (eg, persistent fever and leukocytosis) after several days of antibiotic therapy is concerning for complicated PPE.  Complicated PPEs reflect microbial translocation into the pleural space, which can lead to fibrinous loculation (poor antibiotic penetration).  In addition, complicated PPEs are generally characterized by pH <7.2, glucose <60 mg/dL, leukocytes >50,000 mm3, and markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase (eg, >500 U/L) but falsely negative culture/Gram stain.  **Empyema** represents further progression of infection in the pleural space with frank pus and usually a positive culture/Gram stain.  In addition to antibiotics, definitive drainage (eg, pigtail catheter) is required for treatment. ## Systemic complications - **Sepsis:**  Chest infections are the leading cause of sepsis, an excessive host inflammatory response which leads to distributive shock and multiple organ dysfunction.  Management is supportive (eg, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors) - **Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS):**  Pneumonia is the most common cause of ARDS, reflecting diffuse alveolar and systemic inflammation.  Management involves lung-protective ventilation (eg, low tidal volumes, prevention of barotrauma). Elderly patients who are hospitalized and have pneumonia have a high risk for death (~25%), readmission, and loss of functional status (eg, discharge to institutional care, rather than home). # Summary Pneumonia is an infection of the lung parenchyma that can produce significant local and systemic inflammation.  Community-acquired pneumonia is mainly caused by typical bacteria (eg, pneumococcus), atypical bacteria (eg, *Mycoplasma*), and respiratory viruses, whereas hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia are usually caused by nosocomial bacteria with a high rate of drug resistance.  In most cases, pathogenesis involves aspiration of commensal upper respiratory flora combined with defects in host immune defense.  Clinical pneumonia is defined as a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest imaging and compatible symptoms (eg, fever, chest pain, purulent sputum).  Nonspecific presentations (eg, lethargy, altered mental status) are common, especially in elderly patients.  Treatment involves triage to determine whether hospitalization is needed (eg, CURB-65 score ≥2).  Empiric antibiotic therapy is based on where pneumonia was acquired (eg, CAP vs HAP/VAP) and risk factors for drug-resistant bacteria (particularly MRSA and *Pseudomonas*).  Poor response to antibiotic treatment raises suspicion for an unusual pathogen (eg, zoonotic bacteria, fungi, mycobacteria) or closed-off infection (eg, complicated parapneumonic effusion). ​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​

Risk factors for developing pneumonia

Risk factor

Consequence

  • Advanced age (>65)
  • Coexisting diseases
  • Decreased gag & cough reflex
  • Decreased immune response & lung function
  • Young age (<2)
  • Immature immune system
  • Central nervous system depression
  • Decreased level of consciousness
  • Aspiration of oropharyngeal contents
  • Decreased cough & epiglottal reflexes
  • Chronic disease (cardiovascular, pulmonary)
  • Immunosuppression
  • Inadequate nutrition
  • Compromised immune system & impaired ability to fight infection
  • Prolonged immobility
  • Smoking & air pollution
  • Upper respiratory tract infection
  • Tracheal intubation
  • Impaired mucociliary clearance

Common pathogens in hospital-acquired pneumonia

Gram-negative bacilli

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae
  • Enterobacter species
  • Acinetobacter baumannii
  • Escherichia coli

Gram-positive cocci

  • Staphylococcus aureus
  • Streptococcus species

Tularemia

Epidemiology

  • Transmission:
    • Wild animal (eg, hare, rabbit) hunting/skinning
    • Tick or mosquito bite
    • Bioterrorism agent

Common manifestations

  • Nonspecific systemic symptoms (fever, malaise)
  • Ulceroglandular disease
    • Single papuloulcerative lesion (sometimes absent)
    • Tender, suppurative regional lymphadenopathy
  • Pneumonia

Microbiology

  • Poorly staining, gram-negative coccobacillus
  • Most strains require cysteine for growth
  • Evades most immune defenses & replicates within macrophages/neutrophils

Clinical features of Yersinia pestis

Signs/symptoms

Bubonic plague (80%-90% of cases)

  • Eschars, pustules, or skin necrosis at flea bite site
  • Sudden-onset fever, chills, weakness & headache
  • Painful lymphadenopathy with swelling (bubo), erythema & skin edema
  • Inguinal nodes most commonly affected
  • Rapid progression to sepsis with pneumonia, meningitis, or shock

Septicemic plague (10%-20% of cases)

  • Sudden-onset fever, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting & abdominal pain
  • No lymphadenopathy or bubo
  • Progresses to hypotension, disseminated intravascular coagulation & multiorgan failure

Diagnosis

  • High clinical suspicion with travel to endemic area (eg, southwestern US) or exposure to animals, plus unexplained fever with regional lymphadenitis
  • Blood cultures, fluid culture (eg, cerebrospinal fluid or bubo aspirate), serologic titers

Aspiration: pneumonitis vs pneumonia

Chemical pneumonitis

Aspiration pneumonia

Cause

  • Inhalation of gastric acid leads to direct chemical injury of bronchial & alveolar epithelial cells
  • Inhalation of large inoculate of oropharyngeal or gastric microbes overwhelms host pulmonary defenses

Onset

  • Sudden: within min or hr
  • Indolent: a few days to weeks

Manifestations

  • Abrupt-onset dyspnea, cough, hypoxemia
  • Low-grade fever
  • Diffuse crackles/wheezes
  • Infiltrate in dependent portion of lung
  • Fever
  • Cough with putrid sputum
  • Infiltrate in dependent portion of lung

Management

  • Supportive care
  • Oropharyngeal suction if event is witnessed
  • Antibiotics (eg, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin) that target community-acquired pneumonia pathogens

Legionella pneumonia

Epidemiology

  • Contaminated water
    • Hospital
    • Travel (cruise, hotel)

Clinical features

  • Fever >38.8 C (101.8 F)
  • Relative bradycardia
  • Gastrointestinal: diarrhea, vomiting, cramps
  • Pulmonary: delayed symptoms

Diagnosis

  • Hyponatremia
  • Chest x-ray: lobar infiltrate
  • Sputum Gram stain: PMNs, few/no organisms
  • Urine Legionella antigen

Treatment

  • Respiratory fluoroquinolone or newer macrolide

PMNs = polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

Mycoplasma pneumonia

Epidemiology

  • Respiratory droplets
  • Close quarters/young (eg, school, military)
  • Fall or winter

Clinical

  • Indolent headache, malaise, fever, persistent dry cough
  • Pharyngitis (nonexudative)
  • Macular/vesicular rash

Diagnostic

  • Normal leukocyte count
  • Subclinical hemolytic anemia (cold agglutinins)
  • Interstitial infiltrate (chest x-ray)

Treatment

  • Usually empiric
  • Macrolide or respiratory fluoroquinolone

Common causes of recurrent pneumonia

Same
lung lobe*

Bronchial obstruction

  • Extrinsic: neoplasm, adenopathy
  • Intrinsic: bronchiectasis, foreign body
 

Recurrent aspiration

  • Altered consciousness: seizure, sedatives, antipsychotics, alcohol, recreational drugs
  • Dysphagia: neurologic disorder, esophageal motility issue
  • Poor dental hygiene
  • Gastroesophageal reflux

Different
lung lobes

  • Immunodeficiency: HIV, leukemia, CVID
  • Sinopulmonary disease: cystic fibrosis, immotile cilia
  • Noninfectious: vasculitis, BOOP

*Recurrent aspiration can lead to pneumonia in different dependent regions of the lung depending on the position of the patient during the aspiration event.

BOOP = bronchiolitis obliterans with organizing pneumonia; CVID = common variable immunodeficiency.

Septic organ dysfunction

CNS

  • Delirium ("septic encephalopathy")

Cardiovascular

  • Vasodilation & distributive shock
  • Capillary leak (edema)
  • Myocardial depression (severe)

Pulmonary

  • Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (ARDS)

Renal

  • Acute kidney injury (ATN)

Hematologic

  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation
  • Acute bone marrow suppression (eg, thrombocytopenia)

Endocrine

  • Glucose dysregulation (hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia)
  • Primary adrenal insufficiency

Gastrointestinal
& hepatic

  • Cholestatic & hepatocellular liver injury
  • Paralytic ileus

Neuromuscular

  • Polyneuropathy & myopathy

ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome; ATN = acute tubular necrosis.

Empiric treatment of community-acquired pneumonia

Outpatient

  • Lower risk
    • Amoxicillin (high-dose = 1 g TID) or doxycycline or macrolide 
  • Higher risk (eg, age ≥65, comorbidities, or recent antibiotic use)
    • Respiratory fluoroquinolone* or beta-lactam PLUS macrolide

Inpatient
(non-ICU)

  • Beta-lactam + macrolide (IV)
  • Respiratory fluoroquinolone (IV)

Inpatient
(ICU)

  • Beta-lactam + macrolide (IV)
  • Beta-lactam + respiratory fluoroquinolone (IV)

*Levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, or gemifloxacin. 
ICU = intensive care unit; IV = intravenous; TID = 3 times daily.

Empiric treatment of hospital-acquired & ventilator-associated pneumonia

No risk for MRSA1 or MDR gram-negative pathogens2

Risk for MRSA1 but no risk for MDR gram-negative pathogens2

Risk for MRSA1 & MDR gram-negative pathogens2

One antibiotic active against MSSA & Pseudomonas

 

Beta-lactam preferred; do not use aztreonam, ciprofloxacin, or aminoglycoside monotherapy

One antibiotic active against Pseudomonas

 

PLUS

 

Vancomycin or linezolid

Two antibiotics (from different classes) active against Pseudomonas

 

PLUS

 

Vancomycin or linezolid

Antipseudomonal antibiotics:

  • Beta-lactams: cefepime, piperacillin/tazobactam, imipenem/cilastatin, meropenem
  • Aztreonam
  • Fluoroquinolones: ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin
  • Aminoglycosides: amikacin, gentamicin, tobramycin (should not be used as monotherapy)
  1. IV antibiotic use in the past 90 days, hospital unit with > 20% MRSA resistance, prior MRSA infection and/or MRSA colonization (positive nasal swab), hospitalized ≥ 5 days prior to the onset of VAP.
  2. IV antibiotic use in the past 90 days, hospital unit with > 10% resistance of gram-negative pathogens, hospitalized ≥ 5 days prior to the onset of VAP.

MDR = multidrug-resistant; MSSA = methicillin-susceptible S. aureus; VAP = ventilator-associated pneumonia.

Adult pneumococcal vaccination

Indications

  • Age ≥65
  • Age 19-64 with conditions that increase the risk for serious pneumococcal infection:
    • Diabetes mellitus; chronic heart, lung, liver, or kidney disease

articles.title: Pneumocystis Jirovecii Pneumonia
articles.markdown:
# Pneumocystis Jirovecii Pneumonia # Introduction *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia (PCP, or sometimes PJP) is an opportunistic infection that primarily affects individuals with weakened immune systems, particularly those with advanced HIV infection or those receiving immunosuppressive therapies.  Although the pathogen was previously thought to be a protozoan, it is now classified as a fungus, with some atypical features (eg, cell wall composition), based on molecular studies.  The letters in the acronym PCP previously referred to ***P**neumocystis **c**arinii* **p**neumonia (based on the prior name of *P jirovecii*) and now refer to ***P**neumo**c**ystis* **p**neumonia. # Pathophysiology Healthy patients rapidly clear the inhaled organisms, but those with **impaired cell-mediated immunity** (eg, advanced HIV, chronic immunosuppression) are at risk for a noninvasive infection that fills the alveoli and leads to slowly worsening pulmonary symptoms.  The infection also causes a severe inflammatory response that fills the alveoli with a foamy proteinaceous material, leading to impaired gas exchange and progressive respiratory symptoms. # Risk factors The risk factors for PCP are closely tied to the degree of immunosuppression: - **HIV/AIDS**:  particularly in individuals with a CD4 count <200 cells/mm3. - **Chronic glucocorticoid therapy**:  especially when combined with other immunosuppressants. - **Organ transplantation**:  due to the use of intensive immunosuppressive regimens. - **Hematologic malignancies**:  such as leukemia and lymphoma, often associated with chemotherapy-induced immunosuppression. - **Other immunosuppressive therapies**:  including TNF inhibitors and other biologics. # Pathology The organism appears as **cysts** with distinctive staining properties, typically identified using methenamine silver stain, which reveals the cell walls as crescent shapes structures.  With PCP, there is an interstitial pneumonitis; the alveoli become filled with a frothy exudate composed of the organisms, desquamated alveolar cells, and cellular debris, leading to reduced gas exchange and hypoxia. # Diagnosis The diagnosis of PCP involves a combination of clinical, laboratory, and radiographic findings, along with the identification of the organism in respiratory secretions. ## Clinical manifestations The clinical presentation of PCP varies depending on the underlying immunosuppressive condition. - **In individuals with HIV**:  The disease course is often **indolent**, with symptoms such as progressive dyspnea, a dry cough, and low-grade fever developing over several weeks. - **In immunocompromised individuals without HIV**:  The presentation is typically more acute, with rapid progression to severe respiratory failure. ## Laboratory findings - Nearly 90% of patients have lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels >50 U/L above baseline; an **LDH >450 U/L** is predictive of PCP rather than another pulmonary process. - Arterial blood gas analysis often reveals hypoxemia and an i**ncreased alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient**. - Serum **beta-D-glucan** levels may be elevated (because the cell wall of *P jirovecii* contains beta-D-glucan) but are nonspecific (because beta-D-glucan is a component of the cell wall in most fungi, including *Aspergillus*, *Candida*).  Therefore, this test cannot be used to definitively diagnose PCP. ## Imaging Chest x-ray typically shows diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates ((Image 1)).  However, normal chest x-rays are possible in early disease.  Thin-walled cystic lesions and spontaneous pneumothorax (in ~5% of cases) may also be seen. ## Microscopic identification *P jirovecii* cannot be cultured; therefore, diagnosis relies on the identification of the organism in respiratory specimens using specialized stains, such as **methenamine silver stain** ((Image 2)).  Induced sputum is the least invasive way to obtain respiratory samples; however, diagnostic sensitivity is 50%-90%.  As such, negative results necessitate further testing if PCP is suspected. In patients with suspected PCP with negative induced sputum testing, the next diagnostic test of choice is a fiberscopic bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage ((Image 3)).  This test is highly sensitive (90%-100%) for diagnosis of PCP. # Management The management of PCP involves prompt initiation of antimicrobial therapy and supportive care (eg, oxygen supplementation), with a potential role for corticosteroids. ## Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) is the first-line treatment for PCP.  Patients with mild or moderate disease are treated with oral TMP-SMX, whereas those with more severe disease (eg, large alveolar-arterial gradient, low PaO2, tachypnea) often require intravenous therapy.  Typical duration is 21 days. ## Corticosteroids *P jirovecii* proliferates within the alveoli and triggers a strong inflammatory response.  In addition, hypoxia often worsens with the initiation of antimicrobial treatment due to the release of proinflammatory intracellular macromolecules during lysis of the organism.  Therefore, **concomitant corticosteroids** are generally administered to those with severe PCP to reduce the inflammatory response.  **Indications** include: - a PaO2 ≤70 mm Hg - an A-a gradient ≥35 mm Hg, or - pulse oximetry <92% on room air. ## Alternates to TMP-SMX In patients who cannot tolerate TMP-SMX, alternate regimens are based on disease severity.  For mild disease, oral options include atovaquone, clindamycin plus primaquine, and TMP plus dapsone.  In moderate disease, clindamycin plus primaquine and TMP plus dapsone are used.  Severe disease requires more aggressive treatment, typically with clindamycin plus primaquine or intravenous pentamidine (which has a significant side effect profile, including hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, and nephrotoxicity). Patients being initiated on dapsone or primaquine should be evaluated for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency due to the risk of hemolytic anemia with these medications. ## Antiretroviral therapy In patients with HIV, antiretroviral therapy should also be initiated within 2 weeks (once hypoxia improves) to prevent AIDS progression. # Complications Complications of PCP can be severe and include: - **Respiratory failure**:  due to progressive hypoxemia and diffuse alveolar damage. - **Pneumothorax**:  occurs in about 5% of cases, often due to the rupture of cystic lesions in the lungs. - **Superimposed infections**:  bacterial superinfection can complicate the course of PCP. - **Treatment-related toxicity**:  especially with the use of pentamidine or corticosteroids. # Prognosis The prognosis of PCP depends on the degree of immunosuppression, the timeliness of treatment initiation, and the presence of complications.  With appropriate therapy, the mortality rate in HIV-positive individuals has decreased significantly.  However, non-HIV immunocompromised patients often have a worse prognosis due to the rapid progression of the disease and the severity of underlying conditions. # Prevention **TMP-SMX prophylaxis** (eg, 3 times weekly if double-strength) is effective against PCP and is recommended in HIV-positive individuals with a **CD4 count of <200/mm3**.  It can be discontinued once the CD4 count is above 200 cells/mm3 for more than 3 months. In patients without HIV, TMP-SMX prophylaxis is recommended for those who receive >1 month of daily prednisone (≥20 mg) and if there is also a second source of immunocompromise (eg, hematologic malignancy, additional immunosuppressive medication).  In those receiving immunosuppressive therapy following solid organ transplantation, PCP risk is usually greatest during the 6 months following transplantation, when immunosuppressive regimens tend to be most intensive.  Therefore, primary prophylaxis with TMP-SMX is typically administered during this period.  Because immunosuppressive regimens are generally tapered over time, patients can often stop TMP-SMX prophylaxis 6-12 months after transplant. # Special consideration:  PCP in infancy In children with HIV, PCP is often the initial AIDS-defining illness, and it usually presents at age 3-6 months.  Infants have high baseline levels of CD4 cells due to amplified thymic activity in the months after birth.  Therefore, they frequently develop immunocompromise from HIV at relatively high CD4 counts (eg, 1,000-1,200/mm3).  Common manifestations of PCP include low-grade fever, tachypnea, poor feeding, and progressive dyspnea.  Generalized adenopathy and hepatomegaly are often present.  Patients often have severe hypoxia, and chest x-ray classically shows bilateral perihilar reticulonodular infiltrates that become more diffuse as the illness progresses.  Because the pathogen cannot be cultured, the diagnosis is established when the organism is identified in pulmonary fluid (eg, induced sputum, bronchiolar lavage). # Differential diagnosis The differential diagnosis for PCP includes other causes of pneumonia and pulmonary infiltrates in immunocompromised patients: - **Cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonia**:  Both conditions can present with diffuse interstitial infiltrates and occur in immunocompromised hosts.  However, CMV pneumonia may present with more prominent systemic symptoms (eg, fever, malaise) and "owl's eye" inclusion bodies on histopathology. - **Bacterial pneumonia**:  Both PCP and bacterial pneumonia may present with cough, fever, and dyspnea.  However, bacterial pneumonias typically present with lobar consolidation rather than diffuse interstitial infiltrates and often have productive cough. - **Tuberculosis**:  Tuberculosis and PCP can present chronic cough and weight loss in immunocompromised patients.  However, tuberculosis often presents with upper lobe cavitary lesions, and acid-fast bacilli are identified in sputum samples. - **Cryptococcosis**:  Both PCP and cryptococcosis are fungal infections that occur in immunocompromised hosts.  However, cryptococcosis often presents with focal pulmonary nodules or masses and can disseminate to the central nervous system. # Summary *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia ((Table 1)) is a life-threatening opportunistic infection that predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals.  Prompt recognition and treatment are essential to improve outcomes.  The clinical presentation, diagnostic approach, and management strategies for PCP vary depending on the underlying immune status of the patient.  Despite advances in therapy, PCP remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, underscoring the importance of prophylactic measures in high-risk populations. ​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​

Pneumocystis pneumonia

Epidemiology

  • AIDS (CD4 <200/mm3)*
  • Immunosuppressive medications (eg, chronic glucocorticoids)

Manifestations

  • Indolent (AIDS) or acute respiratory failure (immunosuppressive treatment)
  • Dyspnea, hypoxia, dry cough, fever
  • ↑ Lactate dehydrogenase level
  • Diffuse bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates on pulmonary imaging

Diagnosis

  • Induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage

Treatment

  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole ± corticosteroids
  • Antiretroviral initiation (in AIDS)

*Patients with AIDS (CD4 <200/mm3) & those on chronic glucocorticoid therapy generally receive primary
prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

articles.title: Pleural Effusion
articles.markdown:
# Pleural Effusion # Introduction The pleural cavity is a potential space between the visceral and parietal pleural layers that normally contains a trace amount of fluid (~20 mL) serving as a lubricant during respiration ((Figure 1)).  A pleural effusion is an abnormal accumulation of fluid in this space caused by a variety of hydrostatic, secretory, or inflammatory processes that disrupt the balance of fluid formation and resorption. # Pathogenesis and classification ## Mechanisms Pleural fluid formation is primarily attributed to 4 major mechanisms ((Figure 2)). - **Hydrostatic pressure gradient** (pleural capillary − pleural space):  Increased pleural capillary pressure (eg, from left heart failure) drives extravasation into the pleural space.  Fluid builds up until it tamponades further formation (ie, higher left-sided filling pressures lead to larger effusions). - **Oncotic pressure gradient** (plasma proteins − pleural fluid proteins):  Decreased plasma oncotic pressure (eg, nephrotic syndrome) weakens the colloid drag that pulls fluid back into vessels.  However, plasma hypoproteinemia alone cannot induce an effusion.  Instead, it plays a minor role in maintaining effusions due to primary disease states associated with hypoalbuminemia (eg, renin-angiotensin-system–induced salt-water retention with nephrotic syndrome and cirrhosis, systemic inflammation and vascular permeability with malignancy and malnutrition). - **Vascular permeability**:  Increased vascular permeability (eg, inflammation, pneumonia) allows for plasma to freely filter between endothelial gap junctions and enter the pleural space. - **Lymphatic resorption**:  Pleural fluid is normally reabsorbed by parietal pleural lymphatic channels.  Blockage of these lymphatics (eg, pleural metastases, previous scarring) leads to decreased clearance of fluid. In addition, hepatic hydrothorax and urinothorax are unique causes in which peritoneal free fluid (eg, ascites, urine) seeps upward between tiny fenestrae in the diaphragm (transdiaphragmatic flow). ## Transudates vs exudates - **Transudates** are formed by hydrostatic and oncotic processes (eg, heart failure, cirrhosis), resulting in simpler fluid with lower protein content and specific gravity.  They tend to be bilateral and freely flowing. - **Exudates** are formed by inflammatory processes (eg, pleuritis, infection) that disrupt vessel permeability or lymphatic drainage.  The fluid is more complex, with higher protein content and specific gravity.  Exudative effusions tend to be unilateral and can become loculated (eg, due to fibrinous adhesions). # Clinical features Pleural effusions cause respiratory symptoms based on their size and characteristics. ## Presentation - Small effusions (ie, <500 mL) are usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on imaging.  Larger effusions can cause compressive atelectasis of the adjacent lung, resulting in dyspnea and hypoxemia.  For unilateral effusions, dyspnea is usually improved when lying ipsilaterally (ie, trepopnea) due to gravitational layering of fluid allowing better lung expansion. - When parietal inflammation (eg, parapneumonic, uremic pleurisy) exists, pain is typically pleuritic (ie, sharp and aggravated by deep breathing or coughing). ## Physical examination - Over the effusion, there is dullness to percussion, breath sounds are diminished, and tactile fremitus is decreased.  A friction rub (rasping or squeaky sound with breath excursion) can be heard when there is pleuritis and minimal effusion (ie, pleural layers must be directly in contact). ## Chest imaging - Chest x-ray (CXR):  In adults, ~200 mL of fluid is needed before first being detected as minimal costophrenic angle blunting (normally, the angles should be "sharp enough to pick teeth") ((Image 1)).  Pleural effusions obscure the diaphragm silhouette and have a meniscus due to surface tension ((Image 2)).  Plain CXR cannot reveal the underlying pathology (eg, consolidation, lung mass) behind the effusion because all structures are projected onto a single plane (eg, lobar pneumonia with and without a parapneumonic effusion might appear identical).  Therefore, cross-sectional or 3-D (ultrasound) imaging is often needed, especially for exudative effusions. - Chest CT with contrast:  CT with contrast is the preferred method for imaging pleural effusions when the cause is unknown (eg, suspected malignancy).  Radiocontrast highlights the pleural lining and associated lesions.  Clues toward an underlying cause (eg, mass, interstitial lung disease) can be visualized.  CT can better visualize loculations and pleural rinds that indicate complexity and/or chronicity ((Image 3)). - Ultrasonography:  In general, ultrasound is the preferred method for planning thoracentesis (ie, bedside in real time) and understanding dynamics of effusions (eg, loculated vs free-flowing). # Diagnosis ## Diagnostic thoracentesis Diagnostic thoracentesis involves sampling of 20-50 mL of pleural fluid ((Figure 3)).  It is not needed when the cause is clinically obvious (eg, bilateral effusions in patients with cardiac or renal failure) but is usually indicated in the absence of an obvious explanation, or for unilateral or very asymmetric effusions (especially left > right).  Any parapneumonic effusion with a safe volume (ie, >1 cm fluid stripe on ultrasound) should be sampled to ensure it is not a complicated effusion (ie, pH < 7.2) ((Table 1)) or progressing to empyema (ie, frank pus). ## Light criteria As a house officer, Dr. Richard Light performed thoracenteses on 150 patients and developed a set of rules that could distinguish transudates from exudates ((Table 2)).  The key concept of Light criteria is the **pleural fluid-to-serum** ratio.  An exudate is diagnosed if any one of the following is positive: - Pleural fluid-to-serum protein ratio > 0.5 - Pleural fluid-to-serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) ratio > 0.6 - Pleural LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal for serum LDH Light criteria are highly sensitive for exudates (**only 1 condition needed**).  Due to their sensitivity, they incorrectly classify around 25% of transudates as exudates.  The criteria remain widely used but are gaining criticism for including LDH in 2 items; this redundancy likely contributes to the greater false-positive rate.  Newer systems, such as the pleural fluid only 3-test combination (PFO3) criteria, are potentially more accurate and do not require paired serum testing. ## Exudates When fluid has been classified as an exudate, further analysis is usually required to elucidate the etiology.  Gross appearance can offer important clues: - Cloudy or turbid (ie, cannot read text behind the tube):  usually related to infection (eg, complicated parapneumonic effusion, empyema) - Greenish:  seen with rheumatoid arthritis effusions, empyema, gastric contents (eg, esophageal rupture), or biliary leak - Milky:  indicative of chylothorax, an effusion consisting of frank lymph (eg, disruption of thoracic duct) - Bloody:  could indicate hemothorax (ie, frank bleeding from thoracic vessel) Additional studies are tailored to the suspected scenario: - pH and glucose:  Indicates level of anaerobic metabolism (glycolysis).  Very low pH (ie, <7.2) and glucose (ie, <30) are seen in effusions with florid bacterial or leukocyte cellular activity (eg, empyemas, rheumatoid arthritis effusion). - Cell count differential - Neutrophilic (ie, >50,000/mm³) indicates bacterial infection (parapneumonic, empyema). - Lymphocytic (ie, >50%) is consistent with tuberculosis (usually >80%) or malignant effusion. - Eosinophilic (ie, >10%) has the widest differential, including drug-induced effusions, benign asbestos pleural effusion, malignancy, previous air or blood in the pleural space (ie, after pneumothorax, hemothorax, or surgery), and primary eosinophilic disorders (eg, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis). - Microbiology:  The presence of microbes automatically indicates a **complicated** parapneumonic effusion or, if frank pus is found, **empyema** ((Table 3)).  Therefore, Gram staining and culture are performed on all effusions associated with pneumonia.  Tuberculous empyema can occur without underlying parenchymal infection and is diagnosed with acid-fast bacillus staining and culture. - Cytology:  The sensitivity of a single pleural fluid cytology is ~90% for malignant effusions due to lung cancer, and rises to 98% after a second thoracentesis.  For overwhelmingly lymphocytic effusions (ie, >90%), flow cytometry is indicated to detect clonal expansion (eg, lymphoma). - Others - Albumin:  The pleural-serum albumin gradient (ie, >1.2 mg/dL) can clarify borderline exudative effusions (pseudoexudates), which occur in heart failure after diuretic therapy.  The pleural-serum total protein gradient (ie, >2.5) has a similar function. - Hematocrit:  A pleural fluid-to-blood hematocrit ratio >0.5 identifies true hemothorax (ie, overt bleeding from a thoracic or intercostal vessel).  In contrast, hemorrhagic effusions (eg, malignancy) can appear starkly bloody but are not true hemothoraces (eg, hematocrit ratio <0.5). - Triglycerides and cholesterol:  A high triglyceride level (ie, >110 mg/dL) with low cholesterol level (ie, pleural/serum ratio <1) indicates chylothorax (ie, chylomicron-rich fluid). - Amylase:  Amylase is elevated in effusions due to esophageal rupture (Boerhaave syndrome); it is a supportive finding but not sufficient for diagnosis (requires esophagram).  Amylase is also elevated in pancreaticopleural fistulas, a complication of pancreatitis.   - Adenosine deaminase (ADA):  ADA is elevated in tuberculosis empyema; it is a supportive finding but not sufficient for diagnosis (requires acid-fast bacilli stain, culture, or nucleic acid amplification testing). # Differential diagnosis ## Transudates The 3 most common causes of transudative effusions include:  left heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, and cirrhosis (including hepatic hydrothorax).  Three less common causes include: - Peritoneal dialysis (pleural fluid-to-serum glucose ratio > 1 due to dextrose in dialysate fluid) - Urinothorax (pleural fluid-to-serum creatinine ratio > 1) is the only transudate with very low pH, mirroring urine - Severe hypothyroidism (myxedema) A noteworthy exception is that heart failure effusions (normally transudative) can be borderline exudative, especially after rapid diuresis. ## Exudates The 3 most common causes of exudative effusions include:  infection (eg, viral pleuritis), malignancy (eg, pleural metastases), and autoimmune disorders (eg, lupus serositis).  Three less common causes include: - Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (due to exogenous fertility drugs) - Uremia (due to chronic serosal inflammation, similar to pericarditis) - Drug-induced infusion (eg, valproate, propylthiouracil) Noteworthy exceptions are that pulmonary embolism and malignancy (normally exudative) can be transudative in ~10% of cases. ## Opacified hemithorax When CXR reveals an opacified hemithorax (ie, "unilateral white out"), there are 3 possibilities ((Table 4)). - Massive pleural effusion ((Image 4)):  The trachea and mediastinum are deviated (ie, pushed) to contralateral side when displaced by the fluid volume. - Whole lung atelectasis ((Image 5)):  The trachea and mediastinum are deviated (ie, pulled) to ipsilateral side due to volume loss.  This level of total atelectasis can be caused by an ipsilateral obstruction (eg, tumor or mucus plug) or contralateral mainstem intubation. - Massive consolidation (all lobes):  The trachea and mediastinum remain midline because the alveoli do not change in volume, even though they are full of inflammatory cells. Tracheal deviation is not a reliable indicator when the mediastinal structures are fixed in place (eg, fibrosis, encasing mass). ## Concurrent pneumothorax A concurrent pneumothorax can sometimes accompany the pleural effusion (eg, hemopneumothorax due to rib fracture with intercostal artery laceration).  When air is present in the pleural space, water surface tension is lost.  This condition can be seen on CXR as absence of a meniscus; the top of effusion forms a straight line (ie, air-fluid level) instead. # Management ## Treatment of underlying condition Treating the underlying condition is often sufficient (ie, drainage not necessary) for small-to-moderate effusions that are relatively asymptomatic.  Examples include: - Optimizing diuretic dose and goal-directed medical therapy for decompensated heart failure - Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for viral or autoimmune pleuritis - Antibiotic therapy for uncomplicated (ie, pH >7.2, no organisms) parapneumonic effusion - Chemotherapy or immunotherapy (if appropriate) for metastatic lung cancer A residual chronic effusion (eg, from trapped lung due to previous pleurisy) may not require any specific treatment. ## Drainage Therapeutic thoracentesis is indicated for larger, symptomatic effusions.  The thoracentesis needle is aimed directly above the rib to avoid puncturing the neurovascular bundles that run underneath ((Figure 4)).  Typically, a safe volume for removal is between 1.0-1.5 L.  Removing too much fluid may increase the risk for reexpansion pulmonary edema, a form of inflammatory unilateral injury due to sudden stretch and reperfusion of the collapsed lung. Usually, just enough fluid is removed to relieve dyspnea and improve oxygenation.  However, definitive drainage (ie, removing all fluid possible) is indicated for all complicated parapneumonic effusions, empyemas, and hemothoraces.  This drainage can help with septic source control and prevent future pleural scarring (ie, fibrothorax, trapped lung). Bloody, loculated, or inflammatory effusions often require large-bore "surgical" chest tubes (eg, >24 Fr or >0.8 cm diameter).  For patients with complex infectious effusions, instilling an enzyme cocktail (eg, DNase + tissue plasminogen activator) into the pleural space can break up loculations and is noninferior to surgical decortication. ## Recurrent effusions Recurrence (ie, after initial therapeutic thoracentesis) can happen with both exudates (most commonly malignant and parapneumonic effusions) and transudates (most commonly uncontrolled heart failure, hepatic hydrothorax).  The choice of management depends on whether the lung is expandable or not (ie, trapped). - If the lung is trapped (eg, thick, fibrous rind from prior inflammation), options include surgical decortication (ie, rind removal) if symptomatic and monitoring if asymptomatic (because thoracentesis risks creating a vacuum that will quickly refill with fluid). - If the lung is expandable, creating adhesions between the visceral and parietal pleura (eg, pleurodesis with talc) or placing an indwelling pleural catheter (eg, PleurX™) to allow for self-controlled drainage can be considered. Hepatic hydrothorax tends to be refractory and may require a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt ((Figure 5)). # Summary Pleural effusions can be transudates or exudates based on their formation mechanisms.  Transudates typically arise from hydrostatic or oncotic imbalances (eg, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome), and exudates arise from disrupted vascular permeability or lymphatic drainage (eg, inflammation, malignancy).  Diagnostic thoracentesis (eg, for Light criteria) is performed for effusions with unclear cause (eg, unilateral, asymmetric).  Parapneumonic effusions should always be sampled to evaluate for complicated effusion or empyema, which require definitive drainage for source control.  Additional studies (eg, pH, glucose, cell count) can help clarify the etiology of exudates.  Management involves treatment of underlying cause and therapeutic drainage for large and symptomatic effusions.  Complete drainage (eg, with chest tube or serial thoracentesis) is recommended for highly inflammatory exudates (eg, empyema, hemothorax) to prevent chronic pleural scarring, which can result in trapped lung and restricted pulmonary function. ​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​​​​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌

articles.markdown:
# Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension Of The Newborn # Introduction Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) is characterized by persistently elevated pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) that leads to right-to-left shunting of deoxygenated blood through fetal circulatory pathways (eg, ductus arteriosus, foramen ovale), resulting in a gradient between preductal and postductal oxygen saturations. # Pathogenesis Fetal circulation is characterized by high PVR (due to hypoxic vasoconstriction) and low systemic vascular resistance (SVR) (due to in-parallel connection to low-resistance placental circulation via the umbilical arteries and vein) ((Figure 1)).  Therefore, in utero, PVR is greater than SVR, and the majority of blood is shunted from the high-resistance pulmonary circulation into the low-resistance systemic circulation (ie, right-to-left shunting), through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale.  After birth, pulmonary expansion and aeration normally leads to diffuse pulmonary vasodilation and decreased PVR. However, in PPHN, **PVR remains persistently elevated** after birth, generally in association with an underlying condition that affects the pulmonary circulation, as follows: - **Underdeveloped pulmonary circulation**:  results in fewer pulmonary vessels with abnormal branching and differentiation.  Risk factors for underdeveloped pulmonary vasculature include causes of pulmonary hypoplasia (eg, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, oligohydramnios, bronchopulmonary dysplasia). - **Maldeveloped pulmonary vasculature**:  results in an abnormally thickened pulmonary arteriolar muscle layer.  Risk factors for maldeveloped pulmonary vasculature include meconium aspiration syndrome and fetal pulmonary overcirculation (eg, premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, total anomalous pulmonary venous return). - **Maladapted pulmonary vasculature**:  results in diffuse vasoconstriction of otherwise normally developed pulmonary vasculature.  Risk factors for maladapted pulmonary vasculature include hypoxia, pulmonary parenchymal disease, and bacterial infections (particularly group B streptococcal infections). Although SVR increases after birth, sufficiently elevated PVR (ie, greater than SVR) can lead to right-to-left shunting of deoxygenated blood through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale, often resulting in differential cyanosis with lower postductal oxygen saturation. # Clinical presentation Most patients with PPHN present with **cyanosis** and **respiratory distress** (eg, tachypnea, retractions, nasal flaring, grunting) **within 24 hours of birth**.  In PPHN, cyanosis occurs due to **right-to-left shunting** of deoxygenated blood, and may therefore improve (but will not resolve) with supplemental oxygen.  Oxygen is a potent vasodilator that can decrease PVR and thereby decrease right-to-left shunting.  However, in severe cases, PVR may still be greater than SVR, even with supplemental oxygen at maximal settings.  In these cases, a reduction in PVR is directly proportional to a reduction in the volume of shunted blood, resulting in improved (but not resolved) hypoxemia. In general, the pressure gradient across most right-to-left shunts is relatively low; therefore, the shunt itself rarely creates a murmur.  In PPHN, a holosystolic murmur may be heard at the left lower sternal border due to tricuspid valve insufficiency (ie, tricuspid regurgitation) in the setting of persistently elevated PVR.  In addition, patients with PPHN may have additional physical examination findings related to the underlying condition, such as staining of the skin and nails in meconium aspiration syndrome or flat facies in oligohydramnios (eg, Potter sequence). # Diagnosis In cases of suspected PPHN, diagnostic evaluation includes: - **Preductal and postductal oxygen saturation**:  performed as universal screening for congenital heart disease.  In PPHN, there may be a difference of >10% between the preductal (right hand) and postductal (foot) oxygen saturation, consistent with right-to-left shunting through the PDA.  - This finding is indicative of severe disease and may not always be present.  This difference can also be observed when comparing the preductal arterial partial pressure of oxygen (from the right radial artery) to the postductal arterial partial pressure of oxygen (from the umbilical artery) on arterial blood gas.  - **Chest radiography**:  typically normal but may show reduced pulmonary blood flow. - **Echocardiography**:  the definitive diagnostic test for PPHN.  Echocardiography shows **elevated right ventricle pressure** (RVp) with normal cardiac anatomy (ie, excludes congenital heart disease).  The elevation in RVp relative to systemic blood pressure determines the severity of disease.  In severe cases (ie, RVp is greater than systemic blood pressure), right-to-left shunting through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale can be visualized on echocardiography.  # Differential diagnosis The differential diagnosis for PPHN includes other causes of neonatal respiratory distress, including: - **Respiratory distress syndrome** ((Image 1)):  presents with respiratory distress shortly after birth in preterm (<34 weeks gestation) infants due to surfactant deficiency.  Chest radiography shows widespread alveolar collapse (ie, "ground-glass opacities") and air bronchograms. - **Transient tachypnea of the newborn** ((Image 2)):  a benign, self-limited (ie, resolves in 48-72 hours) condition that presents with respiratory distress immediately after birth in late preterm and term infants due to delayed resorption of retained fetal alveolar fluid.  Distinguishing radiographic features include perihilar linear streaking and fluid in the interlobar fissures. - **Meconium aspiration syndrome** ((Image 3)):  presents with respiratory distress shortly after birth in term and postterm (ie, >41 weeks gestation) infants due to aspiration of meconium in amniotic fluid.  Chest radiograph shows streaky, linear densities and hyperinflated lungs.  This condition may coexist with PPHN, as demonstrated by elevated right ventricle pressure on echocardiography.  - **Neonatal pneumonia**:  presents with respiratory distress and signs of infection.  Chest radiograph shows focal alveolar densities or consolidations.  Pneumonia can coexist with PPHN, as demonstrated by elevated right ventricle pressure on echocardiography.  Therefore, in cases of suspected PPHN, patients should be evaluated for infection (eg, complete blood count, blood culture) and given empiric antibiotics. - **Congenital heart disease**:  can present with cyanosis that does not improve with supplemental oxygen due to right-to-left shunting.  Echocardiography is required for differentiation. # Management Management of PPHN involves supportive care (eg, maintaining normothermia, managing fluids and electrolytes) and specific interventions to improve oxygenation by reducing PVR, including: - **Supplemental oxygen**:  variably improves oxygenation, depending on the presence of right-to-left shunting.  In addition, oxygen is a potent pulmonary vasodilator.  However, exposure to high oxygen concentrations can cause pulmonary injury due to formation of reactive oxygen species, and the fraction of inspired oxygen should be titrated to maintain a goal oxygen saturation of 90% to 95%.  Supplemental oxygen should be administered noninvasively (eg, nasal cannula, continuous positive airway pressure \[CPAP\]) to avoid pulmonary injury (eg, volutrauma, barotrauma). - **Inhaled nitric oxide**:  selectively dilates pulmonary vasculature by increasing cyclic GMP in pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cells ((Figure 2)).  Nitric oxygen should be administered noninvasively in patients with adequate ventilation but persistent hypoxemia (despite supplemental oxygen) due to right-to-left shunting. - **Mechanical ventilation**:  may be considered in severe cases in which hypoxemia persists despite noninvasive supplemental oxygen or nitrous oxide.  Settings (eg, positive end-expiratory pressure) should be adjusted to maintain adequate oxygenation and ventilation while minimizing the risk of chronic ventilatory injury and oxygen toxicity. - **Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation** (ECMO):  may be considered for patients with refractory hypoxemia despite maximal medical therapy, including mechanical ventilation - **Other pulmonary vasodilators**: - Sildenafil:  increases cyclic GMP by inhibiting phosphodiesterase-5 - Milrinone:  increases cyclic GMP by inhibiting phosphodiesterase-3 In addition, management of the underlying condition (eg, surfactant in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, empiric antibiotics in neonatal pneumonia) that is contributing to the pathogenesis of PPHN is essential to avoid disease progression and complications. # Prognosis The prognosis of PPHN depends on the underlying cause, severity, and response to treatment.  Overall, the mortality rate has improved to 5%-10% with newer treatment modalities, including inhaled nitric oxide and ECMO.  However, patients remain at increased risk for neurodevelopmental impairment (eg, cognitive deficit, behavioral problems), especially if there is a history of perinatal asphyxia or ECMO use.  Optimal prenatal care and initial resuscitation and stabilization after delivery minimize the risk of developing PPHN as well as the risk of disease progression in patients with predisposing underlying conditions (eg, congenital diaphragmatic hernia). # Summary Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) ((Table 1)) is characterized by persistently elevated pulmonary vascular resistance that leads to right-to-left shunting of deoxygenated blood through fetal circulatory pathways.  Echocardiography demonstrating normal cardiac anatomy with elevated right ventricle pressure is diagnostic.  Management focuses on pulmonary vasodilation with supplemental oxygen, inhaled nitric oxide, and mechanical ventilation, if necessary. ​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌

Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

Pathogenesis

  • Abnormal persistence of elevated fetal pulmonary vascular resistance
  • Right-to-left shunting across ductus arteriosus

Risk factors

  • Lung hypoplasia (eg, congenital diaphragmatic hernia)
  • Meconium aspiration syndrome
  • Infection (eg, neonatal pneumonia)

Examination

  • ↓ Postductal relative to preductal oxygen saturation
  • Respiratory distress & cyanosis
  • Prominent S2

Treatment

  • Oxygenation & ventilation
  • Inhaled nitric oxide (pulmonary vasodilator)
